arambai.description:
The Burmese unique unit, a ranged cavalry unit that throws darts. It is trained at the Castle in the Castle Age for 75 wood and 60 gold and can be upgraded to Elite Arambai in the Imperial Age.

Arambai hit very hard for a ranged unit, with 12 attack (14 for Elite), but their accuracy is only 20% (30% for Elite) and their range is 5. A dart that misses its target and lands on another enemy still does full damage, so massed Arambai are strong against infantry and clumped units. With 60 HP they die quickly, and archers, Monks, camels and several infantry units counter them.
arambai.tactics:
## Using Arambai in groups
Arambai get better the more of them there are. A handful used for hit-and-run raids does poorly, because low accuracy and short range waste most darts when there are few targets. A large group firing into a packed army turns its misses into hits on neighboring units. Up close they can kill groups of archers in seconds, since archers have low HP and the short distance offsets the poor accuracy. Their speed and rate of fire suit hit-and-run play, and with micro they become much stronger.

## Upgrades and support
Arambai are not mounted archers, so the Fletching line gives them no attack or range, and the Magyar and Tatar team bonuses do not apply. At the Blacksmith only Padded Archer Armor helps them. They do get Ballistics, Chemistry, Bloodlines, Husbandry and Parthian Tactics, which adds +1/+2 armor. Their innate 1 pierce armor (2 for Elite) makes them sturdier than the Burmese Cavalry Archer, though they are still bad at soaking damage. In a full army, Battle Elephants or other cavalry should escort them and take the hits, while Burmese infantry and Monks kill or convert the counter units. Their pierce attack is high enough to hurt archer-resistant units such as Eagle Warriors, Ghulams and Tarkans, and it still works on siege, buildings and ships. Rams, Armored Elephants, unpacked Trebuchets and Siege Towers keep their advantage.

## What beats Arambai
Camel Riders, Mamelukes, Huskarls and Eagle Warriors close the distance and survive the darts. Archers, especially Elite Skirmishers, outrange them, and Monks can convert them before they get many volleys off.

arbalester.description:
The last step of the Archer line, upgraded from the Crossbowman at the Archery Range once the Imperial Age is reached. Only some civilizations have it, and not all get every archer upgrade. The upgrade itself adds +1 attack and +5 HP, for a base of 40 HP, 6 attack (+3 against spearmen) and a range of 5.

Arbalesters work best in large groups, firing volleys at targets that cannot close the distance. Infantry, villagers and camel units suffer most, Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders in particular. Elite Skirmishers, siege weapons and fast units with high pierce armor beat them, and they do almost no damage to rams.
arbalester.tactics:
## Using Arbalesters
The upgrade from Crossbowman is solid, though the Blacksmith technologies matter more. Like most ranged units, Arbalesters need micro to reach their potential. Hit and retreat against cavalry, which they otherwise lose to. On defense they are good behind a wall, where they shoot at attackers from a safe distance, out of reach of melee cavalry.

## Compositions
In a fast Imperial strategy Arbalesters go with Bombard Cannons: the Arbalesters kill everything except buildings, and the cannons take care of those. Halberdiers cover the Arbalester's weakness to cavalry, but that mix still loses to siege, Elite Skirmishers and buildings, so it wants Bombard Cannons or, failing those, Hussars or Light Cavalry against siege and skirmishers, Trebuchets for Castles and Siege Rams for other buildings. With heavy cavalry the Arbalester becomes the support unit and covers the cavalry's problems with Monks, Halberdiers and camels. Because it needs so much gold, this mix is rare in 1v1 and the norm in team games.

## What beats Arbalesters
The Elite Skirmisher is the basic counter: high pierce armor and a bonus against archers, and with Ring Archer Armor it is cost and population effective. Elite Eagle Warriors and Elite Champi Warriors close the distance before they take much damage, and a Coustillier's charge attack kills most Arbalesters in two hits. Cavalry with high pierce armor such as the Tarkan, the Savar and Elite Battle Elephants hold up well, and Hussars are a cheap answer since they cost no gold. Huskarls and Ghulams resist the arrows and move fast enough to reach them. Rams and Siege Towers soak up arrows for the units behind them, while Onagers and Ballista Elephants punish the tight clumps Arbalesters form. Heavy Scorpions only manage this with Siege Engineers, since otherwise the Arbalesters outrange them. Most of these counters need the last armor upgrade to win clearly.

archer.description:
The Archer is the basic foot archer, trained at the Archery Range from the Feudal Age by all civilizations. It costs 25 wood and 45 gold and upgrades to the Crossbowman. With 30 HP, no armor and a low attack it is fragile, but its range of 4 lets it pick off enemy infantry and Villagers from a distance.

Archers are strong against infantry and Villagers and deal +3 bonus damage to Spearmen. They do very little to buildings and lose to Skirmishers, Scout Cavalry and Eagle Scouts. They stay useful into the middle of the game, although Knights, Scorpions and Mangonels reduce their value quickly.
archer.tactics:
## Feudal Age harassment
Archers are a common Feudal Age rush unit. Their range lets them kill Villagers quickly and shoot past small quick walls, and because they cost no food the player can keep saving food for the Castle Age. They need more investment and larger numbers than Men-at-Arms or Scout Cavalry, so most civilizations open with those units early in the Feudal Age. Mid-sized to large groups of Archers harass well while neither side has Knights.

## Towers, defense and upgrades
Tower rushes work better with Archers in support, since Archers can garrison in the attacking Towers and add to the arrows fired. On defense, Archers garrisoned in Watch Towers or placed behind a Wall hold off early raids. Fletching, Bodkin Arrow and Bracer each give +1 attack and +1 range, and the three archer armor technologies add melee and pierce armor. Thumb Ring gives 100% accuracy against stationary targets and a faster rate of fire, and Ballistics lets them hit moving targets.

## What beats Archers
Skirmishers, Scout Cavalry and Eagle Scouts. The Feudal Age answers, Scouts and Skirmishers, cost a lot of food, so a defender who is not prepared for an Archer rush can see the Castle Age delayed a long way. Later in the game Knights, Scorpions and Mangonels beat Archers, and their low HP and armor make them easy to kill once these units arrive.

armored-elephant.description:
The Armored Elephant is the anti-building siege unit of the South Asian civilizations. Bengalis, Dravidians, Gurjaras and Hindustanis train it at the Siege Workshop from the Castle Age in place of the Battering Ram. It counts as cavalry and as an elephant, costs 120 food and 95 gold, and has 180 HP, 140 pierce armor and +90 attack against buildings.

Because it costs food instead of wood, it tends to be worse than rams in the early game and better in the late game. It attacks every 3 seconds, gains armor from the cavalry Blacksmith technologies and can be healed by Monks. Anti-cavalry and anti-elephant units deal bonus damage to it. Its one upgrade is the Siege Elephant.
armored-elephant.tactics:
## Compared with the Battering Ram
A Battering Ram has +150 attack against buildings to the Armored Elephant's +90, but the elephant attacks every 3 seconds instead of every 5, which gives it close to 66% more damage output than the numbers suggest. Its -2 melee armor rises with the cavalry armor technologies, so Villagers, Chu Ko Nu, Scorpions and other low-attack units stop being a threat to it. Monks heal it from 4 tiles away, and it heals while garrisoned in a Castle. Siege Engineers adds 20% attack against buildings, and the single Siege Elephant upgrade is much cheaper than Capped Ram and Siege Ram combined.

Armored Elephants attack nearby units on their own, so without attention they chase faster units or fight ones they cannot beat. Rams speed up with infantry garrisoned inside, while Armored Elephants top out at 0.66 tiles/s with Husbandry.

## Water maps
Armored Elephants are a good choice for soaking up ship fire to protect your own fleet. Wood matters more on water maps, they give more hit points per resource than Battering Rams, and they hit ships near the shore harder than rams do. Bengali ones take 25% less bonus damage, which suits this job.

## Civilization differences
Bengali Armored Elephants resist conversion and attack 20% faster with Paiks. Dravidians lack Bloodlines but regenerate with Medical Corps. Gurjara elephants deal +30% bonus damage in the Castle Age and +40% in the Imperial Age, and Kshatriyas lowers their food cost.

## What beats Armored Elephants
Infantry, cavalry, Mangudai and Mangonels. Huszars, Eagle Warriors, heavy cavalry and heavy infantry beat rams and Armored Elephants alike, and anti-cavalry and anti-elephant units add bonus damage on top. Monks can convert them without Redemption because they are organic, but the Monk has to walk right up to the elephant, and non-Bengali Monks have no armor against its attack.

ballista-elephant.description:
The Khmer unique unit, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. It is an elephant carrying a Scorpion, so its bolts pass through and hit every unit in a line, and it is one of the few units that can cut down trees. It costs 100 food and 80 gold and has 250 HP (280 as Elite) and a range of 5.

Compared with a Scorpion it has far more HP and no minimum range, so it needs less protection and is easier to micro. It is strong against archers, massed infantry and buildings. Onagers, rams, Siege Elephants and anti-elephant units such as Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders beat it.
ballista-elephant.tactics:
## Using Ballista Elephants
The game classes Ballista Elephants as cavalry, so Monks heal them, they can garrison in Castles, and they get Stable and cavalry armor technologies such as Bloodlines, Husbandry and the Barding armors. Siege Engineers adds range and Chemistry adds attack. Their bolts fly only a little past the target before dropping, so a shot at a close target hits the ground early and deals less pass-through damage than a Scorpion bolt would. Hussars are the best escort, since they bring the speed and the anti-siege support the elephants lack.

They are expensive and usually appear in the Imperial Age. The other Khmer option is Elite Battle Elephants with Heavy Scorpions. Ballista Elephants cost less, both to tech into and per unit, which suits 1v1 games, while the Battle Elephant and Heavy Scorpion mix deals more damage and suits team games.

## Cutting trees
They are the only Castle Age unit that can cut down trees, which helps on dense forest maps such as Black Forest or Arena. Each shot removes a single tree, so clearing a path takes time.

## What beats Ballista Elephants
The Onager is the main counter, with heavy bonus damage against them. Rams and Siege Elephants have enough pierce armor to take only 1 damage per bolt and deal bonus damage to siege, so they do severe damage once they get close. Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders have anti-elephant bonuses, although protected Ballista Elephants can hold them off for a while thanks to having no minimum range. Flaming Camels hurt large groups with their blast, but they have no pierce armor and some die on the way in. Monks can convert Ballista Elephants without Redemption.

battering-ram.description:
A siege weapon trained at the Siege Workshop from the Castle Age and upgraded to the Capped Ram in the Imperial Age. Every civilization has it except the Bengalis, Dravidians, Gurjaras and Hindustanis, which get the Armored Elephant instead. The Cumans can build it in the Feudal Age and upgrade it one age earlier.

The ram is built to knock down buildings. It has +150 attack against buildings and +40 against siege weapons, and with 180 pierce armor arrows barely scratch it. Its melee armor is -3, so any melee unit, even a Villager, takes it apart quickly. It is slow, and its damage against ordinary units is negligible.
battering-ram.tactics:
## Taking down buildings
In the Castle Age the Battering Ram is the best unit for destroying structures. Towers and archers do almost nothing to it, though a Castle still deals enough damage that breaking one takes a committed push with several rams. Rams also shield allied units standing right behind them from the arrows of enemy fortifications, so a Villager can repair a ram that is hitting a Castle, even one with Murder Holes. This does not protect against projectiles from enemy units. Siege Engineers adds 20% attack against buildings and 1 line of sight. Rams are also good at killing Trebuchets.

## Garrisoning and soaking arrows
Up to six infantry, foot archers or Villagers can ride inside a ram, and a flag on top shows when it is loaded. Each infantry unit inside adds 0.05 speed and 10 attack against buildings, and the units are safe from enemy fire while inside. A few rams added to an army can also soak up enemy archer fire to protect the main force.

## What beats Battering Rams
Melee units, because of the -3 melee armor. Mangonels and cavalry are the best ways to destroy them, and Magyar Huszars are especially good at it. In an emergency, Villagers can kill a ram as well. Mangudai, Chu Ko Nu and Kipchaks also do well against rams. Castles also deal enough damage that only a dedicated push gets rams through to them.

battle-elephant.description:
A slow, heavy cavalry unit trained at the Stable from the Castle Age, and a regional unit shared by the Bengalis, Burmese, Dravidians, Khmer, Malay and Vietnamese. It costs 100 food and 70 gold, has 250 HP and 12 attack, and deals 25% trample damage around its target. It can be upgraded to Elite Battle Elephant in the Imperial Age, except by the Dravidians.

Battle Elephants beat almost any melee unit cost-effectively, especially early in the Castle Age, and they hit buildings hard. They are very slow, though, take double damage from Spearmen, gain less from upgrades than other cavalry, and make tempting targets for Monks.
battle-elephant.tactics:
## When to make them
A Battle Elephant trains in 24 seconds, and a single Stable produces 280% of the hit points it would make in Knights. That lets a player turn resources into an army very quickly, which suits defending against heavy aggression, forward Stables, sneaking Villagers in before walls go up and landings on water maps. Their low speed matters less when they come out right next to enemy units or buildings. For general use in the Castle Age Knights are often preferred, because elephants cannot force fights and fall off later: Bloodlines gives a Knight 20% more HP but a Battle Elephant only 8%.

## Civilization differences
Every civilization with the unit has a bonus for it. Khmer elephants move 10% faster and get +3 attack from Tusk Swords already in the Castle Age, which makes them the strongest overall. Burmese elephants get extra armor from their civilization bonus and Howdah, plus +4 attack against archers from Manipur Cavalry, so they can screen for Arambai. Bengali elephants take 25% less bonus damage and resist conversion. Malay elephants are 25% cheaper in the Castle Age and 35% cheaper in the Imperial Age but lack Chain Barding Armor. The Malay are also the only elephant civilization with Heresy. Vietnamese elephants get +100 HP from Chatras and act as a meat shield for Rattan Archers. Dravidian elephants miss Bloodlines, Plate Barding Armor and the Elite upgrade, but regenerate with Medical Corps and ignore armor with Wootz Steel.

## What beats Battle Elephants
Pikemen and Kamayuks deal bonus damage to them, and Monks convert them, which hurts more because most elephant civilizations lack Heresy. Ranged units that can kite such a slow target, such as Cavalry Archers, Genoese Crossbowmen and Scorpions, do well against them, as do Mamelukes, War Elephants and Flaming Camels.

berserk.description:
The Viking unique unit, a heavy infantry soldier with axe and shield trained at the Castle from the Castle Age. It upgrades to the Elite Berserk in the Imperial Age. Berserks regenerate 40 HP per minute, so they last a long time between fights and hold up well in pitched battles.

A Berserk costs 65 food and 20 gold and has 65 HP and 12 attack, with small bonuses against shock infantry and standard buildings. It is fast for infantry and can run down small groups of foot archers. Like other infantry it suffers against archers in mass battles, and gunpowder units, Slingers and massed Scorpions do heavy damage to it.
berserk.tactics:
## Berserks or Champions
On land maps a Viking player usually picks either Elite Berserks or Champions, since upgrading both lines costs too much for units with the same role. The Berserk is faster, regenerates and trains in 14 seconds, 12 as Elite. It has fewer HP and less pierce armor than the Viking Militia line, costs 15 more food for the same gold, and is harder to mass from Castles than from Barracks. Fully upgraded, an Elite Berserk has 74 HP, 18 attack and 5/5 armor. Chieftains boosts both lines equally and gives them +5 attack against cavalry and +4 against camels.

## Fighting with Berserks
The regeneration lets Berserks fight, pull back and come back healed, so they wear down armies over a long engagement. Their speed helps against foot archers in small skirmishes, but in a mass battle against archers they should not be the main answer. Use them against Elite Skirmishers, other infantry, cavalry, Eagle Warriors and buildings.

## What beats Berserks
Hand Cannoneers and Slingers do enormous damage to them, and massed Scorpions inflict heavy losses. Among melee units Samurai and Jaguar Warriors threaten them, as do Cataphracts, Teutonic Knights and Boyars. Leitis ignore melee armor, which makes them dangerous, especially with all four Relics. Obuchs strip armor and are cheaper, so equal numbers end close to even and the Berserks are left exposed to archers afterwards. Massed Monaspas overwhelm them with high attack and their own regeneration, and Liao Dao bleed damage outpaces the Berserk's healing.

bombard-cannon.description:
The Bombard Cannon is a gunpowder siege weapon trained at the Siege Workshop in the Imperial Age once Chemistry is researched. Only some civilizations have it, and the Bohemians can upgrade it to the Houfnice. It costs 225 wood and 225 gold, takes 56 seconds to train and fires at a range of 12, with a minimum range of 5.

It outranges all generic ranged buildings and deals large bonus damage to buildings, ships and siege weapons, with a small splash that also hurts friendly units. It is slow and has only 80 HP, so it falls quickly once enemy units reach it.
bombard-cannon.tactics:
## Siege and anti-siege
Bombard Cannons outrange every generic ranged building and counter siege units such as Scorpions, Onagers and Trebuchets. Against Trebuchets they should keep moving so they are not hit back. They can also be used against most other units, as long as those stay far enough away. The splash damages friendly units too, so fire into crowded fights with care. The high cost and the long training time make them hard to mass, but even a few of them support an army well against buildings and siege. Siege Engineers gives +1 range and +20% damage against buildings.

## Compared to the Trebuchet
The Bombard Cannon does not pack and unpack, so it is easier to move around. It is more accurate, splashes units and fires faster with much quicker projectiles. The Trebuchet costs 25 wood and 25 gold less, is available to almost every civilization without Chemistry, takes ranged attacks better and has range 16 against 12. It also deals much more damage per shot, which makes it the better building killer, especially early in the Imperial Age, when Chemistry still needs 100 seconds of research. The Bombard Cannon is the more versatile of the two because it hits both buildings and units.

## What beats Bombard Cannons
Melee units that get close, above all fast ones such as most cavalry, Woad Raiders and Elite Eagle Warriors. Inside its minimum range of 5 a Bombard Cannon cannot fire, and with low HP and slow speed it does not survive long once caught. The article also lists Mangudai as a counter.

boyar.description:
The Boyar is the Slavic unique unit, a heavily armored cavalry unit trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Boyar in the Imperial Age. It costs 60 food and 70 gold, 5 gold less than a Knight, and trains in 15 seconds.

Its strength is melee armor: 4 on the Boyar and 8 on the Elite Boyar, against the Knight line's 2. That makes it very good against light units without big bonus damage, and it has the same pierce armor as the Knight line. It moves a little slower than a Knight, and the Elite Boyar has 30 fewer HP than a Paladin. It loses to the same units that beat Knights.
boyar.tactics:
## Using Boyars
The Castle Age Boyar has +2 attack and +2 melee armor over the Knight, which in melee makes it about as strong as an Imperial Age Cavalier. Since the Slavic Knight line has no Paladin, the Boyar is the better choice for them even before the cost difference. Boyars are the main shock troops: they raid, destroy towns, fight enemy armies head on and can raze Castles. In an army built on siege and infantry, Boyars deal with enemy Siege Onagers and Bombard Cannons.

A steady stream of Boyars needs several Castles. The unique technology Detinets changes the Castle cost from 650 stone to 260 wood and 390 stone, which makes extra Castles easier to build, and Castles placed across the map also help with map control.

## Supporting units
No single Slavic unit fits perfectly next to Boyars, so mix in what the opponent calls for. Light Cavalry handle Monks, Scorpions handle infantry and archers, and infantry handle Heavy Camel Riders. Against enemy heavy cavalry and elephants, converting them with Monks is often better than fighting, and the Slavs have a Monk speed bonus for it.

## What beats Boyars
The usual answers to the Knight line: Monks, Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders, with Monks extra dangerous because the Slavs lack Heresy. War Elephants and Battle Elephants overpower them in melee, and large groups of Monaspa win thanks to their extra attack. Leitis, Wootz Steel infantry and Composite Bowmen ignore armor, so the Boyar's main strength does nothing against them. Because Boyars are slower than Knights, mounted archers such as Mangudai are an even bigger threat. A plain Camel Rider does not counter Boyars outright, though it still trades cost effectively.

camel-archer.description:
The first Berber unique unit, a mounted archer on a camel trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. It costs 50 wood and 60 gold and has 55 HP (60 as Elite), 1 pierce armor and an attack bonus against cavalry archers.

It hard counters other mounted archers and also does well against infantry and most foot archers. As a camel unit it takes the smaller anti-camel bonus instead of anti-cavalry bonus damage, so Camel Riders hurt it less and Mamelukes deal no bonus damage at all. Elite Skirmishers, Genitours and massed Mangonels or Scorpions beat it.
camel-archer.tactics:
## Role in the Berber army
Camel Archers support Berber cavalry against ranged units, and when enemy Halberdiers overwhelm the army they can hit and run against them. With Kasbah they train in 20 seconds, against 30 for a generic Heavy Cavalry Archer, and their short attack delay suits hit-and-run play. Maghrebi Camels lets them regenerate 15 HP per minute. The Berbers lack Parthian Tactics, so Camel Archers are a little less durable than fully upgraded Heavy Cavalry Archers and deal less damage to Spearmen, but they hold up better against units with big anti-cavalry bonuses such as the Heavy Camel Rider.

Pair them with Light Cavalry, which costs only food and can take the front line while the wood and gold go into Camel Archers. They beat the Berber Cavalry Archer in most respects, apart from wood cost, damage against Spearmen and the need for Castles. If gold runs short or the enemy relies on foot archers, switch to Genitours.

## What beats Camel Archers
Elite Skirmishers stay cost effective against them, and massed Camel Archers fall to Mangonels and Scorpions. Genitours take bonus damage and lose one on one, yet still trade well, and they can retreat when melee cavalry arrives to help, which Skirmishers cannot do. Camel Riders, Light Cavalry and Shrivamsha Riders also work decently. Eagle Warriors are a good choice too: they have good pierce armor, more speed than Huskarls or Halberdiers, and an attack bonus against camel units.

camel-rider.description:
An anti-cavalry unit trained at the Stable from the Castle Age by a limited group of civilizations. Every one of them except the Cumans can upgrade it to the Heavy Camel Rider. For the Gurjaras, Camel Scouts turn into Camel Riders for free on reaching the Castle Age and keep the Auto Scout ability.

It has 100 HP and 6 attack, with +9 against cavalry and +5 against camel units and ships, so it hits cavalry for 15 before armor. Camels are the third fastest land unit type in the game. With no armor and a weak base attack they lose to infantry and foot archers, and Cataphracts are immune to their bonus.
camel-rider.tactics:
## Hunting cavalry
Fifteen attack against cavalry is high for a Castle Age unit. Pikemen can scare cavalry away, but horsemen can outrun them, while Camel Riders are fast enough to chase them down and finish them off. In even numbers a group of Camel Riders beats most melee cavalry, landing more hits than Pikemen thanks to a faster attack and more HP. When gold runs short, Pikemen are the better buy. Camels do well against civilizations built around mounted units, such as the Berbers, Franks, Mongols, Persians and Saracens, and the Heavy Camel Rider upgrade in the Imperial Age keeps them competitive.

## Catching mounted archers
Keep Camel Riders on melee cavalry, or use them to ambush groups of mounted archers. Pikemen and Elite Skirmishers hurt mounted archers too, but only Camel Riders are fast enough to force a fight. Some civilizations have stronger versions: Byzantine camels cost 25% less, Saracen camels have 25% more HP, Hindustani camels attack 20% faster, and Gurjara camels deal 30% more bonus damage in the Castle Age and 40% more in the Imperial Age.

## What beats Camel Riders
Infantry and foot archers. The camel's weak armor and low base attack leave it at a disadvantage against both. Cataphracts have a special defense against anti-cavalry bonuses, which takes away the camel's main advantage. Defensive structures are also strong against Camel Riders.

cannon-galleon.description:
A gunpowder siege warship trained at the Dock in the Imperial Age once Chemistry has been researched. Most civilizations have it, though some use a regional replacement such as the Dromon, Lou Chuan or Catapult Galleon instead. It costs 200 wood and 150 gold and can be upgraded to Elite Cannon Galleon.

Its job is to destroy buildings near the shore. It has 13 range, a +200 bonus against buildings and enough range to outshoot Castles and Bombard Towers. Its slow rate of fire, slow projectiles and minimum range of 3 make it nearly useless against ships, and Fire Ships in particular.
cannon-galleon.tactics:
## Clearing the shoreline
Cannon Galleons are close to a sea-going Bombard Cannon, only slightly faster. Their main use is knocking down Towers, Castles and other buildings along the coast from beyond their reach, so those structures cannot use their bonus damage against ships. They can also harass land units at range now and then. Their range equals that of fully upgraded Turkish Bombard Towers, Korean Keeps and Teuton Castles. Like Mangonels and Bombard Cannons they can attack the ground, which can cause friendly fire.

They should always have an escort, usually Fire Ships and Galleons, and should never be sent against enemy ships. Siege Engineers adds 1 range and 20% damage against buildings, and the Dock armor and speed technologies help them survive.

## Spanish Cannon Galleons
The Spanish version is much better than any other. Its projectiles travel at 7 tiles per second instead of 3.5 and hit moving targets as if Ballistics were researched, and it fires about 18% faster.

## What beats Cannon Galleons
Other ships, as long as the enemy has not lost control of the sea completely. A Cannon Galleon cannot hit ships that come close because of its minimum range, and its slow shots miss moving targets. Bombard Cannons on shore can outrange and sink them, and Monks can convert them.

capped-ram.description:
A melee siege weapon upgraded from the Battering Ram at the Siege Workshop in the Imperial Age, for 300 food. Every civilization has it except the Bengalis, Dravidians, Gurjaras, Hindustanis and Wu. It costs 160 wood and 75 gold and later upgrades to the Siege Ram.

Rams tear down walls, buildings and makeshift obstructions and do very well against stationary Trebuchets. With 190 pierce armor the Capped Ram barely notices arrows, but its melee armor is poor, so melee units and Villagers destroy it quickly. It can carry up to six infantry, foot archers or Villagers inside; only garrisoned infantry add speed and attack against buildings.
capped-ram.tactics:
## What the upgrade adds
Compared to the Battering Ram, the Capped Ram has +25 HP, +10 bonus damage against buildings, +1 melee armor and +1 ram armor. It also gains a blast radius of 1.5, so it damages adjacent structures and units, which makes it much better at breaking through massed walls and dense bases. The upgrade is cheap enough that it is almost always worth taking if you build rams. Siege Engineers adds 20% damage against buildings.

## Where it fits
The Capped Ram is usually a step on the way to the Siege Ram. Civilizations without the Siege Ram tend to switch to Bombard Cannons instead, which deal more damage and outrange Castles. Capped Rams still help against an opponent with a lot of walls, or as support for an infantry push. Garrison infantry inside for extra speed and +10 attack against buildings per unit.

## What beats Capped Rams
Melee units, Magyar Huszars in particular, cut rams down because of their negative melee armor. Villagers can do the same when a ram reaches the town. Mangonels damage them, and Mangudai, Chu Ko Nu and Kipchaks are strong against them too. Scorpions counter them only weakly. Arrows from archers and buildings do almost nothing, so keep melee units near your walls to answer a ram push.

caravel.description:
The Caravel is the second unique unit of the Portuguese, a warship trained at the Dock once the Castle Age is reached. It fires bolts like a Scorpion, and each bolt passes through and damages every unit in a narrow line. It costs 90 wood and 34 gold and upgrades to the Elite Caravel in the Imperial Age.

Compared with a War Galley, the Caravel has more HP, pierce armor and line of sight and deals more damage to buildings, but less damage to other ships. It needs no research to become available. Fire Ships counter it hard, and it also suffers against towers, Castles and gunpowder siege.
caravel.tactics:
## Fleet fights
One Caravel loses to one War Galley, and an Elite Caravel loses to a Galleon, but a large fleet of Caravels beats an equal armada of either because each bolt hits several ships. Patrolling into an enemy fleet wastes the pass-through damage once both fleets spread out, so control them by hand and make the enemy chase, which bunches their ships up. Demolition Ships struggle against groups of Caravels, which can sink several of them before they get close. In the late game an economy that can afford both can field Elite Caravels as the main force with Galleons as tanks, though Portuguese Galleons are already strong on their own.

## Against land units
On maps with shallows and river crossings, Caravels work like a durable, fast Scorpion against groups of land units, with less damage per shot. They also punish melee units and dense groups standing on the shoreline. Non-Elite Caravels already have the line of sight and pierce armor of a Galleon, which can make them the better ship before the Elite upgrade.

## What beats Caravels
Fire Ships are the hard counter. The Caravel's bonus damage does not apply to them, and once they close in the pass-through bolts lose most of their value. War Hulks, Turtle Ships, towers, Castles, Mangonels, Bombard Cannons and Thirisadais also beat Caravels.

cataphract.description:
The Cataphract is the Byzantine unique unit, a heavy cavalry unit trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Cataphract in the Imperial Age. It costs 70 food and 75 gold, has +13 attack against infantry (+18 Elite) and carries extra armor against anti-cavalry bonuses, so Camel Riders, Mamelukes and spearmen hurt it far less than other cavalry.

Its base attack and pierce armor are low, which makes it vulnerable to archers and defensive buildings, and the Byzantines lack Bloodlines and Blast Furnace for it. Cataphracts are expensive and need their Imperial Age upgrades to do well.
cataphract.tactics:
## When to use Cataphracts
Cataphracts play a different role from the Knight line and often complement it. In the Castle Age they mostly appear against Native American civilizations, Goths and Hindustanis, which rely on infantry that resists arrows. The Byzantines get no bonus toward an early Castle and the unit is costly, so most players wait for the Imperial Age. There the Elite Cataphract with Logistica, which adds trample damage, attacks very fast and shreds infantry. It can even hold its own against heavy cavalry in big fights, though that is better avoided. The Elite upgrade and Logistica cost a lot of gold, so avoid needless losses.

The counters to Cataphracts are themselves beaten by Halberdiers or Skirmishers, which the Byzantines train at a steep discount.

## What beats Cataphracts
Paladins are one of the best answers: they have more attack and HP than a Byzantine Elite Cataphract and win even in mass fights. War Elephants, Battle Elephants, Leitis, Boyars, Keshiks and massed Monaspa also do well. Massed Arbalesters, Heavy Cavalry Archers and Composite Bowmen exploit the low pierce armor, though they need numbers or a screen because Logistica trample hurts tightly packed archers. Elite Skirmishers work when gold runs out.

Monks are a threat because Byzantine players rarely have gold to spare for Heresy or Faith. Elite Samurai beat Elite Cataphracts cost effectively with their bonus against unique units, and Liao Dao do well until Logistica arrives. Large groups of Halberdiers cost no gold and are a good answer in the late game, but in equal resources the Elite Cataphract wins. Kamayuks, Temple Guards and ordinary Camel Riders do poorly, while Gurjara Camel Riders are the exception and win comfortably.

cavalier.description:
The Imperial Age upgrade of the Knight, trained at the Stable. It costs 60 food and 75 gold and has 120 HP, 12 attack and 2/2 armor. The upgrade from Knight costs 300 food and 300 gold and adds +20 HP and +2 attack. The Burgundians can research it in the Castle Age at half cost, and of the civilizations with Knights only the Saracens and Danes cannot get it.

It is a versatile heavy cavalry unit, fast enough for raiding and flanking and tough enough to screen ranged units and siege on the front line. Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders hard counter it, and Monks can convert it.
cavalier.tactics:
## When to get the upgrade
The upgrade is cheap for what it gives, so it is worth picking up early in the Imperial Age. Even for civilizations with Paladin, the Cavalier is often the more cost-effective unit, especially in 1v1 games where gold is limited. If the army is not built around heavy cavalry, Cavaliers with Bloodlines and Plate Barding Armor are enough. They take arrows worse than even Byzantine Paladins: 35 Arbalester shots or 28 Heavy Cavalry Archer shots kill one, so they are a weaker answer to archers, though in numbers they still last long enough to thin out a larger archer force.

## Civilization differences
Several civilizations without Paladin make up for it. Portuguese Cavaliers cost 20% less gold, Berber ones are 20% cheaper, and Polish ones cost only 60 food and 30 gold with Szlachta Privileges. Burmese Manipur Cavalry adds attack against archers, Malian Farimba adds +5 attack, and Bulgarian Stirrups makes them attack 33% faster, which gives the strongest Cavalier in melee. Roman Cavaliers train fastest thanks to Comitatenses, which also gives them a charge attack. Georgian ones regenerate and take 0.85 population space with Aznauri Cavalry. Sicilian Cavaliers take 40% less bonus damage and get extra armor from Hauberk and conversion resistance from First Crusade. The Burgundians lack Bloodlines, and one of their Stables stops producing during the 80 seconds of Castle Age research.

## What beats Cavaliers
Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders hard counter them with bonus damage, and Monks convert them. Boyars, Teutonic Knights, Berserks, Mamelukes, Kamayuks, Genoese Crossbowmen and the bigger elephants such as War Elephants and Elite Battle Elephants also beat them.

cavalry-archer.description:
A mounted archer trained at the Archery Range from the Castle Age and upgraded to the Heavy Cavalry Archer. Many civilizations have it, but only some get Bloodlines, Husbandry and Thumb Ring and can fully upgrade it in the Castle Age. It costs 40 wood and 60 gold and has 50 HP, 6 attack and 4 range.

Its speed and ranged attack make it a strong harasser and a good counter to infantry, and with enough micromanagement a small group can wipe out whole groups of foot soldiers. It has a long attack delay and needs many technologies to be effective. Enemy attack bonuses treat it as an archer, a cavalry unit and a cavalry archer.
cavalry-archer.tactics:
## Harassing and kiting
Cavalry Archers are among the best harassers in the game, as long as the player micromanages them to keep distance from their targets. They work much better in large numbers, which takes a lot of resources. Slow melee units such as most infantry struggle to deal with them, and their stats are solid enough that they hold up when caught in a fight.

## Upgrades
The unit needs a long list of technologies before it performs. Bloodlines adds 20 HP, Thumb Ring raises the rate of fire by 11% and makes it hit stationary targets every time, and Ballistics lets it hit moving targets. Fletching, Bodkin Arrow and Bracer each add 1 attack and 1 range, and the archer armor line plus Parthian Tactics add armor. Because of this cost it is hard to get a group out in a reasonable time without it being weak.

## What beats Cavalry Archers
Elite Skirmishers counter them very cost-effectively: Cavalry Archers cannot outrange them, and Skirmishers soak up the arrows and deal heavy bonus damage. Mangonels and Scorpions are devastating if their projectiles are not dodged, and rams or Armored Elephants work as damage sponges. Camel Archers deal bonus damage to them, and War Wagons have too much pierce armor to kill. Huskarls, Ghulams and Eagle Warriors combine high pierce armor, bonus damage and enough speed to catch them. Gurjara Shrivamsha Riders have no bonus, but their speed and ability to dodge projectiles make them a hard opponent.

centurion.description:
The Roman unique unit, a heavy cavalry unit trained at the Castle in the Castle Age for 75 food and 85 gold. It can be upgraded to Elite Centurion in the Imperial Age. Its passive ability, Imperium, makes nearby Militia line units move and attack faster.

With 110 HP, 13 attack and 2/3 armor, a Centurion is clearly stronger than a Knight in melee and against Crossbowmen. It is also expensive, especially in gold, and only comes from Castles, so it is hard to mass. Pikemen, Camel Riders and Monks still beat it for their cost, and the Romans have no Heresy.
centurion.tactics:
## Castle Age and Imperial Age use
In the Castle Age the Centurion kills a Crossbowman in three hits where a Knight needs four once the Crossbowmen have armor upgrades, and it takes many more arrows thanks to its pierce armor. In the Imperial Age the Elite Centurion stands in for the Paladin, which the Romans lack. Comitatenses gives it a +5 charge attack and trains it 50% faster. Elite Centurions beat Paladins in equal numbers, except Lithuanian Paladins with 4 Relics, but lose to them for equal resources, since the Centurion is the most expensive cavalry unique unit after the War Elephant. Because of that cost they work better as a support unit than as the main army.

## The Imperium aura
Centurions speed up nearby Militia line units, which is why they pair with Legionaries. The aura is a circle with a radius of 10 (12 for Elite) and gives +10% movement speed (+15% for Elite) and +20% attack speed. Several Centurions do not stack the effect, and the aura does not help allies. A converted Centurion boosts the Militia line of the player who converted it.

## What beats Centurions
Pikemen and Halberdiers, Camel Riders and anti-cavalry unique units such as Genoese Crossbowmen, Mamelukes and Kamayuks all deal bonus damage against them. Monks are a deadly counter because the Romans lack Heresy. Teutonic Knights and Boyars have too much melee armor for them, Battle Elephants and War Elephants overpower them, and Samurai beat them as unique units. Leiciai and Dravidian infantry with Wootz Steel ignore their armor, and Obuch attacks strip it so other units can finish them.

chakram-thrower.description:
The Gurjara unique infantry, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Chakram Thrower in the Imperial Age. It throws metal discs that count as a ranged melee attack and pass through every unit in a straight line, much like a Scorpion bolt. Against buildings there is no pass-through damage.

It costs 65 food and 30 gold, has 40 HP, range 5 and only 3 attack, and moves at 1.15, the same speed tier as Huskarls and Eagle Warriors. Chakram Throwers break up groups of infantry and do well against Elite Skirmishers. With no pierce armor and few HP they die fast to archers and gunpowder, and heavy cavalry and ranged siege beat them.
chakram-thrower.tactics:
## Positioning and massing
The Gurjaras rely on light cavalry and camels, so massed anti-cavalry infantry such as Halberdiers and Kamayuks is a problem for them, and the Chakram Thrower is their answer. The attack is low, and without Blast Furnace an Elite Chakram Thrower tops out at 6, but each disc hits every enemy in its path. In theory 30 Chakram Throwers can kill as many fully upgraded Elite Teutonic Knights in four volleys if every disc hits every knight. This is one of the most micro-intensive units in the game: keep the throwers huddled, aim at tight formations and strike before the opponent spreads out. Small numbers achieve little, and the training time makes massing hard, especially after losing a Castle.

Their speed and melee damage make them good at killing rams and Trebuchets. They are weak against buildings even with Arson, a job the Gurjara Armored Elephant does much better.

## What beats Chakram Throwers
Arbalesters, Hand Cannoneers and Slingers kill them from outside their range, since they have no base pierce armor. Onagers and Scorpions slaughter them, though they take real damage if the throwers reach them. High HP units such as Battle Elephants and Paladins shrug off the low damage, and even a generic Cavalier takes one damage per hit. Shrivamsha Riders block all projectiles. Gurjara Camel Riders cover the weakness to cavalry, and Shrivamsha Riders of their own cover archers and siege.

champion.description:
The Champion is the last tier of the Militia line, upgraded from the Two-Handed Swordsman at the Barracks in the Imperial Age for 650 food and 350 gold. Not every civilization has it. The upgrade adds +2 attack and +5 HP. A Champion costs 50 food and 20 gold, has 70 HP, 14 attack and 1/1 armor, and deals bonus damage to buildings and to the Eagle line.

Few infantry units hit harder, and it beats the cheap trash units, which is why players call it a trash buster. It is still slow and has modest health, so archers, heavy cavalry and splash damage siege weapons beat it.
champion.tactics:
## When Champions work
Champions do best in the early Imperial Age, before their counters are common, and in the late Imperial Age when gold runs short. They defeat Halberdiers, Elite Skirmishers and Hussars with ease. The unique trash units, Genitours and Magyar Huszars, hold up against most civilizations' Champions without clearly beating them. Champions also handle mixed armies of counter units, such as the common Heavy Camel Rider and Elite Skirmisher combination, even for civilizations whose Champions are below average. A Champion army needs a very large food economy, and on lush maps such as Yucatan another army usually fares better if the economy can pay for it.

## Support and civilizations
Pair Champions with cavalry to run down ranged units, or with rams and other siege to raze buildings faster. With a large stockpile of food and gold they can also attack in waves. For several civilizations Champions are a late game deathball: the Malians with +3 pierce armor, the Aztecs and Burmese with extra attack, the Vikings with +20% HP, the Slavs with trample damage, the Teutons with +2 melee armor and the Japanese with a faster attack.

## What beats Champions
Archer units, Heavy Scorpions and Mangonels, which shoot them while they walk in slowly. Heavily armored melee units also win: Cataphracts, Jaguar Warriors, Paladins, Boyars, War Elephants, Elite Battle Elephants, Teutonic Knights and Obuchs. Medium cavalry such as Cavaliers and Magyar Huszars trade about evenly with them.

chu-ko-nu.description:
The Chu Ko Nu is the Chinese unique unit, a foot archer trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Chu Ko Nu in the Imperial Age. Each volley fires several arrows in quick succession: three for the regular unit and five for the Elite. Only the first arrow does full damage, while the extra arrows deal 3 pierce damage each.

It costs 40 wood and 35 gold, more wood than an Arbalester but less gold. It is good against most units and decent against buildings that do not shoot back. Its range of 4 is shorter than most archers, it has no armor, and it is poor at hit and run.
chu-ko-nu.tactics:
## Using Chu Ko Nu
Chu Ko Nu usually fight behind Halberdiers and Light Cavalry, and go with Siege Rams when the target is buildings. Units with no pierce armor, such as Monks, suffer most from the extra arrows. The extra arrows also carry 0 melee attack, which still counts as damage against rams with negative melee armor. Only the first arrow benefits from Fletching, Bodkin Arrow, Bracer and Chemistry, and Thumb Ring makes that first arrow 100% accurate and the unit fire 25% faster. The Chinese bonus makes technologies that benefit Chu Ko Nu 5%, 10% and 15% cheaper in the Feudal, Castle and Imperial Age.

Like the Kipchak, the Chu Ko Nu still does fairly well against units built to resist arrows. Elite Skirmishers survive normal archer fire on pierce armor, but the sheer number of arrows from a group of Elite Chu Ko Nu still wears them down. Even so, it is better to keep away from anti-archer units when you can.

## What beats Chu Ko Nu
Archers with longer range: most other archers outrange the Chu Ko Nu by one tile and can hit and run, while the Chu Ko Nu is bad at kiting because of how its volleys reload and its long attack delay. Huskarls and Ghulams match up especially well against it, and siege weapons with splash damage, such as Mangonels, hurt the clumped, unarmored archers. Scorpions, Eagle Warriors and Genitours also do well against it.

composite-bowman.description:
The Armenian unique foot archer, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. It costs 35 wood and 45 gold and has 40 HP (50 as Elite), 4 pierce attack and a range of 4. Its arrows ignore the pierce armor of every land unit except siege, though the effect does not apply to ships or buildings.

That makes it strong against infantry and most cavalry, including archer-resistant units such as Huskarls, Ghulams and Rattan Archers. The short range is its main weakness: other foot archers can kite it, and siege weapons, which resist its special attack, are a serious threat.
composite-bowman.tactics:
## How the armor-ignoring attack works
The low attack only pays off when the target has armor to ignore. Against the Archer line it needs to cancel at least 1 pierce armor in the Castle Age and 2 as Elite, which the previous Age's armor upgrades usually provide. The only non-spear units where Archers do better are the Monk (except for Bengalis), the Trade Cart and Burmese Archers in the Imperial Age. Against armored cavalry, ignoring armor is like having +4 attack in the Castle Age and at least +6 in the Imperial Age, so Composite Bowmen do very well if they keep their distance. They have melee armor, which the Elite upgrade raises, and their arrows fly straight, so they hit targets moving directly toward or away from them even without Ballistics. A slightly longer attack delay than the Crossbowman and the short range make them weaker at hit and run, and the Armenians lack Thumb Ring.

## Army compositions
Mangonels are the best partner, handling enemy archers and siege, but the Armenians lack Siege Engineers and Bombard Cannons for the late game siege fight. In the middle of the game Warrior Priests make a good meat shield: they are faster than Swordsmen after Fervor and heal each other and the Composite Bowmen.

## What beats Composite Bowmen
Elite Skirmishers still beat them with their bonus damage. Mangonels and Scorpions are unaffected by the armor-ignoring attack and stay very effective, and rams and Armored Elephants soak their arrows as they would any archer's. Ballista Elephants are a strong counter: they resist the attack as siege, cut through groups with pass-through bolts and fight at the same range, though Armenian Monks are a danger to them. Shrivamsha Riders dodge projectiles regardless of armor, which makes them a very strong counter too.

condottiero.description:
The second Italian unique unit, a fast infantry soldier trained at the Barracks in the Imperial Age by the Italians and their allies. It needs no Castle and has no Elite upgrade, so every Condottiero comes out at full strength.

Its job is countering gunpowder. It has +10 attack against gunpowder units and bonus armor that cancels 10 points of anti-infantry damage from Hand Cannoneers, Organ Guns and Grenadiers. Compared with a Champion it moves faster at 1.2, has 80 HP against 70 and trains in 18 seconds, but hits for 10 instead of 14. It costs 35 gold, and with 0 pierce armor it suffers against archers.
condottiero.tactics:
## Countering gunpowder
Up close, Condottieri beat Janissaries, Grenadiers and Hand Cannoneers, and they also trade well against the Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders that usually escort gunpowder armies. Elite Skirmishers handle foot and mounted gunpowder units more cheaply, though they struggle against gunpowder siege, so the Condottiero works best as an emergency counter. Because it needs no upgrades, it is a good answer to a fast Imperial Age into gunpowder on closed maps like Arena, where a few Condottieri can do heavy damage to enemy Bombard Cannons.

## Other uses
Condottieri can stand in for Champions when the upgrade is not ready, or for civilizations that cannot get Champions at all, such as the Persians and Jurchens. Civilizations with weak cavalry, like the Koreans, Malay and Vikings, can use them in place of Hussars against siege and Elite Skirmishers and for some raiding. They also beat Elite Eagle Warriors by forcing fights. On water maps they are very good for landings: they train fast at a cheap Barracks, need no upgrades, and kill a Villager with Loom in 5 hits, or 4 with Forging. The gold cost makes them less efficient as the game goes on.

## What beats Condottieri
Heavy cavalry such as Boyars and heavy infantry such as Serjeants beat them in direct combat, since the Condottiero is a lighter version of the Swordsman line. Samurai are extra dangerous because the Condottiero is a unique unit. With no base pierce armor, it also loses to Arbalesters, archers and Scorpions shooting from long range.

conquistador.description:
The Spanish unique unit, a mounted gunpowder unit trained at the Castle in the Castle Age for 75 food and 60 gold. It can be upgraded to Elite Conquistador in the Imperial Age. In practice it is a Hand Cannoneer on horseback, with 16 attack (19 for Elite) and a range of 6.

Conquistadors are faster and tougher than Hand Cannoneers but lose their bonus against infantry. Few technologies affect them, so they are ready to fight as soon as they are trained, and an early Conquistador rush is hard to stop. They have the shortest range of any gunpowder unit and are expensive to lose, and Monks, camels and skirmishers beat them.
conquistador.tactics:
## Raiding and hit-and-run
Conquistadors do best with hit-and-run tactics, and their short range often forces this anyway when infantry or cavalry chase them. Husbandry alone is enough to make them a strong raiding force and good against non-ranged units, though they should ideally get every technology available to them. Range upgrades do not affect them. In groups they fire volleys that badly damage enemy formations, and with micro they can handle siege weapons. Spanish Blacksmith technologies that help Conquistadors cost no gold.

## Escorting with Light Cavalry
Monks are one of their worst enemies. Conquistadors can shoot Monks, but the Monks usually get enough conversions before dying to make the trade bad. Pairing Conquistadors with Light Cavalry handles Monks, while the Conquistadors supply the damage against everything else.

## What beats Conquistadors
Camel Riders and Mamelukes threaten both the Conquistadors and their Light Cavalry escort. Bolas Riders, Condottieri, Konas, Shrivamsha Riders and Winged Hussars also beat them by a good margin, and Halberdiers hurt them badly if they can catch them. Elite Skirmishers work, although less well than against Cavalry Archers, because the Conquistador's attack gets through their pierce armor. Archers in general beat them for their cost once upgraded, and with Imperial Age technologies and good micro they can win in equal numbers too. Elite Genitours and Camel Archers are also listed as counters.

coustillier.description:
The Burgundian unique unit, a medium cavalry soldier trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Coustillier in the Imperial Age. It costs 55 food and 55 gold and has 115 HP, 8 attack and 2/2 armor.

Its charge attack adds +20 damage (+25 Elite) to the first blow against an enemy unit and takes 40 seconds to build up again. New Coustilliers come out of the Castle fully charged. The charge does not work against buildings. In sustained fights it is weaker than the Knight line because of its lower normal attack, slower attack rate and fewer HP, but it is cheaper and easier to mass.
coustillier.tactics:
## Charge timing and raiding
Coustilliers get the most out of the charge with hit and run: strike, pull back while it reloads, strike again. Timed well, this wears down even Halberdiers, and it works especially well against slow units. Raiding is one of the best uses. With the charge a Coustillier kills a Villager with Loom in three hits, two for the Elite, so draw the enemy army to one front and send the Coustilliers into the back of the base to go after Villagers and leave the buildings.

## Against archers and other cavalry
Cavaliers are usually the better Castle Age pick, but Coustilliers do better against archer and some infantry civilizations. A charged hit plus one normal hit kills a Crossbowman, and the Elite does the same to an Arbalester. They have enough pierce armor to chase Cavalry Archers, and kiting them only gives the charge time to reload. The Coustillier can rival the Burgundian Cavalier and beats most other Cavaliers, Cataphracts and Tarkans for less resources, though the Elite falls well behind the Burgundian Paladin.

## What beats Coustilliers
Camel Riders and Knights, and Halberdiers in large enough numbers. Monks work if they are kept at a distance: a non-Elite Coustillier needs three hits to kill a Monk with Sanctity unless both are charged hits. A converted Coustillier also turns its charge on its former allies. Kamayuks, Genoese Crossbowmen, Mamelukes, Samurai, War Elephants and Boyars also beat it.

crossbowman.description:
The Crossbowman is a foot archer at the Archery Range, upgraded from the Archer once the Castle Age is reached. Every civilization except the Bulgarians and Spanish has it. It costs 25 wood and 45 gold and upgrades to the Arbalester for 450 food and 350 gold. The step up from Archer adds +1 range and +1 attack and cuts training time from 35 to 27 seconds.

Crossbowmen are good against infantry, Villagers and camel units, and in large numbers they kill melee units before those can close in. With 35 HP and no armor they struggle against cavalry, Skirmishers and siege weapons, and they do little to buildings.
crossbowman.tactics:
## The Castle Age power unit
Crossbowmen and Knights are the two traditional power units of the Castle Age. After a Feudal Age Archer rush the Crossbowman upgrade should be a top priority. They work well with infantry, and on the attack they belong inside a group of melee infantry, since arrows are weak against buildings. Pikemen keep cavalry off them, while friendly cavalry handles siege and Elite Skirmishers.

## Knights and Mangonels
Knights have high pierce armor, HP and speed, and they win when both sides have small numbers. Once Crossbowmen reach a critical mass, preferably in a tight space, they can kill Knights in one volley, and a few Pikemen help as well. Mangonels are an effective counter because their area attack kills large groups quickly and cheaply, so that fight comes down to micromanagement. Light Cavalry is a good partner against Mangonels, since it also keeps Monks away and costs different resources. Knights can do the job too, but they drain gold, are slower, see less and are prime targets for Monks.

## Persian Crossbowmen
The Persians cannot upgrade to Arbalester, but their Kamandaran technology replaces the gold cost with extra wood. Their Crossbowmen become a cheap trash unit that is easy to mass with spare wood, and they pair well with Savars or War Elephants, which cost food and gold and shield the archers.

## What beats Crossbowmen
Elite Skirmishers, thanks to high pierce armor and decent damage, although they are of little use against anything except Crossbowmen and Pikemen. Siege units, Mangonels above all, also beat them, as do Huskarls, Eagle Warriors and Rattan Archers.

demolition-raft.description:
The Demolition Raft is a suicide ship trained at the Dock from the Feudal Age, in effect a Petard on water. It is packed with explosives and blows up against enemy ships, Docks, land units in the shallows and buildings close to the shore, dealing 75 damage in an area with +180 against buildings. It upgrades to the Demolition Ship in the Castle Age. Every civilization has it except the Koreans, Portuguese, Saxons and the Northern European civilizations.

It costs 45 wood and 80 gold and is the fastest military ship of the Feudal Age. With 40 HP and no armor, it dies to almost any attack.
demolition-raft.tactics:
## Using Demolition Rafts
Rafts catch enemy ships easily and work best against groups of Galleys and Fire Galleys. They can also destroy enemy Docks quickly, though that is not cost effective. Garrisoning them in your Dock as they are trained lets you mass them up and rush out all at once, before the enemy can react or use its range. That takes some foresight about when enemy ships will come close to the Dock.

Keep them as a complement to a fleet. Because every raft destroys itself, a navy built only on them wins a fight and then has nothing left to hold the water. Mixed with other ships, the rafts do heavy damage and the rest of the fleet finishes off the weakened ships. Against land units caught in the shallows they work very well, since those units have little range to answer with.

## Trading value
Against Feudal Age units, a raft only needs to kill two targets to break even, and gold is rarely short in that Age, so a raft is hard to lose value with even in poor situations. Killing Villagers is worth more than their cost because Villagers are limited by production speed. Careening and Dry Dock add pierce armor, and Siege Engineers adds 40% attack against buildings.

## What beats Demolition Rafts
Towers and ranged units on the shoreline, which kill the fragile rafts before they reach their target. The low HP and zero armor make them easy to stop with any kind of attack if you see them coming.

demolition-ship.description:
A suicide ship packed with explosives, upgraded from the Demolition Raft at the Dock in the Castle Age, with a further upgrade to the Heavy Demolition Ship in the Imperial Age. It costs 45 wood and 80 gold, has 50 HP and deals 95 damage in an area, plus +220 against buildings. The Koreans, Portuguese, Saxons, Danes, Varangians and Vikings cannot build it.

It works like a Petard on water, blowing up against ships, Docks, land units in the shallows and buildings near the shore. It is the fastest military ship and can wipe out groups of ships in one blast, but it dies doing so and is wasted on low HP units.
demolition-ship.tactics:
## The upgrade from Demolition Raft
Compared with the raft, the Demolition Ship has +15 HP, +20 attack, +40 damage against buildings, +1 pierce armor, more speed, a larger blast radius and 14 seconds less training time. The blast also deals full damage to every unit in the radius instead of falling off with distance. Other Feudal Age ships improve just as much in the Castle Age, so the upgrade is almost always worth getting quickly.

## Using Demolition Ships
Send them at high value targets such as fully loaded Transport Ships. The blast destroys most ships or groups of ships in one hit and does not harm friendly units. If the ship explodes early, even when the owner deletes it, the explosion still deals full damage. With their speed, made higher by Dry Dock, they can chase down almost any vessel. They are excellent against Fire Ships, devastating against Transport Ships and good against tight groups of the Galley line if they get close. Opponents tend to target Demolition Ships as soon as they see them, which lets Fire Ships close the distance. A navy built mostly on them falters because each one is spent on a single blast.

## What beats Demolition Ships
Turtle Ships, towers and Castles, and ranged units standing on the shore. Ships with lots of HP spread out also blunt them, since the blast is inefficient against low HP units and needs a tight group to pay off.

dromon.description:
A siege ship trained at the Dock in the Imperial Age by the Armenians, Byzantines, Goths, Huns and Romans. It works much like the Cannon Galleon, but it needs no technology to unlock, while the Cannon Galleon requires Chemistry.

Each shot fires 5 projectiles of 8 attack with +34 against buildings and extra damage against walls and Castles, at a range of 12 and with a 0.8 blast radius. That range outreaches Castles, Keeps and Bombard Towers, except Teutonic, Korean and Turkish ones. It has a minimum range of 3, so it cannot hit enemies close by. It costs 175 wood and 150 gold.
dromon.tactics:
## Clearing the shore
The Dromon's main job is clearing enemy buildings from the shoreline, and now and then harassing land units from range. Because it outranges towers and Castles, it can safely destroy structures that deal bonus damage to ships. It should always have an escort, usually Fire Ships and Galleons. Compared with the Cannon Galleon it has shorter range, a wider blast radius and a faster attack, which makes it better against enemy ships, but it is still expensive and loses cost-efficiently to naval units. It can attack ground and causes friendly fire.

## Civilization differences
The Armenian Dromon is the closest to generic. It fires 6 projectiles instead of 5 for 20% more damage and gets 1 more range from Cilician Fleet. The Byzantine Dromon fires 25% faster, and Greek Fire widens its blast radius by 20%. The Roman Dromon has +1/+1 armor and lacks Dry Dock, and the Romans are the only Dromon civilization with Siege Engineers. Goths and Huns have weaker Dromons, the Goths lacking Dry Dock and the Huns lacking Shipwright.

## What beats Dromons
Other warships, since the Dromon loses cost-efficiently to naval units and cannot shoot anything inside its 3 tile minimum range. Bombard Cannons and Monks are also strong against it.

eagle-scout.description:
A fast infantry scout trained at the Barracks from the Feudal Age, and a regional unit of the Aztecs and Maya. It costs 20 food and 50 gold and takes the place of the Scout Cavalry for these civilizations, which have no cavalry. Both start the game with one Eagle Scout, and the line upgrades to the Eagle Warrior.

Eagle Scouts move quickly, see far, resist conversion and deal bonus damage to Monks and siege weapons. In the Castle Age they also get +3 attack and a small bonus against cavalry. Their weakness is that almost every other infantry unit deals bonus damage against them, and heavy infantry and heavy cavalry beat them.
eagle-scout.tactics:
## Scouting in the Dark Age
The starting Eagle Scout begins in the Stand Ground stance, and every Eagle Scout has an Auto Scout toggle. They cannot attack timid huntables such as Deer. In the Dark Age they move slightly slower than Scout Cavalry and Camel Scouts but see further, which makes them the best scouts of that age. Their combat stats are also good enough to beat the other two scouts and Villagers. Tracking is free in the Feudal Age, which together with the age itself gives them +3 line of sight.

## The Feudal Age Eagle rush
In the Feudal Age Eagle Scouts are much slower than Scout Cavalry and gain no combat bonus, but they are hard to counter because there is no cheap, quickly produced unit that answers them. To balance this they train slowly, 46 seconds each until the Castle Age brings it down to 35. An Eagle rush therefore needs at least two Barracks, which costs the same as the Barracks and Stable a Scout rush needs. Squires is important for them, as for all infantry. The upgrade to Eagle Warrior is cheap but adds little (+5 HP, +1 pierce armor, a bit of speed and +1 attack against mounted units), so Squires or Chain Mail Armor usually come first.

## What beats Eagle Scouts
Heavy infantry such as Long Swordsmen and most other infantry, which deal bonus damage to them. Heavy cavalry also beats them, since their small anti-cavalry bonus only appears in the Castle Age and is not enough against armored horsemen. They do well against Scout Cavalry and foot archers.

eagle-warrior.description:
A fast infantry scout available only to the Aztecs and Maya, upgraded from the Eagle Scout at the Barracks once the Castle Age is reached. It upgrades further to the Elite Eagle Warrior. The Eagle line takes the place of cavalry for these civilizations, and it has a toggleable Auto Scout ability.

An Eagle Warrior costs 20 food and 50 gold and has 55 HP, 7 attack and 0/3 armor. It moves quickly, sees far, resists conversion and has bonus damage against Monks, siege weapons and, to a small degree, cavalry. Almost every other infantry unit has bonus damage against it, and gunpowder units, Slingers and heavy units beat it.
eagle-warrior.tactics:
## Using Eagle Warriors
Eagle Warriors make up for the Aztecs' and Maya's lack of cavalry. Their speed, long line of sight and resistance to conversion make them good at raiding and at hunting archers, siege weapons, Monks and Genitours. Compared to the Eagle Scout, the upgrade adds +1 pierce armor and a few more HP at a reasonable price, so it is useful without being essential. Aztec Eagle Warriors train 15% faster, and Garland Wars gives them +4 attack, while Mayan ones are generic and compete with Plumed Archers as the raiding unit. Squires speeds them up further, and the Blacksmith infantry armor lines apply to them.

## What beats Eagle Warriors
Gunpowder units and Slingers, which have bonuses that cut through their pierce armor. Heavy infantry and most other infantry deal bonus damage to them, and heavy cavalry simply outfights them. Eagle Warriors also cannot attack timid animals like Deer.

elephant-archer.description:
The Elephant Archer is a heavy mounted archer trained at the Archery Range from the Castle Age. It is a regional unit of the Bengalis, Dravidians and Gurjaras and used to be the Indian unique unit. It costs 70 food and 80 gold, has 220 HP and 0/2 armor, and upgrades to the Elite Elephant Archer in the Imperial Age for 900 food and 500 gold.

It is the toughest archer in the game and also the most expensive, yet it has the same attack and base rate of fire as a Cavalry Archer. It is slow, and as both an elephant and a mounted archer it is very vulnerable to Pikemen, Monks and Elite Skirmishers.
elephant-archer.tactics:
## A durable ranged sponge
An army of Elephant Archers has far more HP than an equal-cost army of standard archers but much less damage, so the unit pays off in population efficiency rather than cost. Foot and mounted archers die to one or two Mangonel shots, while an Elephant Archer can take six, and its size means each shot hits only a few of them. The natural 2 pierce armor helps against archers, and unlike melee elephants it can shoot back at Monks. As a ranged unit it stands at the back of a formation, so it works best in front of units with longer range, such as Monks or ranged siege.

## Differences by civilization
Bengali Elephant Archers take 25% less bonus damage, resist conversion and fire 20% faster with Paiks, but they lack Thumb Ring and stay at 70% accuracy. Dravidian ones are the most offensive. Their 25% fire rate bonus makes them the fastest-firing archers in the game, good enough to form the bulk of an army, and Medical Corps gives them 30 HP per minute of regeneration to make up for the missing Bloodlines. Gurjara Elephant Archers train faster and cost 25% less food with Kshatriyas. They lack Ring Archer Armor but get +4 melee armor from Frontier Guards, so they hold up better against melee units and worse against archers.

## What beats Elephant Archers
Pikemen and Monks, as with all elephants, and Elite Skirmishers, since they are mounted archers. Flaming Camels deal 200 damage in total to elephant units and are lethal to packed groups. Kamayuks, Camel Riders, Mamelukes, Eagle Warriors, Huskarls and Scorpions also beat them.

elite-battle-elephant.description:
The Elite Battle Elephant is the Imperial Age upgrade of the Battle Elephant, trained at the Stable. It is a regional unit of the Bengalis, Burmese, Khmer, Malay and Vietnamese; the Dravidians have Battle Elephants but not this upgrade. It costs 100 food and 70 gold and has 300 HP, 14 attack and 25% trample damage.

It is slow, tough and powerful, a smaller and cheaper version of the Elite War Elephant. It beats most melee units, takes a long time to die to arrows and is good at hitting buildings. Spearmen, Kamayuks and Monks are its main problems, and every civilization that has it gives it some bonus or unique technology.
elite-battle-elephant.tactics:
## Using Elite Battle Elephants
The trample damage makes them stronger the bigger the fight, and they hold up against melee units even when those have moderate bonuses against them. Heavy Camel Riders do poorly against them. They cannot catch foot archers, but even the weakest Elite Battle Elephant survives 50 Arbalester shots, so they make a good meat shield for your own ranged units. They do best in pitched battles, are poor raiders, and are population efficient once you reach the population limit.

## Civilization differences
Bengali elephants take 25% less bonus damage, resist conversion and attack 20% faster with Paiks. Burmese ones get extra armor from a civilization bonus and Howdah, plus Manipur Cavalry for +4 against archers. Khmer elephants move 10% faster and reach 21 attack with Tusk Swords, the strongest version overall. Malay elephants cost 35% less but lack Chain Barding Armor and Bloodlines, so they crush melee units and die to archers. Vietnamese elephants get +100 HP from Chatras and shield their Rattan Archers.

## What beats Elite Battle Elephants
Halberdiers and Kamayuks deal almost double bonus damage to them. As slow, valuable units they are a prime target for Monks, and most elephant civilizations lack Heresy. Elite Mamelukes hit and run with high attack and a bonus against cavalry, and Flaming Camels deal about 200 damage to elephants, which is lethal to a packed group. Genoese Crossbowmen, mounted archers and War Elephants also beat them. Foot archers are the usual answer for the elephant player, because they handle all of these counters and keep pace once Husbandry is researched.

elite-cannon-galleon.description:
A gunpowder siege warship, upgraded from the Cannon Galleon at the Dock in the Imperial Age for 525 wood and 500 gold. Only some civilizations have it. It costs 200 wood and 150 gold and has 150 HP, 60 attack with +275 against buildings, a range of 15 and a minimum range of 3.

Its job is destroying buildings from the water. It outranges Castles and Bombard Towers, which makes it close to a seagoing Bombard Cannon that moves a little faster. A slow rate of fire and slow projectiles make it weak against Galleons and other ships, Fire Ships above all, so it needs an escort.
elite-cannon-galleon.tactics:
## Clearing the shoreline
Compared with the Cannon Galleon, the elite version has +30 HP, +10 attack, +75 attack against buildings, +2 pierce armor, +2 range and a slightly larger blast. The range lets it hit Towers and Castles, which deal bonus damage to ships, from outside their reach, and removing such structures is its main use. Keep it on buildings along the shore and away from enemy ships. Siege Engineers adds range and damage against buildings, Careening and Dry Dock add pierce armor, and Shipwright makes it cheaper and faster to build.

Always send an escort, usually Fire Ships and Galleons. Spanish Elite Cannon Galleons are much better than anyone else's: their projectiles travel at 7 tiles per second instead of 3, hit moving targets as if Ballistics were researched, and they fire 18% faster. Turkish ones get +25% HP and +2 range from Artillery.

## What beats Elite Cannon Galleons
Enemy ships, Fire Ships in particular. The slow shots do little against moving ships, and it cannot attack anything closer than 3 tiles. Bombard Cannons and Monks also beat it.

elite-eagle-warrior.description:
The last tier of the Eagle line, upgraded from the Eagle Warrior at the Barracks in the Imperial Age for 800 food and 500 gold. This infantry unit is available only to the Aztecs and Maya, whose Eagle line takes the place of cavalry.

It is fast, has 8 line of sight, 4 pierce armor, conversion resistance and the Auto Scout ability, plus attack bonuses against Monks, siege weapons and mounted units. It cannot attack timid huntables like Deer. Almost every other infantry unit deals bonus damage to it, and it does not counter heavy cavalry.
elite-eagle-warrior.tactics:
## The Elite upgrade
Over the Eagle Warrior, the upgrade gives +2 attack, +2 more damage against Monks and siege, +5 HP, +1 pierce armor, +0.15 speed and 15 seconds less training time. It is moderately expensive, but the Eagle Warrior's attack is low, and both civilizations use the unit heavily enough that they will want it. Thanks to its bonus, the Elite Eagle Warrior hits cavalry as hard as a Champion does. It is better against cavalry than its base stats suggest and is viable against light cavalry.

## Aztec and Mayan Eagles
Each civilization has a unique technology that changes how its Eagles are used. The Aztec Garland Wars adds 4 attack, which makes them better raiders that kill a Villager in three hits. Because they are weak to other infantry, Aztec players sometimes pair them with Jaguar Warriors, or with Arbalesters if they went Crossbowmen in the Castle Age. The Mayan Holcans gives the Eagle line 40 extra HP, for 100 in total, so they hold up in pitched battles. Plumed Archers go well with them because they counter the infantry that threaten Eagles and move at a similar speed. Mayan Elite Eagle Warriors are the most well rounded and generally considered the best.

## What beats Elite Eagle Warriors
Other infantry, since almost all of it deals bonus damage to Eagles, and heavy infantry in particular. Heavy cavalry, gunpowder units and Slingers also beat them. Elite Eagle Warriors are strong against archers, siege weapons, Monks, Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders.

elite-elephant-archer.description:
The Imperial Age upgrade of the Elephant Archer, a slow, heavy mounted archer trained at the Archery Range. It used to be the Indian unique unit and is now a regional unit of the Bengalis, Dravidians and Gurjaras. It costs 70 food and 80 gold and has 270 HP, 7 attack and a range of 4.

It is the toughest archer in the game and also the most expensive one. Its attack and base rate of fire match a Heavy Cavalry Archer's, so for the same cost it brings far more HP and far less damage, which makes it population efficient. Halberdiers, Monks, Elite Skirmishers and Flaming Camels are its main threats.
elite-elephant-archer.tactics:
## A damage sponge at the back
Compared to the Elephant Archer, the Elite version has 50 more HP, +1 attack and 15% more accuracy, so the upgrade matters. Elite Elephant Archers survive far better than other archers: most archers die to one or two Onager shots, while an Elite Elephant Archer can take five, and its size means an Onager only hits a few at once. Its 2 base pierce armor also helps against archers, and unlike melee elephants it can at least shoot back at Monks. Its HP suggests using it as a damage sponge, but as a ranged unit it usually stands at the back. Monks and ranged siege weapons, which outrange it, solve that.

## Civilization differences
Bengali elephants take 25% less bonus damage, resist conversion and fire 20% faster with Paiks, which lets them hold against Halberdiers and Monks in similar numbers. Dravidian elephants fire 25% faster from their civilization bonus, making them the fastest-firing archers in the game. They lack Bloodlines but regenerate 30 HP per minute with Medical Corps, and they work as the bulk of an army. Gurjara elephants train 25% faster, can cost 25% less food with Kshatriyas, and get +4 melee armor from Frontier Guards, but they lack Ring Archer Armor and Faith. The Elite Shrivamsha Rider fills a similar anti-archer role, so for them the unit is a niche choice.

## What beats Elite Elephant Archers
Halberdiers and other anti-elephant units deal heavy bonus damage, and Monks convert them. As mounted archers they also take bonus damage from Elite Skirmishers.
