Flaming Camels deal 200 damage to elephant units and are lethal against packed groups. Mamelukes, Heavy Camel Riders, Huskarls and Heavy Scorpions also beat them.

elite-skirmisher.description:
An anti-archer foot archer upgraded from the Skirmisher at the Archery Range once the Castle Age is reached. Every civilization has it except the Turks, and the Mapuche can also train it at the Settlement. The Vietnamese and their allies can upgrade it further to the Imperial Skirmisher.

It costs 25 food and 35 wood, no gold, and has 35 HP, 3 attack and 4 pierce armor. Bonus damage against archers, Spearmen and Cavalry Archers lets it beat ranged units cheaply. With a weak, slow attack and a minimum range of 1, it does almost no damage to infantry and cavalry, and melee units and siege weapons beat it.
elite-skirmisher.tactics:
## The upgrade and the role
The Elite Skirmisher upgrade gives +1 attack, +1 bonus damage against archers, +2 against Cavalry Archers, +1 pierce armor and +1 range. It is cheap enough to get early almost every time. Skirmishers are made to answer archers: their pierce armor and bonus make them useful against any archer player, especially for civilizations whose bonuses favor infantry or heavy cavalry. The +4 bonus against Pikemen lets a group shoot down approaching spearmen, which together with the low cost makes them good support for cavalry.

## Massing in the late game
One Elite Skirmisher does little damage, but they cost no gold and count as trash units, so they can be massed until a single volley kills its target. A large blob also keeps enemy melee units from reaching every skirmisher at once. They matter most late in the game, when gold runs out and armies rely on food and wood, and in a trash war their bonus against the Spearman line becomes more useful. Bracer, Ring Archer Armor and Thumb Ring are the upgrades that decide how far a civilization's skirmishers can go.

## What beats Elite Skirmishers
Melee units of almost every kind, since the minimum range and weak attack leave the skirmisher unable to hurt them. Even Pikemen can reach them if the skirmishers are caught at close range. Siege weapons beat them too, and apart from archers, Hand Cannoneers and Pikemen, they lose to most of what they meet.

elite-steppe-lancer.description:
The Elite Steppe Lancer is the Imperial Age upgrade of the Steppe Lancer at the Stable, available to the Cumans, Jurchens, Khitans, Mongols and Tatars. It is light cavalry with a lance that attacks from a range of 1. It costs 70 food and 40 gold, has 80 HP, 11 attack and 0/2 armor, and trains in 20 seconds.

The upgrade gives +20 HP, +2 attack, +1 pierce armor and 4 seconds less training time. Its attack and cost sit between the Scout Cavalry and Knight lines. It beats Hussars, Elite Skirmishers, Villagers and siege weapons, and loses to heavier cavalry, Halberdiers, Monks and camel units.
elite-steppe-lancer.tactics:
## Massing and support
Elite Steppe Lancers are most effective in large groups, because their range lets units behind the front line attack too, much like the Inca Kamayuk. They do well in choke points and behind sturdier units such as Cavaliers, attacking over their backs. They also pair well with Halberdiers, Elite Skirmishers and Hussars, which end up as a buffer between the Lancers and dangerous opponents. The upgrade pays off when many Steppe Lancers are in use, although it is expensive and the Steppe Lancer is much stronger in the Castle Age than in the Imperial Age. The unit needs micromanagement.

## Raids and defense
Speed and range let them hit and run like Cavalry Archers. Several Lancers can strike one Villager or siege unit at once and kill it while other cavalry would still be moving into position. The short training time also makes them useful on defense.

## Civilization differences
Cuman Elite Steppe Lancers move a little faster and train twice as fast with Steppe Husbandry. Jurchen ones attack faster and are the strongest in melee. Khitan ones lack Bloodlines and Blast Furnace but get double melee attack upgrades and regenerate in combat with Ordo Cavalry. Mongol ones have +30% HP, and Tatar ones deal +20% damage from higher ground and get Silk Armor.

## What beats Elite Steppe Lancers
Camel units, especially Mamelukes and Imperial Camel Riders, as well as Genoese Crossbowmen and Kamayuks. Masses of Halberdiers and Viking infantry with Chieftains are a strong threat because of their bonus against cavalry. One on one they lose to heavily armored cavalry such as Cavaliers and Paladins, and Monks also beat them.

fast-fire-ship.description:
The Fast Fire Ship is the Imperial Age upgrade of the Fire Ship, trained at the Dock. It carries a flamethrower on the bow and has an attack bonus against other ships, but it has to come very close to them, with a range of 2.5. Many civilizations do not have it.

It costs 75 wood and 45 gold and has 140 HP, 3/7 armor and a speed of 1.56. Compared with the Fire Ship it has 20 more HP, more attack against ships, more pierce armor and a little more speed. It is good against Galleons, Cannon Galleons, Transport Ships and Fishing Ships, and weak against other close range ships and against towers and Castles.
fast-fire-ship.tactics:
## Fast Fire Ships against Galleons
In a close fight the Fast Fire Ship beats a Galleon, but Galleons are usually preferred because they cost less and have more range, which also helps with scouting. In a large battle a Galleon fleet beats a Fast Fire Ship fleet comfortably thanks to that range. With proper support from other ships, though, a group of Fast Fire Ships can sink a Galleon fleet easily. They also deal with buildings on the shoreline and melee units standing in the shallows.

Careening and Dry Dock add pierce armor, Carvel Hull and Clinker Construction add speed, and Shipwright makes them cheaper and faster to train. Byzantines get +1 range from Greek Fire and a faster attack from their civilization bonus.

## What beats Fast Fire Ships
Demolition Ships and Turtle Ships, which also fight at close range, along with Carracks and Longships. Towers, Castles and ranged siege on the shore also outrange and sink them.

fire-galley.description:
A Feudal Age ship trained at the Dock that sprays fire at close range, available to all civilizations. It costs 75 wood and 45 gold, has 110 HP, 1/4 armor and a range of 2.5, and deals melee damage with a bonus against long-range warships. Researching the War Galley upgrade turns every Fire Galley into a Fire Ship.

It is the main ship of Feudal Age water fights and beats Galleys one on one and in groups, thanks to its high pierce armor and the Galley's lack of melee armor. Hulks hard counter it, and its short range leaves it open to Demolition Rafts.
fire-galley.tactics:
## Feudal Age water fights
Early on, nobody has much of a navy to answer them, so Fire Galleys make fairly effective harassment ships, and with good micro they can burn down enemy Docks. They are also good against Transport Ships, rams, melee units standing in the shallows and buildings on the shoreline. Unlike other ranged units, their attacks can be blocked by enemy units or buildings standing between the Fire Galley and its target. Careening and Dry Dock add pierce armor, and the Byzantines get +1 range from Greek Fire.

## What beats Fire Galleys
Hulks hard counter them: they soak up the melee damage, deal bonus damage to Fire Galleys and hit back with melee damage of their own. Fire Galleys also cannot outrun Hulks, cost more and take longer to train. Demolition Rafts reach them before the short-ranged Fire Galleys can shoot them down, though that only pays off when several Fire Galleys are caught in one explosion. Towers and ranged siege units on the shoreline beat them as well.

fire-ship.description:
A warship trained at the Dock from the Castle Age by every civilization. It carries a flamethrower on the bow, so it has to get very close to enemy ships, and then it spews fire about 4 times per second. Fire Galleys become Fire Ships automatically when the War Galley upgrade is researched. Most civilizations can upgrade them to Fast Fire Ships in the Imperial Age, and the Chinese get Dragon Ships instead.

The Fire Ship has 120 HP, 2/4 armor, a range of 2.5 and an attack bonus against other ships. It sinks most ships quickly, the Hulk line excepted, but its short range leaves it open to Demolition Ships and massed War Galleys.
fire-ship.tactics:
## Using Fire Ships
Compared with the Fire Galley, the Fire Ship has +20 HP, +1/+1 attack, +2 attack against Fishing Ships, +2 pierce armor, +0.05 speed and 29 seconds less training time. The War Galley upgrade that brings it also improves the Galley and the Demolition Raft just as much, so it is worth researching right away. Each flame does little damage, but the attack is very fast, and the high pierce armor lets Fire Ships close the distance under fire and tear into enemy ships.

Fire Ships work mostly as support for other ships, because they quickly sink masses of Galleons, Cannon Galleons and other Fire Ships. Together with Galleons they make a good escort for Transport Ships. They are strong against Transport Ships, Fishing Ships, buildings on the shoreline and rams, and they can even fight melee units standing in the shallows.

## What beats Fire Ships
Demolition Ships are excellent counters, since a Fire Ship has to come right up to its target to attack. Korean Turtle Ships are also a threat. The short range lets War Galleys engage much more easily in large numbers, so War Galleys win big fights, and the Castle Age Fire Ship is slower than a War Galley, which lets micromanaged Galleys hit and run against it. War Hulks, Longships, towers, Castles and ranged siege units on the shoreline also beat Fire Ships.

fishing-ship.description:
The basic civilian ship of every civilization, trained at the Dock from the Dark Age for 75 wood. It gathers food from fish and builds Fish Traps, which work like Farms on water. It cannot be upgraded into another unit, and like a Villager it has a Drop Off command that sends it to the nearest Dock and straight back to work.

On deep-sea fish close to a Dock it gathers food about 50% faster than a Villager on a Farm, while costing about 50% more. Fishing Ships can also collect gold from Oysters and Whales. With 50 HP and no attack they cannot defend themselves.
fishing-ship.tactics:
## Fish and Fish Traps
A Fishing Ship gathers 0.42 food per second from deep-sea fish, 0.24 from shore fish and 0.35 from Fish Traps, and carries 15 food at a time. The rate depends heavily on the distance to the Dock, so once the nearby deep-sea fish are gone, walking time cuts into the income. Fish Traps solve this. They take long to build and gather a little slower, but a trap gives 715 food for 100 wood, much more per wood than a Farm, and needs no Mill upgrades. Farms only become more wood efficient after Crop Rotation, or Heavy Plow for the Sicilians. After Gillnets, Fishing Ships on Fish Traps gather faster than Villagers on Farms.

## Upgrades and gold
Fishing Lines and Gillnets each add 10% work rate and 5 carry capacity. Shipwright makes them 20% cheaper and faster to train, and Careening and Dry Dock add pierce armor. On maps with Oysters or Whales, the ship collects gold at 0.4 per second from Oysters and 0.5 per second from Whales. Several civilizations boost them: Japanese Fishing Ships have double HP, +2 pierce armor and a work rate bonus that grows each age, Dravidian ones carry 15 more, and Maya ones get 15% more out of fish and Oysters.

## What beats Fishing Ships
Fishing Ships have 50 HP and 1/1 armor and no attack, so any armed enemy ship can sink them. They depend on the player controlling the water near their Docks. Gurjara Fishing Ships can garrison in Docks.

flemish-militia.description:
The second Burgundian unique unit, an anti-cavalry infantry soldier trained at the Barracks from the Feudal Age. It sits between the Spearman and Militia lines and has no Elite upgrade. Instead it gains HP and attack for free with each Age: 40 HP and 5 attack in the Feudal Age, 60 HP and 11 attack in the Imperial Age.

It costs 35 food and 25 gold. The Flemish Revolution technology also turns every Burgundian Villager into Flemish Militia, though these can no longer gather or build. It has bonus damage against cavalry, camels, elephants and ships, beats other foot units in melee, and shares the usual infantry weakness to archers and siege.
flemish-militia.tactics:
## Flemish Militia or Spearmen
Compared to Spearmen, the Flemish Militia has 1 more melee and pierce armor and attacks every 2 seconds instead of every 3. That gives it a clear edge against foot units other than Monks, and against siege units, where the Spearman does poorly against anything not mounted. Its bonus damage against cavalry is far smaller than a Spearman's, though, and it costs gold where the Spearman costs wood, so Spearmen give more value per resource against cavalry. Squires, the Blacksmith infantry lines and Arson all apply.

## Flemish Revolution
Researching Flemish Revolution converts every Villager into a Flemish Militia with the same share of HP left. They cannot build, repair or gather, but Villagers can still be trained afterwards.

## What beats Flemish Militia
Archers, Hand Cannoneers and Slingers, like most infantry, along with ranged siege and fortifications. Cataphracts absorb all of its bonus damage, and Samurai are strong against it because it counts as a unique unit. Teutonic Knights and Jaguar Warriors beat it as well.

galleon.description:
The Galleon is the Imperial Age upgrade of the War Galley, trained at the Dock after Heavy Warships is researched. Every civilization except the Aztecs, Khitans and Malians has it. It costs 90 wood and 30 gold and has 155 HP, 9 pierce attack, 0/6 armor and a range of 7, with bonus damage against long-range warships, buildings and rams.

The upgrade adds +30 HP, +2 attack, +4 attack against long-range warships, +2 pierce armor and +1 range, which makes it close to mandatory. The Galleon is the standard late game warship for most civilizations. It struggles against Fast Fire Ships, heavy warships, towers and Castles.
galleon.tactics:
## Backbone of the late game navy
Galleons should be built in numbers to take out enemy navies. In groups they destroy Heavy Demolition Ships and enemy Galleons easily, and they work best in large numbers paired with Fire Ships. They are cost-effective against unique ships that fill the same role, such as the Caravel and the Longship, and against long-ranged siege ships. Carracks lose to them at long distance. Bracer, Dry Dock and Shipwright fully upgrade the Galleon, and only some civilizations have all three.

## Shoreline combat
Galleons are useful against enemy units and buildings near the shore, including melee units standing on the shoreline. Towers, Castles and ranged siege units are the exception, and Galleons should avoid fighting them from the water.

## What beats Galleons
Fast Fire Ships, to which Galleons are somewhat vulnerable, and heavy warships such as the Turtle Ship and the Thirisadai. Carracks win at close distance, and Elite Longships are also listed as a counter. From land, towers, Castles and ranged siege units on the shoreline beat them.

galley.description:
The Galley is the basic ranged warship, trained at the Dock by every civilization from the Feudal Age. It is a small, fast ship used for scouting and for attacking vulnerable units near the water, and it upgrades to the War Galley in the Castle Age.

It costs 90 wood and 30 gold and has 110 HP, 6 pierce attack, a range of 5 and 0/3 armor, with bonuses against buildings, rams and long range warships. It is weak on its own and becomes effective in numbers. It is good against Transport Ships, Fishing Ships and anything on the shoreline, and loses to Fire Galleys, towers and Castles.
galley.tactics:
## Using Galleys
A large enough group of Galleys takes out enemy ships with ease, and Galleys are good at wiping out Fishing Ships and other economic units close to the coast. Shore bombardment is where they have a niche of their own, since neither the Demolition Raft nor the Fire Galley can do that job. The archer technologies Fletching, Bodkin Arrow and Bracer add attack and range, Ballistics lets them hit moving targets, and Careening and Dry Dock add pierce armor.

In the Feudal Age the Fire Galley is usually the better default choice. The Galley tends to become the better pick in the Castle Age, once it can be upgraded to the War Galley.

## What beats Galleys
Fire Galleys beat them without needing to be massed. Towers, Castles and ranged units on the shoreline also outshoot them. Hulks win at close distance, while Galleys come out ahead when they keep the Hulk at long range.

gbeto.description:
The Malian unique infantry, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. Gbetos throw knives, dealing melee damage at a range of 5 (6 as Elite). They cost 50 food and 40 gold and have 40 HP (50 as Elite), 10 attack (13 as Elite), no base armor and a high movement speed.

They have more range and attack than the other ranged melee units, the Mameluke and the Throwing Axeman, and they deal a lot of damage quickly. With no armor and little HP they are fragile, so foot archers, Hand Cannoneers and ranged siege beat them.
gbeto.tactics:
## Hit and run
Gbetos are fast enough to hit and run against almost every infantry unit except Elite Eagle Warriors, Woad Raiders and Condottieri, and their range and melee attack defeat Eagle Warriors quickly anyway. Of the whole infantry branch, only the Teutonic Knight holds up against them. Because the damage is melee, they also kill units with high pierce armor such as Huskarls, Elite Skirmishers and rams, which Cavalry Archers struggle with, and they still win against Pikemen that get close.

## Raids and compositions
With Arson, Gbetos can burn down unprotected bases and retreat safely when the fight turns. They pair well with cavalry, especially Light Cavalry, since both are fast. The cavalry takes the hits and kills the siege and archers that threaten Gbetos, while the Gbetos add damage from behind and keep Pikemen off the cavalry. Forging, Iron Casting, the infantry armor upgrades and Squires all apply to them.

## What beats Gbetos
Foot archers outrange them, and their low HP and pierce armor make them vulnerable to most ranged units. Hand Cannoneers are also quite effective. Onagers and Heavy Scorpions can be lethal, though a small, well microed group of Gbetos can get close to the machines and destroy them. Boyars and Teutonic Knights also beat them in melee.

genitour.description:
The second Berber unique unit, a mounted skirmisher trained at the Archery Range from the Castle Age and upgraded to the Elite Genitour in the Imperial Age for 500 food and 450 wood. It is also the Berber team bonus, so any ally of a Berber player can train it. It costs 40 food and 35 wood, and since it needs no gold it counts as a trash unit.

Genitours have bonus damage against every archer unit and beat almost all of them, the Genoese Crossbowman being the exception. None of their strengths apply against cavalry or siege weapons, and anti-cavalry units such as Camel Riders and Pikemen hurt them.
genitour.tactics:
## Against archers
The Genitour fills the same anti-archer role as the Elite Skirmisher from the same age. It is 40% faster, has 15 more HP (20 more as Elite, and more again with Bloodlines) and can hit and run against infantry, and the Elite Genitour has 1 more attack than the Elite Skirmisher. In exchange it needs 60% more food, has 1 less range and is vulnerable to anti-cavalry units. Cavalry Archers are better at hit and run against infantry because of their higher base attack. Genitours are also good Monk deterrents: they have range and speed, and a converted Genitour is of little use to the enemy, especially against Berber cavalry.

## When to pick Genitours
The Berbers usually prefer them in the Imperial Age, because they keep up with a Berber cavalry army where Skirmishers lag behind. Genitours are a good choice against civilizations that use Cavalry Archers. The Turks have no Elite Skirmisher and get very strong Genitours thanks to Sipahi. The Japanese gain from their larger than usual bonus against archers, which threaten Japanese infantry armies.

## What beats Genitours
Camel Riders and Pikemen, since the Genitour is a cavalry unit and takes their anti-cavalry bonus. Siege units are another bad matchup, as the Genitour's bonuses do nothing against them. Huskarls, Eagle Warriors, Woad Raiders and Ghulams also beat Genitours, and the Genoese Crossbowman is the one archer that holds up against them.

genoese-crossbowman.description:
The first Italian unique unit, a foot archer trained at the Castle in the Castle Age for 45 wood and 40 gold. It can be upgraded to Elite Genoese Crossbowman in the Imperial Age. It trains in 14 seconds, about half the time of a Crossbowman.

Its bonus damage against cavalry, elephants, camels and ships makes it a genuine counter to mounted units. It has more HP than a Crossbowman and 100% accuracy, but only 4 range and no bonus against Spearmen. Skirmishers, Huskarls, siege and fast armored infantry beat it.
genoese-crossbowman.tactics:
## Against cavalry and elephants
Massed Genoese Crossbowmen are a strong defense against Knights, including the durable Sicilian ones. War Elephants and Battle Elephants die quickly to large groups, and they even beat Bengali Elephant Archers for their cost. When massed they hold up against infantry as well. Against mounted archers they have a big bonus and no range disadvantage. Cavalry can still win one on one if it reaches melee range. Shrivamsha Riders dodge their shots, Savars deal extra damage to archers, and Tiger Cavalry gets stronger with each kill, so a small group of Genoese is in danger against all three.

## Compositions and ships
Italian Hand Cannoneers are cheap and pair well against infantry that threatens archers. Hussars and Bombard Cannons deal with siege, with the Hussar adding speed and the Bombard Cannon handling buildings. The unit also has a bonus against all ships: two Elite Genoese Crossbowmen can sink a fully upgraded Galleon, a job that takes about ten Arbalesters. The Italians pay 33% less for Chemistry and Ballistics.

## What beats Genoese Crossbowmen
Elite Skirmishers and Huskarls have good pierce armor and bonus damage against archers. Genitours may lose in equal numbers but cost no gold, so they are still a cost-effective answer. Eagle Warriors and Ghulams are fast and armored enough to close in. Mangonels and Scorpions hurt them, although a Genoese Crossbowman survives one Mangonel shot. Among unique archers, Longbowmen outrange them, Rattan Archers take only 1 damage per shot, and Composite Bowmen ignore their pierce armor while being cheaper.

ghulam.description:
The Hindustani unique unit, a fast infantry soldier trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Ghulam in the Imperial Age. It is used to kill archers and to raid. A Ghulam costs 30 food and 45 gold, trains in 12 seconds and has 60 HP, 9 attack, +5 against archers and 0/3 armor.

Its spear thrust also hits the unit behind the target for 50% damage, so clumped archers suffer most. High pierce armor and speed let it reach foot archers where most infantry cannot, and it also does well against Villagers, siege and Eagle Warriors. With no base melee armor it loses to heavy infantry, heavy cavalry and Monks.
ghulam.tactics:
## Hunting archers
Ghulams are the Hindustani answer to archers. Their Hand Cannoneers and Camel Riders are built to fight infantry and cavalry, and Ghulams cover the weakness both have against archers. The thrust only reaches the second unit when two enemies stand in a row, so tightly packed archer groups are the best target. Their speed also lets them run down siege weapons, and in the Castle Age they stand in for the Knights the Hindustanis lack. They have one less attack than a Knight and are slightly slower, but are cheaper, smaller and faster to train, and the Hindustani economy makes a Castle for them affordable.

The Ghulam reaches full armor quickly. The Hindustanis only need the Elite upgrade, which brings pierce armor to 6, while Eagle Warriors need both Plate Mail Armor and their Elite upgrade, at a higher combined cost. That helps when catching up to an enemy archer rush. Compared to Huskarls, Ghulams cost much less food for a little more gold.

## What beats Ghulams
Melee units, because the Ghulam has no base melee armor. Champions, Jaguar Warriors, Samurai and Teutonic Knights beat it, as does heavy cavalry. Monks can also convert it. Pair Ghulams with Camel Riders or Hand Cannoneers so they are not left alone against these units.

halberdier.description:
The Halberdier is an infantry unit upgraded from the Pikeman in the Imperial Age at the Barracks, the Sicilian Donjon or the Mapuche Settlement. Not every civilization has it. It costs 35 food and 25 wood with no gold, which makes it a trash unit, and it is one of the cheapest military units in the game per population. It has 60 HP, 6 attack and no armor.

Its job is countering cavalry, with +32 bonus damage against cavalry and large bonuses against elephant and camel units. Against every other unit type it is weak, and archers in particular kill it quickly.
halberdier.tactics:
## Anti-cavalry duty
The upgrade from Pikeman adds +10 attack against cavalry, +8 against camel units and +13 in total against elephant units. That makes it almost always worth it, although the high cost can be hard to justify if the enemy makes little cavalry. The cavalry bonus is so large that two Halberdiers can bring down a Paladin. Halberdiers need to be massed, and then they are cost-effective against all cavalry, even Cataphracts. They cannot force a fight, so they suit guarding units that would otherwise fall to cavalry, such as siege weapons.

## Trash wars
Halberdiers become more valuable in the late Imperial Age, when gold usually runs low and games turn into trash wars. There they hold an advantage over Hussars.

## What beats Halberdiers
Archers, especially in mass. Halberdiers have little HP and pierce armor and also take the archers' bonus damage against Spearmen. Other infantry beats them as well, since their base damage is very low and they have no bonus against infantry. Cavalry Archers can handle them with proper micromanagement, and Elite Cataphracts trade about evenly with them.

hand-cannoneer.description:
The Hand Cannoneer is a gunpowder unit trained at the Archery Range once the Imperial Age is reached and Chemistry is researched. Only some civilizations have it, and the Bohemians can train it from the Castle Age. It counts as an archer for attack bonuses as well as a gunpowder unit.

It costs 45 food and 50 gold and has 17 pierce attack, +10 against infantry and a range of 7. It hits very hard but fires slowly, has only 40 HP and is inaccurate at long range. It is deadly against infantry and good against Heavy Camel Riders, and it is vulnerable to Skirmishers, siege and towers.
hand-cannoneer.tactics:
## Using Hand Cannoneers
The shots fly off in random directions around the target, so long range accuracy is poor. Cavalry are big targets, so accuracy matters less against them, and up close Hand Cannoneers are deadly. Their bonus against infantry applies to all infantry except the Condottiero, plus +1 against spearmen. Handled well, they also kill siege weapons efficiently, though Onagers can still outrange them.

Compared with the Arbalester, the Hand Cannoneer is better against targets with high pierce armor, while the Arbalester is better against targets with little. The food cost makes them awkward to fit into a build, so they usually need a special plan such as a fast Imperial Age strategy on closed maps.

## Civilization differences
Italians get 90% accuracy and pass-through damage from Pirotechnia, Portuguese ones track moving targets with Arquebus, and Hindustanis get +2 range from Shatagni. Turkish Hand Cannoneers have more HP, Spanish ones fire 18% faster, and Burgundians deal 25% more damage. Burgundians, Franks, Georgians and Gurjaras lack Ring Archer Armor.

## What beats Hand Cannoneers
Elite Skirmishers, Ghulams and Huskarls have attack bonuses against archers, and Huskarls also have high pierce armor against the shots. Condottieri and Winged Hussars have bonuses against gunpowder units, and Genitours also beat them. Being low HP foot units, Hand Cannoneers die quickly to Mangonels, Onagers and Scorpions, and they do poorly against towers and Castles.

heavy-camel-rider.description:
The Imperial Age upgrade of the Camel Rider, researched at the Stable for 325 food and 360 gold. Every civilization with Camel Riders gets it except the Cumans, and the Hindustanis can go one step further to the Imperial Camel Rider. It costs 55 food and 60 gold and has 120 HP, 7 attack, +18 against cavalry and +9 against camel units.

It is a fast, durable anti-cavalry unit that can also chase down mounted archers. Low armor and base attack make it poor against infantry, foot archers and buildings, and defensive structures deal extra damage to it.
heavy-camel-rider.tactics:
## Against cavalry
Heavy Camel Riders deal about as much damage to cavalry as Halberdiers but are much more durable, and as the second fastest land unit type after light cavalry they can force fights. They also beat mounted archers, which kite Halberdiers to death. The Spearman line does better against elephants and other camels, since it has an extra bonus against elephants and a smaller penalty against camels. Most of the time the tech tree decides anyway: most camel civilizations lack Halberdiers or have weak ones, and the Gurjaras and Turks do not even have Pikemen. Against siege they do decently thanks to their speed.

The upgrade gives +20 HP, +1 attack and +9 bonus damage against cavalry. It is cheap and worth getting before other technologies when the enemy fields cavalry.

## Civilization differences
Saracen Heavy Camel Riders have 170 HP, and Hindustani ones attack 20% faster. Gurjara ones get +40% bonus damage, +4 melee armor from Frontier Guards and an Auto Scout ability, since they count as scouts. Berber ones are 20% cheaper and regenerate with Maghrebi Camels, Byzantine ones cost 25% less but lack Bloodlines, and Malian ones get +5 attack from Farimba.

## What beats Heavy Camel Riders
Infantry and foot archers, which their low armor and base attack cannot deal with. They cost far more than a Halberdier, which makes them worth converting for enemy Monks. Cataphracts and defensive structures also beat them.

heavy-cavalry-archer.description:
The upgraded Cavalry Archer, researched at the Archery Range in the Imperial Age, or in the Castle Age for the Khitans. Many European civilizations have the Heavy Mounted Crossbowman in its place. It costs 40 wood and 60 gold and has 60 HP, 7 attack with +4 against spearmen, 4 range and 1/0 armor.

It is fast enough to hit and run and durable when caught in a fight, but it is strong only in large numbers, which makes it expensive to use. Enemy bonuses treat it as an archer, a cavalry unit and a cavalry archer, so Elite Skirmishers, Camel Archers and Onagers punish it hard.
heavy-cavalry-archer.tactics:
## The upgrade
Over the Cavalry Archer it gains 10 HP, 1 attack, 2 more attack against spearmen, 1 melee armor and 30% accuracy, and trains 7 seconds faster. That makes it an important upgrade against Spearman line units. The accuracy gain matters most for civilizations without Thumb Ring, or when the unit fights before Thumb Ring is researched. The Georgians and Khmer benefit most. A fully upgraded Heavy Cavalry Archer has Bloodlines, Bracer, Ring Archer Armor, Parthian Tactics and Thumb Ring, which the Japanese, Magyars, Saracens, Turks and Tatars all get.

## Compositions
The most popular pairing is with Hussars. Heavy Cavalry Archers cost wood and gold, so the food goes into Hussars that give the army melee support, and the result is a mobile and dangerous force. Heavy cavalry can replace the Hussars if gold allows, though that is uncommon because both units cost a lot of gold. Heavy Cavalry Archers are strong against slow melee units and, with Parthian Tactics and Ring Archer Armor, against foot archers.

## What beats Heavy Cavalry Archers
Elite Skirmishers and Onagers are devastating against mounted archers. Heavy Camel Riders are also very good, being faster and dealing bonus damage to all mounted units, as long as they are not microed down. Halberdiers can deal with them in theory, but in practice they usually die before they reach them. Elite Eagle Warriors, Heavy Scorpions, Genoese Crossbowmen, Huskarls, Mamelukes, Camel Archers and Rattan Archers also beat them.

heavy-demolition-ship.description:
A suicide ship packed with explosives, upgraded from the Demolition Ship at the Dock in the Imperial Age. Many civilizations have it, but not all. It costs 45 wood and 80 gold and blows up on contact, damaging enemy ships, Docks, land units in the shallows and anything close to the shore.

Its explosion deals 120 damage, with +280 against buildings, over a wide area. Together with the Demolition Ship it is the fastest military vessel in the game, so it can chase targets down. As a suicide unit it is lost with every attack, which makes it a poor base for a navy.
heavy-demolition-ship.tactics:
## Picking targets
Compared to the Demolition Ship it has 10 more HP, 30 more attack, 60 more damage against buildings and a blast radius 0.5 larger. One hit destroys most ships. It is excellent against Fire Ships, devastating against loaded Transport Ships and good against Cannon Galleons. It also works against the Galley line if it can get close. Docks and other buildings on the shoreline, and melee units standing in the shallows, are good targets too.

A Heavy Demolition Ship also explodes when it is killed, damaging nearby units, but it causes no friendly fire to its own side. Siege Engineers adds 40% damage against buildings, and Carvel Hull and Clinker Construction make it even faster. Armenians get a 20% larger blast radius from Cilician Fleet.

## What beats Heavy Demolition Ships
Turtle Ships are listed as a counter. Towers and Castles shoot them down before they reach the shore, and ranged units standing on the shoreline do the same. Their 70 HP is low, so they need to reach the target before anything with range can focus them.

heavy-scorpion.description:
A light siege weapon upgraded from the Scorpion at the Siege Workshop once the Imperial Age is reached. It costs 75 wood and 75 gold and has 60 HP, 14 pierce attack, range 7 and a minimum range of 2. Its bolts pass through every unit in a straight line, and unlike Mangonel shots they never hurt friendly units, which helps in crowded close fights.

Heavy Scorpions are slow, fire slowly and must be protected. They shred tightly grouped infantry, foot archers and elephants. Fast melee units close the gap and dodge the bolts, and longer ranged siege such as Onagers and Bombard Cannons destroys them.
heavy-scorpion.tactics:
## Upgrade and compositions
The Heavy Scorpion upgrade adds +20 HP, +4 attack and +1/+1 armor. It is cheap for what it gives, so take it whenever you use Scorpions in any number. A medium group can wipe out armies of infantry and archers very quickly and even holds up against cavalry in large enough numbers. Halberdiers are the usual escort against cavalry, a mix especially common for the Bulgarians, Celts, Chinese, Ethiopians, Khmer, Slavs and Teutons, whose bonuses help both units. Siege Engineers adds 1 range, Chemistry adds 1 attack and Ballistics lets the bolts hit moving targets.

## Scorpions or Arbalesters
Fully upgraded Heavy Scorpions have the same range as fully upgraded Arbalesters, which are cheaper and easier to mass, so Arbalesters are usually the better choice. Civilizations without Bracer or Arbalesters, such as the Celts, Franks, Slavs and Teutons, get more out of Heavy Scorpions.

## What beats Heavy Scorpions
Cavalry and other fast melee units such as Woad Raiders, Elite Eagle Warriors, Ghulams and Huskarls dodge the bolts and reach the scorpions quickly, and the minimum range leaves them helpless once that happens. Cavalry Archers, Mangudai in particular, kill them when microed well. Onagers and Bombard Cannons outrange them and destroy them from a distance.

huskarl.description:
The Huskarl is the unique unit of the Goths, an infantry unit trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, and at the Barracks once Anarchy is researched. It costs 57 food and 27 gold in the Castle Age and 53 food and 25 gold in the Imperial Age. It has 60 HP, 10 attack and 0/6 armor. The Elite Huskarl upgrade in the Imperial Age raises that to 70 HP, 12 attack and 0/8 armor.

High pierce armor and bonus damage against archers and buildings make it one of the best raiders in the game and a nightmare for archers. With no melee armor and fairly low HP it does poorly in melee.
huskarl.tactics:
## Raiding and breaking archers
Archers do little against the Huskarl's pierce armor, and its bonus damage kills them fast. The pierce armor, the bonus against buildings and the Goth infantry bonus against buildings also let Huskarls take down a Castle with little effort. The drawback is the Castle they need, both to train them and to research Anarchy, so the opponent can mass archers before Huskarls arrive and the Goths need Elite Skirmishers until then. In the Castle Age a small group struggles to reach a large archer army, so avoid trickling them in. With Perfusion and Anarchy the Goths can produce enough Huskarls to overwhelm almost any archer army.

## Against melee and gunpowder
Huskarls should only fight weak melee units such as Camel Riders, Light Cavalry, Halberdiers and Eagle Warriors. The Goths can make them cheaply and quickly enough to swamp Paladins or Champions, but Champions and Halberdiers are the more efficient answer to enemy melee. Hand Cannoneers and Slingers have bonus damage and range against Huskarls, yet an Elite Huskarl kills either in two strikes, so they need numbers or melee cover.

## What beats Huskarls
Melee units with high armor such as Boyars and Teutonic Knights, units with bonus damage against them such as Jaguar Warriors, Cataphracts and Samurai, and hard hitters such as Shotel Warriors, Leitis, Obuchs and Urumi Swordsmen. War and Battle Elephants crush them with HP and splash damage. Throwing Axemen, Gbetos, Mamelukes and Chakram Throwers deal melee damage from range, so the pierce armor does not help. Onagers and Mangonels are a threat too, while Scorpions, Organ Guns and Hussite Wagons are not.

hussar.description:
The Hussar is light cavalry upgraded from the Light Cavalry at the Stable in the Imperial Age. The upgrade costs 500 food and 600 gold, and only some civilizations have it. The Poles and Lithuanians get the Winged Hussar as an alternative.

It costs only 80 food, moves fast and has 75 HP, 2 pierce armor, a line of sight of 10, resistance to conversion and +12 attack against Monks. It is used for scouting, raiding and hunting down archers, siege weapons and Monks. In a straight fight it is weak, and it loses to infantry, heavier cavalry and Genoese Crossbowmen.
hussar.tactics:
## The Hussar upgrade
The upgrade gives +15 HP, a Monk bonus of 12 instead of 10, and a slightly faster attack every 1.9 seconds instead of 2. Because of the faster attack, a Hussar without Bloodlines beats a Light Cavalry with it. The upgrade is expensive, so research it after the Blacksmith upgrades and only if you will use Hussars a lot.

## Using Hussars
Hussars raid economies and defend against siege weapons and Monks. Because they cost only food they count as trash units and matter most in the late game, when gold runs low. Among trash units they beat Elite Skirmishers and lose to Halberdiers, and they are the most versatile of the three since they also handle siege and raiding. A common pairing is Hussars with mounted archers: the gold goes into archers and siege, while Hussars deal with Elite Skirmishers, siege and Monks and soak up infantry, heavy cavalry and Heavy Camel Riders for the archers.

Some civilizations stand out. Turks get the upgrades for free and +1 pierce armor, Bulgarians fight best in melee with Stirrups, Magyars get free attack upgrades, and Berbers and Magyars field them cheaper. Cumans have the fastest Hussars, Mongols get 30% more HP, and Tatars get extra armor from Silk Armor.

## What beats Hussars
Halberdiers are the classic answer, as the trash unit that counters light cavalry. Infantry and heavier cavalry also beat Hussars in a direct fight because of their poor combat stats. Genoese Crossbowmen, with their bonus against cavalry, beat them too.

hussite-wagon.description:
The first Bohemian unique unit, a gunpowder siege wagon trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. It costs 110 wood and 80 gold and has 160 HP (230 as Elite), 7 pierce armor (10 as Elite) and a range of 6. Each shot fires one main bullet and five weaker ones at the same time. It does not need Chemistry.

Enemy projectiles that pass through the wagon deal only half damage to the units behind it, and the wagon takes the other half. That makes it a moving shield for Bohemian ranged units. Mangonels, Bombard Cannons, cavalry and armored infantry beat it.
hussite-wagon.tactics:
## The wagon as a shield
The Hussite Wagon works like a mobile tower. In formation it always sits in front of ranged units and behind melee units, and the Box formation is useful for sheltering units behind it. The shield ability applies to pierce and melee projectiles, but melee units that do not fire projectiles are unaffected, attack ground shots ignore it, and the high arc of Bombard Cannon and Trebuchet shots gets past it. In practice the wagon usually draws enemy fire itself and plays the role of a Skirmisher or ram that soaks up arrows, more than a damage dealer. It is expensive and asks for little micro, so experienced players find the ability hard to use well, and it is not a required part of the Bohemian late game army. Siege Engineers adds 1 range and Wagenburg Tactics adds speed.

## Raiding
A few wagons sent into an enemy base can shut down the economy for a short time, because the enemy has to invest to kill something this durable. Villagers deal +6 damage to Hussite Wagons, though, so stay away from a Villager counterattack. Against an opponent making Villagers from four or more Town Centers the raid is likely a net loss, given the cost of the unit and its upgrade.

## What beats Hussite Wagons
The Mangonel and Bombard Cannon lines, which deal extra damage to the Heavy Siege armor class on top of their anti-siege bonus. Cavalry, Throwing Axemen, Huskarls, Samurai and Condottieri also beat them. As siege, they need Villagers to repair them, and Monks can convert them once Redemption is researched. They are not archers or cavalry, so Halberdiers, Heavy Camel Riders and Elite Skirmishers get no bonus against them.

imperial-camel-rider.description:
The second Hindustani unique unit, upgraded from the Heavy Camel Rider at the Stable in the Imperial Age. It is already the final upgrade of the line and has no Elite version. At 55 food and 60 gold it is cheaper than a Knight.

It has 140 HP and 8 attack, with +18 against cavalry and +9 against camel units and ships. It is fast, durable and easily kills most cavalry in one on one fights. With no base armor and a weak base attack it does much worse against foot units.
imperial-camel-rider.tactics:
## Role in the Hindustani army
The Hindustanis have no Knight line at all, so camels are their fast and resilient unit. Imperial Camel Riders can shield weaker units while still cutting down mounted units, and they are among the most versatile cavalry in the game. The Hindustani civilization bonus makes them attack faster and the team bonus gives them +2 attack against standard buildings, so they are fairly good at putting pressure on enemy towns. That makes up for the missing Cavaliers and Paladins to some degree, though the camels remain weaker against those units in most respects.

## The upgrade
Compared with the Heavy Camel Rider, the Imperial Camel Rider has +20 HP and +1 attack and trains 10% faster. The upgrade is expensive, but it is generally worth it because of how well the unit fits the Hindustani army.

## What beats Imperial Camel Riders
Foot units in general, since the camel has no base armor and a low base attack. Foot archers and Genoese Crossbowmen shoot it down, and Halberdiers and Kamayuks deal anti-cavalry damage to it. Heavy melee units such as Teutonic Knights, Berserks and Elite Cataphracts also beat it. Imperial Camel Riders are strong against Elite Skirmishers, siege weapons and cavalry.

imperial-skirmisher.description:
An anti-archer foot archer upgraded from the Elite Skirmisher at the Archery Range in the Imperial Age. It is a shared unique unit: the Vietnamese and every player allied with them can get it, except the Turks, who have no Elite Skirmisher. It costs 25 food and 35 wood and no gold.

It has 5 pierce armor and bonus damage against archers, Spearmen, cavalry archers and Mamelukes, which makes it a cheap answer to archer armies. Its attack is weak and slow and it has a minimum range, so infantry, cavalry and siege beat it.
imperial-skirmisher.tactics:
## Late game trash unit
Compared to the Elite Skirmisher, the Imperial Skirmisher has +1 attack, +1 pierce armor and +1 bonus damage against archers and cavalry archers. Against Arbalesters this means it takes half the damage and deals about 28.5% more. Because it costs no gold it becomes most useful late in the game, when gold runs low. Its +4 bonus against Spearmen lets groups of them kill approaching Pikemen quickly, though the minimum range and low melee armor leave them exposed. As a generic unit it does not take the Samurai's bonus against unique units.

## Researching it in team games
Unlike the Condottiero or the Genitour, each allied player has to research the upgrade at their own Archery Range. Being a trash unit, it matters less in team games than in 1v1. Civilizations with strong Skirmisher bonuses get the most out of it, especially the Aztecs, Britons, Byzantines, Dravidians, Inca, Koreans, Lithuanians and Maya. For the Aztecs, whose Arbalesters are weak, Imperial Skirmishers boosted by Atlatl are better in most respects, from cost efficiency to training time.

## What beats Imperial Skirmishers
Melee units of nearly every kind, since the Skirmisher deals almost no damage to infantry and cavalry and cannot fire at close range. Siege units also beat them. They do well against archers, some gunpowder units such as Hand Cannoneers and Conquistadors, and to a degree Pikemen.

jaguar-warrior.description:
The Aztec unique unit, an anti-infantry foot soldier trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Jaguar Warrior in the Imperial Age. It costs 60 food and 30 gold and has 65 HP, 15 attack with +5 against infantry, and 1/2 armor.

Each enemy military unit it kills gives it +1 attack, up to +4. Monks, warships, Transport Ships and Kings count for this. The anti-infantry bonus lets it beat any other infantry one on one except Teutonic Knights and Samurai, and its speed of 1 lets it catch Champions. Like most infantry it struggles against heavy cavalry, and gunpowder units, Scorpions and Mangonels beat it.
jaguar-warrior.tactics:
## When to use Jaguar Warriors
The Jaguar Warrior is less cost effective against units other than infantry, and the Aztec Champion and Siege Onager compete with it for the same job while being more well rounded. It is usually worth making only against civilizations that lean heavily on infantry. Garland Wars adds +4 attack, which lets the Elite Jaguar Warrior beat Elite Samurai one on one, though the Samurai is cheaper and so still the cost-effective answer.

## Jaguars with Eagle Warriors
Eagle Warriors cover what Jaguars lack: they have bonuses against Monks and siege and are very good against foot archers, while Jaguars handle the infantry that troubles Eagles. The pair is common in Aztec armies, and Monk support helps both. Hand Cannoneers and mounted archers are the biggest threat to this combination, and Onagers are the usual answer when they appear. Monks can convert Cataphracts if those show up.

## What beats Jaguar Warriors
Cataphracts, Hand Cannoneers, Scorpions, Mangonels and War Elephants. Samurai beat them on cost. Obuchs need higher numbers but strip armor with each hit, and Urumi Swordsmen with Wootz Steel ignore melee armor and win most even fights. The Liao Dao is the one unique infantry that reliably beats Jaguar Warriors, thanks to bleed damage and damage reflection from Lamellar Armor. Against those infantry the Aztecs can turn to Arbalesters, since all of them have low pierce armor.

janissary.description:
The Janissary is the unique unit of the Turks, a gunpowder unit trained at the Castle from the Castle Age. It plays like a Hand Cannoneer with longer range and no minimum range. It costs 60 food and 55 gold and has 44 HP, 17 attack, a range of 7 and 1/0 armor, with only 50% accuracy. The Elite Janissary upgrade in the Imperial Age raises this to 50 HP, 22 attack, range 8 and 65% accuracy.

Janissaries are fragile but hit very hard, and they are strong against infantry and buildings. Elite Skirmishers, siege weapons and fast cavalry with bonus damage are their main threats.
janissary.tactics:
## Castle Age pressure
In groups Janissaries fire volleys that kill or badly wound units that come too close. They are strong against infantry, although Hand Cannoneers do more to infantry thanks to their +10 bonus. Their pierce attack is enough to get through the pierce armor of buildings, and in sufficient numbers they can destroy a Town Center given time. They cannot outrange Castles or towers, and aggressive use leaves them open to Elite Skirmishers or Knights catching them out of position. One Mangonel shot that connects does heavy damage. On Arena, a Castle drop into Janissaries is a popular strategy. They counter Castle Age siege easily, and two or three Mangonels in support deal with enemy foot archers, which makes this one of the strongest Castle Age compositions.

## Imperial Age support
Onagers, and Heavy Scorpions with Siege Engineers, threaten them with splash damage, but the Turks can answer with Bombard Cannons, unlocked as soon as they reach the Imperial Age. Archers and mounted archers exploit the low accuracy, low pierce armor and long reload. Turk Light Cavalry, with free upgrades and extra pierce armor, covers that weakness.

## What beats Janissaries
Elite Skirmishers counter them cost-effectively, since Janissaries have low HP and take bonus damage as archers. Mangonels, Scorpions and Bombard Cannons hit them with splash damage or from long range. Huskarls overwhelm them in numbers. Ghulams, Condottieri, Konas and Winged Hussars combine bonus damage with fast movement. Shrivamsha Riders block projectiles with their shields, and the Janissary attacks slowly enough for the shields to recharge.

kamayuk.description:
The Kamayuk is a unique unit of the Inca, an anti-cavalry infantry unit with a very long spear, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Kamayuk in the Imperial Age. It costs 53 food and 30 gold in the Castle Age and 50 food in the Imperial Age, and trains in 10 seconds.

Its spear gives it a range of 1, so Kamayuks can attack from behind one another. It has big bonuses against cavalry, camels and elephants and trades decently with generic infantry in large groups. Archers, siege and specialized infantry are its weak points.
kamayuk.tactics:
## Using Kamayuks
Kamayuks work best in large groups, where the back rows strike over the front rows and engage melee units without walking around each other. The range also lets them hit through walls, which makes them good at defending or attacking walled areas and at stopping rams. They train quickly and the Inca have cheaper Castles, so they are easy to mass.

They are better than Pikemen against infantry thanks to a faster attack and higher base attack, and can handle generic infantry such as Champions. Pair them with Slingers to deal with Jaguar Warriors, Teutonic Knights and similar infantry, and add Champi Warriors to protect them from archers and siege. With +1 pierce armor and +10 HP over Champions, plus Fabric Shields, they hold up against foot archers far better than their description suggests. When gold runs short, mix in cheaper Halberdiers; with gold available, Kamayuks are the better cavalry counter.

## What beats Kamayuks
Hand Cannoneers decimate them and also handle Champi Warriors. Siege Onagers and Heavy Scorpions punish the way Kamayuks clump together. Cataphracts dominate them with resistance to anti-cavalry bonuses, bonus damage against infantry and trample damage. Mounted archers still work despite the Kamayuk's bonus against them, and Mamelukes, Samurai, Teutonic Knights, Jaguar Warriors, Janissaries, Plumed Archers and Rattan Archers also beat them.

karambit-warrior.description:
The Malay unique infantry, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. It costs only 25 food and 15 gold, trains in 6 seconds and takes half a population slot. It has 30 HP (40 as Elite) and 7 attack (8 as Elite) and moves faster than most infantry.

Karambit Warriors are meant to be massed. They are good for raids, emergency defense against siege and swarming light units, and they beat Eagle Warriors, Halberdiers, Elite Skirmishers and Light Cavalry. Their low HP makes them weak against splash damage, gunpowder units, heavy cavalry and heavy infantry.
karambit-warrior.tactics:
## Swarming and raiding
Always use them in a swarm to make up for their low HP. They still cost gold, so mass them with a purpose and with proper micro, and do not trickle them into an enemy army where they get picked off one by one. Their attack and HP are lower than a Shotel Warrior's, while they cost three quarters of the gold of a Militia line unit.

A group can raid an unprotected base, kill Villagers and retreat when troops arrive, as long as there are no defensive buildings, ranged units or heavy cavalry nearby. With Arson, and the +1 bonus against Standard Buildings as Elite, a large group can surround buildings and wear them down. Gold-free Long Swordsmen and cheaper Battle Elephants help with this.

## Other uses
They train fast, so a few can be made on the spot to kill Rams or Trebuchets attacking the base. Against Onagers or Scorpions, send them in staggered or flank formation; Scorpions still punish them. A swarm can also surround light infantry and light cavalry and keep them away from units such as Bombard Cannons. Their bonus against shock infantry makes them deadly to Eagle Warriors, Fire Lancers and Jian Swordsmen, and Monks are ineffective against them. They can also fill rams quickly, which helps a Castle Age ram rush. Their smaller collision size lets them pack tightly and path well.

## What beats Karambit Warriors
Splash damage from Mangonels and Scorpions, since they cluster tightly and have little HP. Gunpowder units, heavy cavalry, elephants and heavy infantry also beat them, as do defensive buildings when they raid.

keshik.description:
The first Tatar unique unit, a medium cavalry unit trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to the Elite Keshik in the Imperial Age for 700 food and 600 gold. It costs 60 food and 40 gold, far less gold than a Knight.

A Keshik generates a slow trickle of gold while it attacks enemy units, though not buildings. It has 120 HP against the Knight's 100 and is slightly faster, but has 1/2 armor and less attack. It is a good raider and very cost-effective, yet it falls quickly to anti-cavalry units and heavier cavalry, and with no Faith or Heresy in the Tatar tree it is very easy to convert.
keshik.tactics:
## Timing
If the player starts with a Castle, Keshiks are a better rush unit than Knights in the early Castle Age, being much cheaper and generating gold. They are not strong enough to justify building a Castle early just for them. The Elite upgrade is expensive but finishes in 40% of the Cavalier upgrade time, so it can turn the game in the early Imperial Age. Late in 1v1 or free for all games, the gold they generate helps keep a gold economy going and delays the trash wars, though the player should still take Relics and add trash units.

## Gold generation
The gold comes from time spent attacking units, not from each hit. Micromanaging attacks can therefore produce less gold, and attack upgrades or the Elite upgrade lower the gold earned per kill because targets die faster.

## In the army
The Keshik keeps up with mounted archers, which makes the two the ideal late game Tatar composition when gold is available. With the Swordsman line almost useless for the Tatars, Keshiks are their answer to Eagle Warriors. Against a Cavalier the fight can go either way, but the Keshik's extra HP and pierce armor make it more durable, especially for raiding. Its lower melee attack than a Paladin's makes it harder to break an army, a job the Tatar Cavalry Archers help with.

## What beats Keshiks
Anti-cavalry units such as Pikemen, Kamayuks, Camel Riders and Mamelukes, and stronger melee units such as Paladins, Teutonic Knights, Samurai, Boyars, Konniks, Leitis and elephants. Keshiks need other units to protect them. Monks are a serious threat, so Tatar players should use their Hussars to kill them.

king.description:
A special civilian unit that appears in campaign scenarios and Regicide games. It can never be trained, though it is available in the Scenario Editor. A King cannot attack or help the economy, cannot be converted and, unlike heroes, does not regenerate.

In Regicide a player whose King dies loses the game at once. The King has 75 HP and no armor, but moves almost as fast as a Knight, has a long line of sight from the start and is ignored by predators. Each architecture set has its own King sprite and icon.
king.tactics:
## Scouting and keeping him safe
The King's speed and vision make him a good early scout around the player's own town. Going deep into enemy territory is risky because of Town Center and Castle fire. Every player in Regicide starts with a Castle, and once the surroundings are scouted the King should be garrisoned inside it. Later in the game he belongs behind Walls in a safe Castle. Khmer Kings can also garrison in Houses (up to 5), and Armenian and Georgian Kings in Fortified Churches (up to 10).

## What beats Kings
Any armed unit, since the King has 75 HP, no armor and no way to fight back. Because killing him ends the game, the enemy King's location should be the focus of a player's attacks.

kipchak.description:
The Cuman unique unit, a mounted archer trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Kipchak in the Imperial Age. It costs 60 wood and 35 gold and has 40 HP and range 4. Each volley has three arrows, four for the Elite. Only the first arrow uses the listed attack and benefits from attack technologies. The others deal 3 pierce damage each.

Because every arrow does at least one damage, a Kipchak deals at least 3 per volley, which helps against high pierce armor units, rams and Monks. It harasses well and is strong against slow melee units. Archers and camel units, the Camel Archer above all, beat it.
kipchak.tactics:
## Using Kipchaks
Play Kipchaks like Cavalry Archers: mass them and harass slow units. They fire slightly slower but have half the attack delay of Cavalry Archers, which makes micro easier. The extra arrows also deal melee damage to Battering Rams and Capped Rams and pierce damage to Monks, so Kipchaks handle both better than most archers. Halberdiers and Kamayuks are dangerous up close, but good hit and run keeps them at bay.

Cumans should prefer Kipchaks to Cavalry Archers in most games, since they cost less gold and do more against pierce armor. Cavalry Archers have more HP and attack 9% faster, so they are better for soaking damage, for example against archers, and Steppe Husbandry speeds up their training, which does not apply to Kipchaks. Without enough Castles, Cavalry Archers are the easier army to build. Light Cavalry, which costs only food, or Steppe Lancers make good partners in front of the Kipchaks.

## Cuman Mercenaries
After a Cuman player researches Cuman Mercenaries, every allied player can train up to 5 free Elite Kipchaks per Castle, in any Age, in 12 seconds each. The technology stacks, so it helps even a team made up only of Cumans.

## What beats Kipchaks
Camel units, especially the Camel Archer, and foot archers, which outshoot the fragile Kipchak with its 0/0 armor. Halberdiers and Kamayuks threaten them up close if the Cuman player does not keep moving.

knight.description:
The Knight is the heavy cavalry unit of the Stable, available from the Castle Age. Native American, Indian and Three Kingdoms civilizations lack it, although Shu, Wei and Wu have the Hei Guang Cavalry in its place. It costs 60 food and 75 gold and has 100 HP, 10 attack, 2/2 armor and a speed of 1.35. It upgrades to the Cavalier for 300 food and 300 gold.

In the Castle Age the Knight is often the main fighting force, unmatched against most infantry, foot archers, light cavalry and siege weapons. Its high gold cost and lack of conversion resistance are its main drawbacks, and Pikemen, Camel Riders and Monks counter it.
knight.tactics:
## Early Castle Age strength
Knights are best in the early Castle Age, when there are few effective counters to them. As the primary shock unit of most armies they are very effective at disrupting enemy villages, destroying colonies and thinning out an enemy garrison. Their high attack, HP and natural armor let them stand up to most opposition. Pairing archers with Knights helps against the three units that counter them best: Camel Riders, Pikemen and Monks.

## Later in the game
Knights lose value as the economy develops and unique units, Pikemen, Camel Riders and siege weapons appear. Crossbowmen in a critical mass can also stand up to them by then. The large gold cost means that over time infantry becomes easier to mass and can outnumber the Knights. Knights and their upgraded forms still play a significant role in the late game.

## What beats Knights
Camel Riders, the only unit that matches the Knight in both attack power and speed, and Mamelukes. A line of Pikemen or Kamayuks is a good defense, provided they can catch the Knights. Monks are a threat because Knights are expensive, strong enough to be prime targets and have no conversion resistance. Heavily armored or hard-hitting melee units such as Boyars, Teutonic Knights, Berserks, War Elephants and Battle Elephants also win, as do Genoese Crossbowmen and overwhelming firepower.

konnik.description:
The Konnik is the Bulgarian unique unit, a cavalry unit that turns into an infantry unit, the Dismounted Konnik, when it is killed. It is trained at the Castle and the Krepost from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Konnik in the Imperial Age, which also upgrades the dismounted form.

It costs 60 food and 70 gold and trains in 16 seconds. The mounted form has 100 HP and 12 attack but a slow attack rate of 2.4. With two lives it is durable, and each form shrugs off the counters to the other, so opponents need two kinds of answer. Neither form is especially strong against archers.
konnik.tactics:
## Using Konniks
The Castle Age unique technology Stirrups makes the mounted form attack 33% faster, bringing it to 1.8 like a Knight. With Stirrups a Konnik matches a Knight, and a fully upgraded Elite Konnik beats a Cavalier without Stirrups. That makes it a strong shock unit for raiding and soaking damage, and since it keeps fighting as infantry after death, it is usually preferred over the Knight line.

The Dismounted Konnik comes back into the fight after 3 seconds. It uses the infantry Blacksmith technologies, Arson and Squires, and has +4 against standard buildings. It is a little weaker than a Long Swordsman apart from its higher attack, and Stirrups does not speed it up.

Konniks are prime targets for conversion. Without Heresy you can delete a mounted Konnik that is being converted, which turns it into the dismounted form and forces the Monk to start over, sometimes long enough for the infantry to reach it.

## What beats Konniks
Units with high all round stats beat both forms without needing bonuses: War Elephants, Battle Elephants, Boyars, Teutonic Knights and veteran Jaguar Warriors. Leitis, Composite Bowmen, Bolas Riders and Liao Dao also handle both. Samurai have a bonus against unique units and attack faster. Genoese Crossbowmen, Mamelukes and Flemish Militia use their anti-cavalry bonus on the rider, then their stats on the infantry. The Dismounted Konnik has no bonus against shock infantry, so Varangian Guards and Temple Guards do well against it. Any mix that covers cavalry and infantry, such as Pikemen, swordsmen and archers, works too.

leitis.description:
The Lithuanian unique heavy cavalry, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. It costs 70 food and 50 gold and has 100 HP (130 as Elite) and 13 attack (16 as Elite). Its attack ignores the armor of every land unit except siege, but not of ships or buildings. Like other Lithuanian cavalry, it gains +1 attack for each Relic in a Monastery, up to +4.

Compared with the Knight line it is faster and cheaper in gold and hits harder, but has less HP and armor. It shreds armored melee units and suffers against archers and the usual anti-cavalry units.
leitis.tactics:
## Leitis or Knight
The Lithuanians have little economy bonus in the Castle Age besides extra food per Town Center, so most of the time Knights are the better pick until the late Castle Age. Once Castles are up, or when the game starts with one as in Regicide, Leiciai beat Knights in a few ways: in the Castle Age they ignore melee armor and have +3 attack over a Knight, and in the Imperial Age their upgrade is cheaper and much quicker. With a strong economy and at least three Castles they can replace the Knight line, as long as the enemy is not making archers. Every armor technology the enemy researches is wasted against them, while Blacksmith attack upgrades make them stronger.

In the late game, Elite Leiciai suit 1v1 games, few archers and match-ups against units with high melee armor. Paladins are better in team games, especially in a pocket position, against large groups of archers and for destroying bases, thanks to their higher HP and pierce armor. As raiders, Elite Leiciai with two Relics kill a Villager in two hits, though they are more vulnerable to defensive structures. Against archer civilizations, pair them with the Lithuanian Skirmishers.

## What beats Leiciai
Halberdiers and Camel Riders counter them cost effectively, although Elite Leiciai with two Relics kill Halberdiers in three hits and can sometimes trade well with Camel Riders. Avoid Battle Elephants and Imperial Camel Riders. Samurai, Kamayuks, Genoese Crossbowmen, Mamelukes, Bolas Riders, War Elephants and Monks also beat them, and Blackwood Archers, Jaguar Warriors, Urumi Swordsmen and Liao Daos give them trouble. Large groups of foot archers, mounted archers and Hand Cannoneers hurt them because of their low HP and pierce armor. Their special attack does nothing against Bombard Cannons, Trebuchets and siege with Ironclad.

light-cavalry.description:
The second step of the Scout Cavalry line, upgraded from Scout Cavalry at the Stable in the Castle Age for 150 food and 50 gold. Every civilization has it except the Aztecs, Inca, Mapuche, Maya, Muisca, Teutons and Tupi. It upgrades further to the Hussar, or to the Winged Hussar for the Lithuanians and Poles.

It costs 80 food and nothing else, is very fast, resists conversion and has the Auto Scout ability. Its line of sight is 8 in the Castle Age and 10 in the Imperial Age. It kills Monks, siege weapons and archers well, but it fights poorly against other melee units.
light-cavalry.tactics:
## Hunting Monks and siege
The upgrade from Scout Cavalry adds 15 HP, 2 attack and 4 attack against Monks, which is a lot for its low cost. Light Cavalry has the speed and attack to run down and kill groups of siege weapons, Elite Skirmishers or Monks, and it is also strong against Villagers and archers. Its solid pierce armor helps it get to those targets. It should avoid fights with melee units. Like the rest of the Scout line, it cannot attack timid huntables such as Deer.

## Raiding on a food budget
In the Castle Age the Knight is generally the better unit because of its much stronger stats. As gold becomes more valuable later in the game, the Light Cavalry turns into a useful raider because it costs only food, and it is a viable choice whenever a player is short on other resources. Its line of sight, which grows by 2 with every age, also makes it a good scout.

## What beats Light Cavalry
Most melee units. Its combat ability against heavy cavalry, camels and infantry is very limited, so any of those wins a straight fight. Genoese Crossbowmen are also strong against it.

long-swordsman.description:
The third tier of the Militia line, upgraded from the Man-at-Arms at the Barracks in the Castle Age for 150 food and 65 gold. Almost every civilization has it. The Jurchens and the South American civilizations, which use the Champi Warrior instead, are the exceptions. It costs 50 food and 20 gold and later upgrades to the Two-Handed Swordsman, or to the Legionary for the Romans.

Long Swordsmen are the basic Castle Age infantry. They beat every standard Castle Age unit one on one except the Knight and the Cavalry Archer, and they have a bonus against buildings and shock infantry. They are slow and weak against archers, heavy cavalry and Mangonels.
long-swordsman.tactics:
## When Long Swordsmen are worth it
The upgrade from Man-at-Arms adds 15 HP, 3 attack and 1 melee armor, so it should come quickly if the line sees any real use. In most games, though, the Long Swordsman is a niche counter to trash units, Camel Riders, Eagle Warriors and other shock infantry. It costs little gold but a lot of food, which is hard to justify given its low speed and durability, and it needs two unit upgrades where Knights need none. Two Long Swordsmen do beat one full health Knight. In general it is usually better to make Pikemen as a counter, mass Crossbowmen, or put the food into a boom or the Imperial Age.

The Goths are a special case. Against them, massing Long Swordsmen is a good move, since they trade well with Huskarls and their later upgrades do progressively better against Elite Huskarls.

## Upgrades and civilization bonuses
Like all basic infantry they get a bonus against standard buildings, and with Arson that makes them useful raiders. Squires and Gambesons complete their upgrades, and many civilizations boost them: Burmese get extra attack, Celts move faster, Japanese attack 33% faster, Vikings get 20% more HP and Teutons extra melee armor. Roman Long Swordsmen get double effect from Scale and Chain Mail Armor and the Centurion's aura.

## What beats Long Swordsmen
Archers of almost every kind, which shoot them before they close the distance. Scorpions and Mangonels punish groups of them. Heavy cavalry such as Cataphracts and Boyars beats them in melee, as do Teutonic Knights and Jaguar Warriors. Monks can also convert them. Long Swordsmen in turn do well against Pikemen, Light Cavalry, Camel Riders, Elite Skirmishers, Eagle Warriors and Rams.

longboat.description:
The Longship, formerly called the Longboat, is a fast warship trained at the Dock from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Longship in the Imperial Age. It is a regional unit for the Danes, Saxons, Varangians and Vikings. It costs 100 wood and 50 gold and has 125 HP, 0/3 armor and range 6.

Each volley fires four arrows at once, and every arrow deals the full 5 pierce damage, so its real damage is much higher than its attack and rate of fire suggest. Large masses of Longships can beat most navies and punish units and buildings near the shore. They stack easily, which leaves them open to splash and pass-through attacks.
longboat.tactics:
## Massing Longships
Longships train faster than most warships and need no Medium Warships upgrade, so the usual plan is to go all in on them once the Castle Age is reached, destroy the enemy navy early and keep the opponent off the water. In large enough numbers they can replace every other warship except the Catapult Galleon. Longship civilizations have no Demolition Raft line, so Longships are also their best answer to units in the shallows. Their speed and tight stacking make micro easy. In small groups they struggle even against Galleys and Hulks.

## Differences between civilizations
Danish Longships are faster, the only ones that outrun the Fire Ship line. Saxon Longships have more HP but lack Clinker Construction and Carvel Hull, so they are the slowest, though they do best against Hulks and Caravels. Varangian Longships reload faster and are the strongest in the Castle Age at equal numbers. Viking Longships are cheaper and easiest to mass, and win at equal resources.

## What beats Longships
Units with splash or pass-through damage exploit the tight stacks: Mangonels, Bombard Cannons, Dromons, Caravels and Turtle Ships. Fast micro can dodge many of these shots and even makes Demolition Ships mostly ineffective, but massed Demolition Ships and Caravels remain dangerous. Fire Ships beat small groups. Turtle Ships and Thirisadai have high pierce armor, and Longships have a hard time against them, though both come late or cost a lot, which favors a fast Castle Longship push. Towers, Castles and ranged siege on the shore also beat them.

longbowman.description:
The Longbowman is the unique unit of the Britons, a foot archer trained at the Castle from the Castle Age. It costs 35 wood and 40 gold and has 35 HP, 6 attack and 70% accuracy. With the Briton range bonus it shoots from 6 tiles in the Castle Age. The Elite Longbowman upgrade in the Imperial Age costs 850 food and 850 gold and adds HP, attack, pierce armor, accuracy and range.

Fully upgraded, an Elite Longbowman reaches a range of 12, more than any other archer, so it outranges Castles, towers, Onagers and Galleons. It keeps the usual archer weaknesses against cavalry, Skirmishers and melee charges.
longbowman.tactics:
## Massed range
Longbowmen and Briton Arbalesters play much the same way. A single Longbowman is no threat, but a group mows down enemies from long range before they can attack. They are valuable for base defense behind walls, and with infantry or cavalry in front they hold their ground against most units. Groups can also hit and run, backing up while killing the closest enemy, though not as well as Cavalry Archers. Britons lack Thumb Ring, so their archers fire slower and miss more often, which also limits overkill when a group focuses one target, and stray arrows can hit nearby enemies.

## Range against buildings and siege
Blacksmith upgrades, Yeomen and the Briton civilization bonus take an Elite Longbowman to 12 range. Against massed Siege Onagers or Heavy Scorpions, that range lets them destroy one siege weapon at a time. With a Saracen ally they get bonus damage against standard buildings and outrange them, and only Teutonic Castles, Korean Keeps and Turkish Bombard Towers can fire back. Trebuchets should still come along for sieges. Since Longbowmen need Castles and Briton Archery Ranges work faster, they are harder to mass and show up mostly in the very late game.

## What beats Longbowmen
Without protection they fall to mass cavalry, Skirmishers, Huskarls, Ghulams and Eagle Warrior charges. Elite Skirmishers, Rattan Archers and Genitours cause trouble even though Longbowmen outrange them. Siege weapons are a heavy threat, though Longbowmen handle them better than other archers. Rams placed in front of an army soak up arrows, and Coustilliers badly wound them with their charge attack.

magyar-huszar.description:
The Magyar Huszar is the Magyar unique unit, a light cavalry unit with an attack bonus against siege weapons. It is trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Magyar Huszar in the Imperial Age. It costs 35 food and 45 gold, and the Corvinian Army technology turns that into 80 food, which makes it a trash unit.

It is fast, cheap and trains quickly, with 80 HP and an attack every 1.8 seconds, a rate only Knights and Cataphracts match among cavalry. It is ideal against siege and for raiding. Its low armor and modest attack mean it rarely wins one on one against melee units, though its low cost keeps it cost effective.
magyar-huszar.tactics:
## Raiding and anti-siege
Magyar Huszars complement Cavalry Archers well. They deal with enemy siege weapons and Elite Skirmishers, the main threats to Cavalry Archers, and leave the rest to the archers. In the Castle Age they raid better than Light Cavalry, killing a Villager with Loom in 4 hits instead of 5. In the Imperial Age the Elite Magyar Huszar needs 3 hits to the Hussar's 4, and by then Corvinian Army has usually removed the gold cost.

The regular Hussar still competes for the raiding role. It has a much bigger line of sight, trains from Stables, which are easier to mass from than Castles, and costs less. It also resists conversion and has a bonus against Monks, which the Magyar Huszar lacks.

## What beats Magyar Huszars
Pikemen deal huge bonus damage to them, though their low speed and lack of range often means they only chase Huszars off. Camel Riders are a real threat, as are Kamayuks, Mamelukes and Genoese Crossbowmen with their anti-cavalry bonuses. Samurai deal bonus damage to unique units. Heavy melee units like Teutonic Knights and Berserks outfight them, since the Huszar's weak attack and armor make one on one melee fights almost impossible to win.

mameluke.description:
The Saracen unique unit, a camel rider that throws its scimitar at a range of 3, dealing melee damage. It is trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. It costs 55 food and 85 gold and has 100 HP with the Saracen bonus, 8 attack (10 as Elite) and +9 against cavalry (+12 as Elite), but that bonus does not apply to camel units.

Its speed, range and strength against cavalry make it one of the hardest units to counter, and a well controlled group can take down almost anything. The high cost offsets that. Foot archers, Camel Riders and Monks beat it.
mameluke.tactics:
## Using Mamelukes
Mamelukes suit most combat situations. Only larger numbers of foot archers and ranged infantry such as Throwing Axemen and Gbetos beat a well controlled group, and they cannot be countered by trash units. Teutonic Knights are the exception: Mamelukes can kite them forever but deal only 1 damage per shot.

Good partners are Camel Riders, Onagers, Bombard Cannons and Hussars, all of which the Saracens get at least fully upgraded. Camel Riders deal with other camels and siege, Onagers with archers, Hussars with siege and Monks, and Bombard Cannons with buildings and siege. Hussars also make a cheap meat shield. Cavalry Archers fill a similar role and fit poorly, except when facing Teutonic Knights. With a Hindustani ally, Mamelukes get +2 attack against Standard Buildings.

## What beats Mamelukes
