Mamelukes are in both the camel and Mameluke armor classes, so Spearmen, Pikemen, Halberdiers and Heavy and Imperial Camel Riders deal extra damage to them. Camel Riders are a strong counter: Mamelukes get no bonus against them, and they are faster. Camel Archers have longer range, take no cavalry bonus and cost less. Genoese Crossbowmen have a bonus against camels, and other foot archers also work. A well placed Siege Onager shot can wreck a group. Shrivamsha Riders handle small groups by dodging, and Bolas Riders slow them down and deal bonus damage to camels. Monks are effective because Mamelukes are expensive and need at least 5 shots (4 as Elite) to kill a Monk with Sanctity.

man-at-arms.description:
An infantry unit upgraded from the Militia at the Barracks in the Feudal Age for 100 food and 40 gold, and the step before the Long Swordsman. Every civilization with the Militia has it, which leaves out the Inca, Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi, who have the Champi Runner instead. It costs 50 food and 20 gold.

It has 45 HP and 6 attack, with +3 against shock infantry and +2 against standard buildings. Men-at-Arms beat most units of the Feudal Age, so they are good at disrupting an opponent's economy. They are slow, weak against archers, and die easily when outnumbered.
man-at-arms.tactics:
## Feudal Age raids
The Man-at-Arms does the same job as the Militia but with 2 more attack, a 50% increase, which makes it better at harassing Villagers and razing buildings. How well that works in practice depends on how developed the enemy is. The upgrade is cheap enough to be almost always worth it, especially against Eagle Scouts or buildings. Men-at-Arms are somewhat effective against Scout Cavalry, but they get mobbed and die quickly when outnumbered.

They work best with support troops. A good raiding party is around a dozen Men-at-Arms, some Skirmishers against enemy Archers, and optionally a few Spearmen if the enemy makes many Scout Cavalry, as the Franks might. Adding some of the player's own Archers gives much better raiding results. Murder Holes is not available in the Feudal Age, so Men-at-Arms can avoid tower fire by zig-zagging to the base of the tower, where it cannot target them.

## Into the Castle Age
Upgrade to Long Swordsman as soon as possible when moving to the Castle Age, because the enemy's larger technology tree gives them many effective counters.

## What beats Men-at-Arms
Archers, because Men-at-Arms are slow and cannot catch them. Scorpions are also strong against them. Scout Cavalry in large enough numbers can mob and kill them.

mangonel.description:
A ranged siege unit trained at the Siege Workshop from the Castle Age for 160 wood and 135 gold. Every civilization has it except the Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans and Koreans, which use the Rocket Cart instead. It upgrades to the Onager in the Imperial Age.

The Mangonel fires a heavy shot with splash damage, plus five extra projectiles, and is strong against archers, slow units in dense groups, siege and buildings. Its range of 7 outranges Town Centers. The shot travels slowly, the Mangonel has a minimum range of 3, and its blast hits friendly units too, so it needs an escort and careful control.
mangonel.tactics:
## Pairing and control
Mangonels almost always need other units with them. Pikemen or Monks protect them from cavalry in early Castle Age pushes, and archers join them on open maps against enemy archers. Ranged units are less likely to be caught in their blast. The attack ground command helps when the player can predict where enemy troops will move. A common plan, especially on Arena, is a fast Castle Age with Mangonels and Monks: the Mangonels kill the Crossbowmen that threaten Monks, and the Monks convert the Knights that threaten Mangonels. It takes intense micro.

Against massed archers a single good shot can turn a battle, so Mangonels act as an equalizer for the player behind in an archer war. In high level archer wars the main answer to a Mangonel is another Mangonel. Siege Engineers adds 1 range and Chemistry adds 1 attack.

## Mangonel or Scorpion
The Mangonel hits much harder per shot, hits more units, deals melee damage that destroys other siege, has more HP and gains more from its two upgrades. The Scorpion costs about half as much, causes no friendly fire, fires nearly twice as fast and has shots that are harder to dodge.

## What beats Mangonels
Fast melee units, especially Eagle Warriors and Magyar Huszars. Eagle Warriors resist conversion, deal bonus damage to siege and cost little food. Light Cavalry and Mangudai also close in quickly. Monks with Sanctity survive a full hit and can convert Mangonels with Redemption. Conquistadors, Janissaries and Arambai have pierce attack high enough to cut through its 6 pierce armor, and well microed archers can split to dodge its shots.

mangudai.description:
The Mongol unique unit, a mounted archer trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Mangudai in the Imperial Age. It costs 55 wood and 65 gold and has 60 HP, 6 attack, range 4 and bonus damage against siege weapons.

Mangudai are effective against slow units such as Monks, Villagers and infantry, and they can pick off archers caught off guard. The siege bonus lets them kill rams from behind fortifications. A low attack delay makes them easier to micro than Cavalry Archers, and they have 20% more HP. Camel units, Elite Skirmishers, Light Cavalry in numbers and heavy cavalry are the main threats.
mangudai.tactics:
## Using Mangudai
The 0.5 second attack delay is the Mangudai's main practical edge, since it lets you stop, fire and move on with little lost time. Their base rate of fire is slightly slower than a Cavalry Archer's, but Thumb Ring helps them more, so after it they attack a little faster. Even with the bonus against siege, do not charge massed Scorpions or Mangonels unless you have enough Mangudai to kill a machine in one volley and can dodge the shots.

## Compositions
Mangudai are usually paired with Hussars, Steppe Lancers and siege weapons, because the Mongol civilization bonuses and the unique technology Drill boost all of them. Parthian Tactics adds armor and bonus damage against Spearmen, and Bloodlines and Husbandry also apply.

## What beats Mangudai
Camel Riders and Mamelukes are a threat, though their low pierce armor means they take heavy damage themselves on the way in. Elite Skirmishers and Light Cavalry in large numbers are dangerous. Heavy cavalry, the Savar above all, and Genitours and Japanese Heavy Cavalry Archers beat an equal value of Mangudai without support. Genoese Crossbowmen, Camel Archers and Rattan Archers also beat them.

militia.description:
The Militia is the first military unit, trained at the Barracks, and the only one available in the Dark Age. Every civilization has it except the Inca, Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi, who get the Champi Scout instead. It costs 50 food and 20 gold and has 40 HP, 4 attack and 0/1 armor. It upgrades to the Man-at-Arms for 100 food and 40 gold.

Militia are weak and die easily, but they give a player early offense. They beat Skirmishers, Scout Cavalry and Spearmen. Against walls, other buildings and upgraded units they are extremely ineffective, and archers beat them.
militia.tactics:
## The Dark Age rush
The Militia's only real use is the Dark Age rush, or drush: a small band trained quickly and sent into the enemy base to harass, disrupt the economy and often prevent early walling. Killing Villagers is not the priority. The player's scout can block fleeing low HP Villagers so the Militia can finish them. Dark Age towns defend poorly, so this works if the opponent is caught off guard. Villagers without Loom die quickly, but Villagers with Loom can win if they strike first, and they can also garrison in the Town Center.

## Follow-ups
A drush either disrupts enemy walling or buys time for the player's own walls. In the first case the player goes up to the Feudal Age quickly and gets the Man-at-Arms upgrade, which kills Villagers, scouts and walls faster. Infantry civilizations such as the Celts, Dravidians, Japanese and Malians do well with a Man-at-Arms rush, and the Bulgarians end up with one anyway because their Militia upgrade is free. Archers usually follow, since Men-at-Arms already counter a scout rush and prevent walling. In the second case the drush is followed by walling and a fast Castle Age for power or unique units, a common plan for the Aztecs, Bulgarians, Goths and Portuguese.

## What beats Militia
Archers, and walls, which Militia barely damage. Upgraded units of any kind also beat them, and Villagers with Loom can fight them off. Massing Militia without a plan wastes resources that are better spent on the economy and the Feudal Age.

missionary.description:
The Missionary is the second Spanish unique unit, a mounted Monk trained at the Monastery from the Castle Age. It converts enemy units and heals friendly ones like a Monk, can pick up Relics, and has no Elite upgrade. It costs 30 food and 100 gold.

It moves at 1.1 against the Monk's 0.7, so it can flee from almost everything except non-elephant cavalry. As a mounted unit it benefits from cavalry technologies other than attack upgrades, and Bloodlines gives it more HP than a Monk. In exchange its conversion range is 7 instead of 9, and it takes bonus damage from anti-cavalry units.
missionary.tactics:
## Using Missionaries
A few Missionaries added to a Knight army can swing a drawn out battle, healing the Knights and converting enemies while keeping up with them. All Monastery technologies apply, along with Inquisition, which adds 1 range and speeds up conversions. With Bloodlines and Sanctity a Missionary reaches 65 HP, enough to survive two direct Mangonel or Onager hits. The Spanish get Chain Barding Armor and Plate Barding Armor without a gold cost.

In the early Castle Age the shorter range is a real drawback, so when they can be kept safe behind other units or buildings, regular Monks do the job better. Once the technologies are in, Missionaries are usually the better pick for their flexibility. Their best targets are slow melee units, especially elephants, and Knights.

## What beats Missionaries
Light Cavalry deal bonus damage to Monks and are fast enough to catch them. The cavalry armor class makes Missionaries much more vulnerable than Monks to the Spearman line and to camel units. Archers, Eagle Warriors, Halberdiers and defensive structures also beat them.

monaspa.description:
The Georgian unique heavy cavalry, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, with an Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age. It costs 60 food and 45 gold, trains in 14 seconds and has 70 HP (80 as Elite), 12 attack (14 as Elite) and 3/2 armor (5/2 as Elite). It gains +1 attack for every seven of its own Monaspas or Knights within 15 tiles, up to +4.

Compared with the Knight it hits harder, moves faster and has more melee armor, but has far less HP. That makes it a damage dealer that works in large groups, while archers and units with big anti-cavalry bonuses beat it.
monaspa.tactics:
## Massing Monaspas
The Monaspa does not count itself for the bonus, so groups of 8, 15, 22 and 29 get +1, +2, +3 and +4 attack. The aura does not chain along a line of units, and Knights near Monaspas get no attack themselves. A converted Monaspa or Knight counts for its new owner. At 14 seconds, a Castle trains Monaspas slightly faster than two Stables train Knights, which helps reach the numbers the ability needs. Opening with Knights and mixing in Monaspas later also works, since Knights count toward the bonus.

Its low gold cost helps in 1v1 games. Like the Leitis it is a glass cannon, and both can reach 22 attack as Elite. The Elite upgrade gives +10 HP, +2 melee armor, +2 attack and +1 line of sight but does not change the ability. The Georgian bonuses help: Monaspas regenerate 8 HP per minute in the Castle Age and 14 in the Imperial Age, take less damage on higher ground, and with Aznauri Cavalry take 20% less population space. Being fast, they can leave a fight and heal somewhere safe.

## What beats Monaspas
Units with large bonuses against cavalry: Pikemen, Camel Riders and especially the ranged Mamelukes and Genoese Crossbowmen. Halberdiers kill them in three hits. Teutonic Knights, Boyars, War Elephants, Leiciai and Dravidian infantry with Wootz Steel also beat them, though Monaspas beat Boyars for equal resources. Archers hurt them because of their low HP, but their pierce armor is decent and a full group of 29 Elite Monaspas kills Arbalesters without Ring Archer Armor in two hits. Monks, Kamayuks, Berserks and Battle Elephants also beat them.

monk.description:
A non-combat unit trained at the Monastery from the Castle Age by every civilization, for 100 gold. Monks convert enemy units from a range of 9, heal friendly units except ships and siege weapons, and carry Relics to the Monastery, where each one produces a steady trickle of gold.

Monks have 30 HP and move slowly, so almost any unit kills them quickly. They never convert on their own and need constant micromanagement, and after a conversion they must recharge for 62 seconds. Converting one Knight or other expensive unit can pay for the Monk even if it dies right afterwards.
monk.tactics:
## Conversion and the Monk rush
In the Castle Age, Monks can back up a rush because they outrange almost every unit. Civilizations with good Monks can do a Monk rush, which works because the defender usually has no anti-conversion technologies yet and gold is plentiful at that stage. It is often combined with Mangonels or Scorpions in a Monk and siege push: the siege handles archers and buildings while the Monks deal with Knights.

## Monastery technologies
Redemption is the most important, since it lets Monks convert Mangonels and Scorpions, and Bombard Cannons on closed maps. Sanctity lets a Monk survive one Mangonel shot. Atonement matters only when the opponent makes Monks, and Fervor is a modest boost. In the Imperial Age, Block Printing lets Monks outrange almost every unit, Onagers included, and Theocracy cuts the micromanagement needed for groups. A civilization without both Redemption and Sanctity should not rely on Monks for conversion. Aztec Monks gain 5 HP for every Monastery technology and reach 100 HP.

## Relics and healing
A Relic in the Monastery gives about as much gold as one gold miner without mining upgrades. A Monk carrying a Relic loses 2 line of sight and cannot heal or convert. One Monk heals a unit at 150 HP per minute, and each extra Monk on the same unit adds only half that. Monks cannot heal while moving, so training them just for healing rarely pays off outside slow games.

## What beats Monks
In the Imperial Age almost every infantry or cavalry unit kills a Monk in three hits, and archers need about five. Siege weapons make short work of Monks that lack Redemption. Light Cavalry, Eagle Warriors and Heroes are also strong against them. In big battles on several fronts it becomes almost impossible to micromanage Monks well.

obuch.description:
The Polish unique infantry unit, trained at the Castle in the Castle Age for 55 food and 20 gold in only 12 seconds. It can be upgraded to Elite Obuch in the Imperial Age. Each of its hits lowers the target's melee and pierce armor by 1, down to 0, until that unit is healed back to full HP. Buildings are not affected.

Obuchs have more HP and armor than the Militia line, which makes them very durable frontline infantry. In exchange they hit for less, see less and move slower than a Two-Handed Swordsman. Archers, ranged siege, Monks and units with bonuses against infantry beat them.
obuch.tactics:
## Breaking armor
Obuchs are good against units with heavy melee armor. They hard counter Serjeants and Bulgarian Two-Handed Swordsmen with Bagains, and against Teutonic Knights and Boyars they lose in equal numbers but win for equal resources. They also strip pierce armor from Huskarls, War Wagons and Elephant Archers, so pairing them with archers works well. Armor bonuses against bonus damage, such as the Cataphract's anti-cavalry armor, stay untouched. A fully upgraded Elite Obuch beats a fully upgraded Champion thanks to its durability and the armor it tears off.

## Army composition
Obuchs hold the front while fragile damage dealers such as Arbalesters, Hand Cannoneers and siege do the killing behind them. Low-attack units gain the most from the armor reduction, Elite Skirmishers and Winged Hussars with Lechitic Legacy in particular. Arbalesters and Siege Rams are a strong combination with them, and the Polish economy and the infantry's low gold cost keep it affordable. Winged Hussars also deal with enemy Monks.

## What beats Obuchs
Archers, ranged siege and mounted archers kite them. Heavy Cavalry Archers, Plumed Archers, Conquistadors and Mamelukes are especially deadly. Cataphracts, Jaguar Warriors and Samurai have bonus damage against them, and Battle Elephants and War Elephants overpower them because the Poles lack Halberdiers. Berserks regenerate between fights, Urumi Swordsmen with Wootz Steel ignore their armor, and Legionaries, Liao Dao, Throwing Axemen and Gbetos are also strong against them. Monks are a problem too: the Poles have no Heresy, Monks have no armor to reduce, and healing a unit to full HP restores its armor.

onager.description:
A ranged siege weapon upgraded from the Mangonel at the Siege Workshop once the Imperial Age is reached, and the step before the Siege Onager. Every civilization has it except the Chinese, Huns, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans and Turks. It costs 160 wood and 135 gold and has 60 HP, 55 attack, range 8 and a minimum range of 3.

Its shots deal splash damage, which makes it devastating against archers, slow units and tight groups, and strong against buildings and most siege. It can attack the ground and cut down trees. The projectile is slow, it cannot fight units that reach it, and its blast also hurts your own units.
onager.tactics:
## The upgrade
The Onager upgrade costs 800 food and 500 gold. It adds +10 attack, +10 attack against buildings, +1 range, +1 pierce armor, +0.25 blast radius and +10 HP, which makes it worthwhile whenever several Mangonels are in use. Onagers can also cut down trees, which on maps with large forests such as Black Forest lets a player open a path and attack from behind the trees. Siege Engineers adds 1 range and 20% damage against buildings.

## Protecting Onagers
Onagers need guarding in most situations. Archers are a common escort because your own melee units get caught in the blast, but archers do not cover the main weakness, which is cavalry. That is why Onagers are often paired with Halberdiers or Monks as well.

## What beats Onagers
Fast melee units that close the distance before the slow projectile lands, Magyar Huszars and Elite Eagle Warriors above all. Once they are inside the minimum range the Onager cannot hit them. Mangudai are fast enough to dodge and have bonus damage against siege. Bombard Cannons outrange and kill them. Monks with Block Printing and Redemption can convert them from a distance.

organ-gun.description:
The Organ Gun is the first unique unit of the Portuguese, a gunpowder siege weapon trained at the Castle from the Castle Age without Chemistry. It costs 80 wood and 56 gold and fires a cone-shaped volley of five bullets with 6 attack each at a range of 7, with a minimum range of 1. It has 50 HP and 2/4 armor. The Elite Organ Gun in the Imperial Age has 70 HP and 6 pierce armor and fires six bullets of 8 attack.

It is meant for masses of foot units with low pierce armor. Buildings, cavalry and siege weapons are its weak spots.
organ-gun.tactics:
## Against massed foot units
Each bullet tends to hit a different unit, and each one is reduced by the target's pierce armor. Organ Guns therefore do very well against units with low pierce armor and lose much of their effect against units with high pierce armor or pierce armor upgrades such as Blacksmith technologies, Gambesons or Fabric Shields. Bonus damage against infantry and Skirmishers helps them get through the moderate armor of those units. Buildings have high pierce armor, so Organ Guns do little to them. Infantry and archers in dense formation are the best targets.

## Protecting them
The minimum range and slow rate of fire leave Organ Guns open to melee and siege attacks, so keep them protected at all times. Firing from behind friendly units and buildings stops enemies from getting inside the minimum range. Halberdiers and Hand Cannoneers pair well with them and guard them against melee attacks.

## What beats Organ Guns
Cavalry and siege weapons. Bombard Cannons and Siege Onagers are especially dangerous, and an Elite Organ Gun barely survives one hit from a regular Onager. Rams are a bad matchup as well: despite the bonus against rams, each bullet deals only one damage, while a ram ordered to attack an Organ Gun does devastating damage. Against Condottieri, Huskarls, Mangudai and Eagle Warriors the fight is closer.

paladin.description:
The Paladin is the top heavy cavalry unit of the Knight line, upgraded from the Cavalier at the Stable in the Imperial Age. Only a few civilizations have it: Burgundians, Byzantines, Celts, Cumans, Franks, Huns, Lithuanians, Magyars, Spanish and Teutons. The Persians have the Savar instead.

It costs 60 food and 75 gold and has 160 HP, 14 attack and 2/3 armor. It is one of the strongest and most durable units in the game, and a large group can wreck an unprepared town or army. The unit and its upgrade are expensive, and it trades badly against Halberdiers, Heavy Camel Riders and Monks.
paladin.tactics:
## Using Paladins
Compared with a generic Cavalier, the Paladin has 40 more HP, 2 more attack with a slightly slower attack, and 1 more pierce armor, which helps a lot against archers. The upgrade costs 1,300 food and 750 gold, so research it only when Paladins will be the backbone of your army. Against ordinary infantry, archers, siege and unguarded towns they dominate, but mistakes with such expensive units are costly.

## Civilization differences
Frankish Paladins have 192 HP from their HP bonus despite lacking Bloodlines, and Chivalry makes their Stables work 40% faster. The Huns train and upgrade them 20% faster through their team bonus. Cuman Paladins are the fastest, Teuton ones get +2 melee armor for long melee fights, and Lithuanian ones gain +1 attack per Relic, up to 4. Burgundians get the upgrade 50% cheaper and earliest. Magyar and Spanish Paladins are generic, while Burgundian, Byzantine and Celtic ones fall below generic.

## What beats Paladins
Halberdiers lose one on one but win by a wide margin in cost efficiency. Heavy Camel Riders beat Paladins in both cost and population efficiency. Monks are a serious threat because each Paladin costs so much gold. Onagers used carefully can deal a lot of damage, though siege is otherwise ineffective. Elite Battle Elephants, War Elephants, Boyars, Teutonic Knights, Berserks, Kamayuks, Mamelukes and Genoese Crossbowmen also beat them.

petard.description:
A suicide siege unit trained at the Castle (and the Krepost) from the Castle Age, available to all civilizations. It costs 65 food and 20 gold, has 50 HP and explodes on contact for 25 damage, with +900 against walls and gates, +500 against all buildings, +100 against Castles and +60 against siege weapons.

Petards are faster than most siege and are used to blow up walls, key buildings and enemy siege. The blast covers a very small area. Ranged units are the main danger, since they kill Petards before they arrive.
petard.tactics:
## Using Petards
They suit quick strikes on key enemy buildings or siege near your own Castles in the Castle Age, and breaching walls: two take down a piece of Stone Wall, or one with Siege Engineers. For general building destruction they are less cost effective than other siege units. In Sudden Death they can take out the starting Town Center quickly, and in Regicide they can destroy the building where the King is garrisoned. Siege Engineers adds 40% damage against buildings.

Line them up in staggered formation, especially against Castles, so each volley of arrows only hits one Petard.

## Petards needed per building
Without Siege Engineers, a Town Center takes 5 Petards (6 if fully upgraded), a Keep or Bombard Tower 5 (6), a Castle 8 (12) and a Wonder 10 (12). Gates take 2, and Fortified Walls and Fortified Gates take 3. With Siege Engineers, the Town Center drops to 4 (5), the Keep and Bombard Tower to 4, the Castle to 6 (9) and the Wonder to 7 (9). The fully upgraded figures assume Masonry, Architecture and Hoardings.

## What beats Petards
Ranged units, which kill them from a distance without taking any damage. Arrow volleys from Castles and towers also pick them off if they come in a tight group.

pikeman.description:
An anti-cavalry infantry unit upgraded from the Spearman at the Barracks in the Castle Age and upgraded again to the Halberdier for 300 food and 600 gold. Every civilization has it except the Gurjaras and Turks, and the Sicilians can also train it at Donjons. It costs 35 food and 25 wood, with no gold, which makes it a trash unit.

It has 55 HP and 4 attack, with +22 against cavalry, +18 against camels and +47 in total against War Elephants. It is an excellent counter to cavalry and one of the cheapest military units in the game, but it is weak against nearly everything else, archers above all.
pikeman.tactics:
## The upgrade from Spearman
The Spearman deals +15 to Knights, +12 to Camel Riders and +30 to War Elephants. The Pikeman raises that to +22, +18 and +47, an increase of more than 45%, and adds 10 HP, so the upgrade is extremely important to get. Pikemen still cannot force fights against enemy cavalry, elephants aside, because cavalry can simply move away. For civilizations that have Camel Riders, camels are the better choice against Knights for that reason.

## Using Pikemen
Pikemen are useful when attacking a player whose army is built on cavalry, and when defending against cavalry raids. They are frail, so they should fight in groups. They are an excellent escort for siege weapons, protecting them from enemy melee cavalry. Outside the cavalry matchup they lack the offensive power to win fights, but they are as cheap as a military unit can be and work well as cannon fodder.

## What beats Pikemen
Archers, which deal with their low HP and zero pierce armor from range, and Scorpions. Other infantry beats them too, since the Pikeman has very little attack outside its bonuses. Cataphracts also defeat Pikemen.

plumed-archer.description:
The Maya unique unit, a fast, well armored foot archer trained at the Castle in the Castle Age. Its base cost of 55 wood and 55 gold drops to 44 each in the Castle Age and 39 each in the Imperial Age through the Maya civilization bonus, which makes it one of the most cost-effective archers. It can be upgraded to Elite Plumed Archer in the Imperial Age.

Compared to standard archers it has much more HP and moves fast enough to keep up with some cavalry, plus a bonus against infantry. It has less range in the Castle Age and less attack in the Imperial Age. Skirmishers, siege and some unique archers beat it.
plumed-archer.tactics:
## Hit-and-run archers
Plumed Archers move at 1.2, against 0.96 for the Archer line, so they can raid and kite the way Cavalry Archers do, and for the Maya they take that role. The bonus against infantry makes them effective against most infantry in the game. Their speed and HP also let them handle cavalry and siege much better than the Archer line. Against Paladins they do less well than Arbalesters because of their lower attack. Eagle Warriors move at a similar speed, so the two units can work together. They benefit from the full set of archer upgrades at the Archery Range, Blacksmith and University, including Thumb Ring and Ballistics.

## Against siege
Like all foot archers they are vulnerable to siege weapons, Onagers in particular, though less than most. An Elite Plumed Archer with 65 HP survives two Onager shots, while a Siege Onager still kills it in one. Their speed also makes siege shots easier to dodge.

## What beats Plumed Archers
Elite Skirmishers and Genitours are cost-effective and cheap to spam against them. Rattan Archers beat them easily despite the Plumed Archer's own pierce armor. Composite Bowmen ignore pierce armor and can threaten them, although the Elite Plumed Archer's lower cost and better range can make up for it. Huskarls, War Wagons and siege weapons also beat them.

ratha.description:
The Bengali unique unit, a chariot trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Ratha in the Imperial Age. It costs 60 wood and 60 gold and has 100 HP. With a button it switches between a bow (5 pierce attack, range 4) and a sword (10 melee attack with 20% splash damage). New Rathas come out in ranged mode.

The Bengalis have neither Knights nor Cavalry Archers, and the Ratha covers both roles. It is one of the tankier units, but in either mode it keeps the archer and cavalry archer armor classes, so Elite Skirmishers, camel units and other anti-archer units beat it. It is also slower than most mounted archers.
ratha.tactics:
## Switching modes
In ranged mode Rathas hit and run slow melee units such as Champions and Halberdiers, though Halberdiers are dangerous if they close the gap. In melee mode they go after siege and Skirmishers, which they cannot shoot well because of the minimum range, and they get +2 against Skirmishers. Pick the mode by the target's armor: ranged against Teutonic Knights, which have heavy melee armor and poor pierce armor, melee against Huskarls, which are the other way round. The melee splash damage lets massed Rathas beat even generic Paladins.

## Upgrades
Rathas take a lot of technologies to reach full strength: Blacksmith attack for both modes, the archer armor line (cavalry barding does not apply), Bloodlines, Husbandry and Paiks, which adds 20% attack speed. The Elite upgrade gives modest gains, +10 HP, better accuracy, +1 pierce armor and more attack in both modes, but costs no gold. Training from Castles also makes them harder to mass. As a cavalry archer the Ratha is cheaper and faster than the Bengali Elephant Archer.

## What beats Rathas
Anti-archer units, because the Ratha keeps the archer armor classes even in melee mode: Elite Skirmishers, and Huskarls, Ghulams, Eagle Warriors and Rattan Archers to a lesser degree. Camel Riders and Camel Archers are a major threat. Genoese Crossbowmen and Monks also beat them. In melee mode Kamayuks and Samurai give them trouble, and in ranged mode Paladins and other heavy cavalry do.

rattan-archer.description:
The Rattan Archer is the first unique unit of the Vietnamese, a foot archer trained at the Castle from the Castle Age. It costs 50 wood and 45 gold and has 42 HP, 6 attack, a range of 4 and 4 pierce armor, close to a Huskarl's. The Elite Rattan Archer upgrade in the Imperial Age, for 800 food and 750 gold, raises that to 48 HP, 7 attack, range 5 and 6 pierce armor.

It is the second fastest foot archer after the Plumed Archer and holds up well against archers and other ranged fire. With no melee armor it is vulnerable to cavalry, fast infantry and Huskarls.
rattan-archer.tactics:
## Ranged duels and raids
The high pierce armor lets Rattan Archers hold off enemy ranged units even without a bonus against them. Elite Skirmishers and Genitours struggle to kill them, though they stay cost-effective. Scorpion bolts and arrows from towers and Town Centers do little to them. Their speed lets them chase retreating archers, pull back from massed Skirmishers and siege, and raid for Villagers. Composite Bowmen ignore their pierce armor, but the Armenians lack Thumb Ring, so the fight still favors the Rattan Archers.

## Mangonels and escorts
With Bodkin Arrow, Rattan Archers deal 2 damage per shot to Mangonels, unlike Castle Age Crossbowmen, and their speed makes Mangonel shots easier to dodge. With good micromanagement they can destroy the usual hard counter to massed archers, despite having 1 less range than a Crossbowman. They work best escorted by Battle Elephants and infantry, which soak damage and fight melee units. The wood cost is high for a foot archer and can cut into buildings, ships and siege.

## What beats Rattan Archers
Cavalry, Huskarls and fast infantry such as Eagle Warriors and Ghulams, which exploit the missing melee armor. Rattan Archers fare better against cavalry than the Archer line, but worse for their total cost, and their long attack delay makes hit and run against fast melee units harder. In the Imperial Age several Onagers make short work of them. Tupi foot archers with Curare, especially Blackwood Archers, overwhelm them with stacking poison damage that bypasses pierce armor.

samurai.description:
The Samurai is the Japanese unique unit, a fast attacking infantry unit trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Samurai in the Imperial Age. It costs 45 food and 30 gold, trains in 9 seconds and has +10 attack against unique units (+12 Elite).

With the Japanese infantry attack speed bonus it strikes every 1.43 seconds, and it charges up +1 attack and gains 25% speed when running at a nearby enemy. That makes it a strong hunter of enemy unique units in the late game. It has less pierce armor than a Champion with Gambesons, so archers, Scorpions and heavy cavalry are its problems.
samurai.tactics:
## Using Samurai
The Samurai looks like the Barracks swordsman of its Age. It has 1 more attack than a Long Swordsman and attacks faster, and the Elite Samurai beats a Champion despite 2 less attack because it attacks so much more often. Its bonus against unique units makes it cost effective even against anti-infantry units such as Cataphracts and Jaguar Warriors, though against Cataphracts it needs to outnumber them. Unique upgrades of common units, unique buildings and Camel Scouts do not take the bonus.

The charge, which adds 25% speed when the target is 2 to 6 tiles away (7 for Elite), helps make up for the low pierce armor. Samurai close the gap on moderate groups of archers and push back siege better than other infantry.

## Army compositions
Pikemen, who also get the Japanese attack speed bonus, cover the Samurai against cavalry. Against archers, add ranged support: Japanese Cavalry Archers with their bonus against archers, Elite Skirmishers or Scorpions.

## What beats Samurai
Like most swordsmen, Samurai struggle against the Knight line, Scorpions and archers, and Paladins, Battle Elephants and Hand Cannoneers also beat them. Chakram Throwers and Slingers are not cost effective targets because of their ranged attacks and bonus against infantry. Legionaries beat them outright: they do not count as unique units, have bonus damage against infantry, cost less and train from any Barracks.

scorpion.description:
A light siege weapon trained at the Siege Workshop from the Castle Age, available to every civilization except the Shu. It costs 75 wood and 75 gold and has 40 HP, 11 pierce attack, a range of 7 and a minimum range of 2. Its bolts pass through and hit every unit in a line, with half damage to everything after the first target. It upgrades to the Heavy Scorpion in the Imperial Age.

It is strong against slow, tightly grouped units such as infantry, foot archers and elephants, and it never hurts friendly units. Fast cavalry, high pierce armor units, Mangonels and Bombard Cannons beat it.
scorpion.tactics:
## Using Scorpions
Scorpions usually need to be massed, except against foot archers, where even one has an advantage. A medium-sized group can wipe out armies of infantry and archers and holds out against cavalry in enough numbers. They are slow, so keep them protected. Pikemen are the usual escort against cavalry, a mix the Celts and Slavs favor since they have bonuses for both. Genoese Crossbowmen also protect them from cavalry and help against other units. Ballistics lets them track moving targets, Chemistry adds attack, and Siege Engineers adds range.

## Compared with the Mangonel
Mangonels hit harder, deal melee damage that is very effective against siege, have more HP, can attack ground and get two upgrades. Scorpions cost about half as much, need little micro since they do not damage friendly units, attack nearly twice as fast and move a little faster. Their bolts keep flying 3 tiles past maximum range, reaching units 10 tiles away (11 with Siege Engineers), and reach targets faster, so hit-and-run archers struggle to dodge them. The Heavy Scorpion upgrade costs 800 food and 750 wood with no gold, much less than the two Onager upgrades together. Scorpions also have one more pierce armor and a shorter minimum range.

## What beats Scorpions
Mangonels, whose melee damage tears through siege. Khmer Scorpions and those of their allies outrange Mangonels and are less vulnerable to them. Bombard Cannons and Longbowmen outrange Scorpions. Fast melee units such as most cavalry, Eagle Warriors, Woad Raiders and Mangudai dodge the bolts or close the gap quickly, and Huskarls, Ghulams and Eagle Warriors shrug off the bolts with high pierce armor.

scout-cavalry.description:
A light cavalry unit trained at the Stable, and the unit most players start the game with. Every civilization has it except the Aztecs, Inca, Mapuche, Maya, Muisca and Tupi, and all of those except the Gurjaras start with one. It costs 80 food and upgrades to Light Cavalry in the Castle Age for 150 food and 50 gold.

In the Dark Age its 3 attack is too weak for fighting, so it scouts. On reaching the Feudal Age it gets +2 attack, +2 line of sight and +0.35 speed and becomes a quick raider against Villagers and archers. It resists conversion and has +6 attack against Monks, but it loses to infantry and other cavalry.
scout-cavalry.tactics:
## Dark Age scouting
In the Dark Age the Scout finds and brings home Sheep and other herdables and locates Berry Bushes, forests, huntables, and gold and stone mines. On water maps it should look for a good place for a Dock. Later it explores the rest of the map to find the enemy base, enemy resources and Relics. The starting Scout begins in Stand Ground stance. Every Scout Cavalry has the Auto Scout ability, and none can attack timid huntables like Deer.

## The Scout rush
In the Feudal Age, Scouts are often used to harass enemy Villagers. The Lithuanians with their extra food, the Magyars with cheaper Scouts and free attack upgrades, and the Mongols with faster hunters and extra vision and HP for the Scout line are especially good at it. Scouts stay useful a little into the Castle Age, but Pikemen and growing numbers of Archers and Crossbowmen make them less and less effective.

## Castle Age and beyond
Stables usually switch to Knights in the Castle Age, which train just as fast and are much stronger. In high level games Scouts still appear in the early Castle Age because they counter Monks, and on Arena and other closed maps the Scout and Eagle Scout lines are the only effective answer to a Monk and siege push. The Light Cavalry upgrade, available to every non-American civilization except the Teutons, is worth getting, and Light Cavalry make better trash units late in the game.

## What beats Scout Cavalry
Infantry and other cavalry. Pikemen and large groups of Archers also kill Scouts easily.

shotel-warrior.description:
The Ethiopian unique unit, a fast infantry unit trained at the Castle in the Castle Age for 50 food and 30 gold. It can be upgraded to Elite Shotel Warrior in the Imperial Age. It trains in 8 seconds, and the Elite version in 4.

Shotel Warriors hit very hard for their cost, with 16 attack (18 for Elite), and move quickly, which makes them strong raiders and a fast emergency defense. They are also very fragile: 45 HP and almost no armor, with the Elite upgrade adding only 5 HP and 1 pierce armor. Archers and any unit with good damage output kill them quickly.
shotel-warrior.tactics:
## Raiding
Raiding is what Shotel Warriors do best. In the Imperial Age they kill a Villager in two hits, and with Arson an uncontested group can destroy a Town Center in seconds. They should stay away from defensive structures. A Shotel Warrior rush is somewhat better than the Ethiopian Knight rush, because Ethiopian Knights lack Bloodlines, Plate Barding Armor and the Paladin upgrade. The unit still costs a fair amount of gold, so its use is situational, and Ethiopians often have better options such as an Archer rush.

## Other uses
In the early Castle Age they can protect an offensive Castle by killing enemy rams. In open battles they are good against siege and Monks, and they cover for the Ethiopian lack of Gambesons and Champions by dealing with Eagle Warriors and Huskarls that threaten archers and siege. Royal Heirs makes them take 3 less damage from mounted units, which can decide a fight against cavalry. Groups of them can also ride inside rams into an enemy town and unload there, if the rams are upgraded and escorted.

## What beats Shotel Warriors
Foot archers, Hand Cannoneers, Janissaries and Scorpions kill them before they reach their target. Paladins, Champions and other heavy infantry beat them in melee, as do Cataphracts and War Elephants. Shotel Warriors in turn do well against Villagers, buildings, Elite Skirmishers, Pikemen, Eagle Warriors, Light Cavalry, Camel Riders, Elephant Archers and Monks.

shrivamsha-rider.description:
One of the three Gurjara unique units, a fast cavalry rider trained at the Stable from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Shrivamsha Rider in the Imperial Age. It costs 70 food and 30 gold and has 55 HP, 8 attack, 0/1 armor and a speed of 1.6, which makes it the second fastest land unit.

A second, regenerating shield bar lets it dodge five projectiles (seven for the Elite) in 20 seconds, whatever their damage. Melee attacks bypass the shield completely. That makes it strong against archers, mounted archers, siege and Villagers. Its plain stats are mediocre for the cost, so Camel Riders, Halberdiers and most melee units beat it.
shrivamsha-rider.tactics:
## Dodging and raiding
Each dodged projectile uses up part of the shield, about 20% for the regular rider and 14% for the Elite. Once the shield runs low, ranged hits go through. A large group of riders still does very well against most ranged units, and the shield also cancels the charge and slow effect of Bolas Riders. It offers no protection against non-projectile ranged attacks such as those of Kamayuks and Steppe Lancers.

The Shrivamsha Rider is a good raider even without Blast Furnace. Towers are little danger, though Town Centers and Castles can overwhelm the shield with many arrows. Its speed lets it escape bad fights, chase down fleeing Cavalry Archers and catch Trade Carts. Bloodlines, Husbandry and the Barding armor line apply, and Kshatriyas cuts the food cost by 25%.

## What beats Shrivamsha Riders
Camel Riders are its worst enemy, and Halberdiers are very cost effective against it. Knights win on cost, and Samurai deal bonus damage to it as a unique unit. With no base melee armor it does poorly against melee units in general, though it can outrun most of them. Chu Ko Nu and Kipchaks fire several projectiles per volley and drain the shield quickly, especially in numbers, and Genoese Crossbowmen and Blackwood Archers with Curare are very deadly once the shield is gone.

siege-elephant.description:
The Siege Elephant is the Imperial Age upgrade of the Armored Elephant at the Siege Workshop. It is a regional unit of the Bengalis, Dravidians, Gurjaras and Hindustanis and takes the place of the Capped Ram. It costs 120 food and 95 gold and has 220 HP, 4 attack with +105 against buildings and +35 against siege weapons, and -2/150 armor. It is an elephant unit and counts as cavalry.

It is great at taking down massed buildings and absorbing pierce damage. Infantry, cavalry, Mangudai, Onagers and Flaming Camels beat it, and it takes bonus damage from anti-cavalry and anti-elephant units.
siege-elephant.tactics:
## Compared to the Capped Ram
The Siege Elephant works much like a Capped Ram and lags a bit behind the Siege Ram. It costs food instead of wood, and food is harder to mass. It cannot carry infantry for extra speed and building damage, but Monks can heal it from 4 tiles away, so no Villager has to come to the front to repair it. That suits the Monk and siege pushes common on Arena. Cavalry armor technologies at the Blacksmith raise its melee armor, so it holds up better against low-attack units. It attacks every 3 seconds instead of every 5, and its blast hits every unit and building nearby at 33% force. It can also garrison in Castles and allied Kreposts.

## Handling them
Siege Elephants attack non-siege units on their own, so without micromanagement they may chase faster units or fight ones they cannot beat. Monks can convert them without Redemption but have to stand next to them, which is risky with the blast damage.

## Civilization differences
Bengali Siege Elephants take 25% less bonus damage, resist conversion, attack faster with Paiks and get the highest building damage through Siege Engineers. Dravidian ones lack Bloodlines, Siege Engineers and Plate Barding Armor but regenerate with Medical Corps and ignore melee armor with Wootz Steel. Gurjara ones deal +40% bonus damage, cost less food with Kshatriyas and train faster.

## What beats Siege Elephants
Infantry, cavalry and Mangudai. Like rams, they are weak to Huszars, Eagle Warriors, Onagers, heavy cavalry and heavy infantry. Halberdiers and Flaming Camels hit them hard as elephants, and Monks can convert them up close.

siege-onager.description:
The Siege Onager is the final upgrade of the Mangonel line, upgraded from the Onager at the Siege Workshop in the Imperial Age. Only some civilizations have it. It costs 160 wood and 135 gold and fires a 75 damage shot with splash damage at a range of 8, and it can attack the ground and cut down trees.

It is arguably the strongest siege weapon for killing units, devastating against dense groups of archers, slow units and other siege. It is slow, has a minimum range of 3, only 70 HP and a slow projectile, costs a lot, and its blast hurts friendly units too.
siege-onager.tactics:
## Using Siege Onagers
Siege Onagers cannot defend themselves against most melee units, so they need a guard. Halberdiers are the usual partner: they buffer melee attackers and hurt cavalry. Bulgarians, Celts, Ethiopians, Slavs and Teutons all have bonuses that help both units. Archers are an option because your own melee units are at risk from the blast, but archers do not cover well against cavalry, the Onager's main weakness.

The upgrade from Onager gives +10 HP, +25 attack, +15 attack against buildings and a larger blast radius that makes shots harder to dodge. It is one of the most expensive upgrades in the game, so in 1v1 weigh whether it is worth it, though a few good shots can turn a game. A Siege Onager kills a Bombard Cannon in one shot and survives two, which narrows that matchup, but the Bombard Cannon's longer range still wins with equal numbers and control. Cutting trees lets Siege Onagers attack through forests on maps like Black Forest.

## What beats Siege Onagers
Fast melee units, especially Magyar Huszars and Elite Eagle Warriors, reach them before they can fire again. Cavalry in general is their main weakness. Mangudai can pick them off from range while dodging shots, and Monks with Block Printing and Redemption can convert them from a distance. Bombard Cannons outrange them.

siege-ram.description:
The final ram upgrade, researched from the Capped Ram at the Siege Workshop in the Imperial Age for 1,000 food. It costs 160 wood and 75 gold and has 270 HP, -1 melee armor, 195 pierce armor and +200 attack against buildings. Up to six infantry, foot archers or Villagers can garrison inside, and each garrisoned infantry unit adds speed and damage against buildings.

It is the best ram at knocking down buildings and soaking up arrows, and it does very well against Trebuchets. Melee units, Mangonels and Villagers beat it.
siege-ram.tactics:
## The upgrade
Compared with the Capped Ram, the Siege Ram has +70 HP, +50 damage against buildings, a larger blast radius, +1 melee armor and +1 ram armor, and it is slightly faster. The upgrade is expensive but costs no gold, which makes it worth getting for a unit this costly. Siege Engineers adds 20% damage against buildings and +1 line of sight. Each garrisoned infantry unit adds 0.05 speed and +10 damage against buildings, and the Siege Ram cannot be converted from a distance.

## Siege Rams with infantry
Siege Rams pair very well with infantry. The rams take the ranged fire and tear down buildings, while the infantry kills the enemy melee units that threaten the rams. Even with -1 melee armor, a Siege Ram has enough HP to survive 15 hits from a Champion.

## What beats Siege Rams
Melee units, since the ram's melee armor is negative, with Magyar Huszars especially effective. Villagers can also attack them. Mangonels deal melee damage that hurts siege. Mangudai, Chu Ko Nu and Kipchaks deal enough damage to break them despite the pierce armor. Scorpions are listed as a counter too.

siege-tower.description:
A siege weapon trained at the Siege Workshop from the Castle Age by every civilization, for 100 wood and 120 gold. It cannot attack at all. Its job is to carry up to 10 infantry, foot archers or Villagers and unload them on the other side of an enemy wall.

With 100 pierce armor it takes almost no damage from arrows, though Bombard Towers and Trebuchets still hurt it, and it moves faster than a ram. Its melee armor is -2, so melee units destroy it quickly. The ability is only useful against a fully walled base, and a second layer of walls behind the first stops it.
siege-tower.tactics:
## Unloading over walls
To drop troops over a wall, order the Siege Tower to attack the wall section. Simply ungarrisoning makes the units appear around the tower instead. Once the tower is assigned to a wall, any units garrisoned into it afterwards are dropped on the far side automatically, as long as there is room. If the space is blocked, the tower unloads as soon as it clears. This lets an army bypass fortifications, avoid alerting the enemy too early and save the time spent breaking down walls. Pathfinding is a real problem: Siege Towers often do not move where the player intends, especially when positioned next to a wall. Escort the tower until it reaches the wall and the troops are out.

## Compared with rams
A Siege Tower absorbs pierce damage about as well as a Capped Ram or Siege Elephant, and it has more garrison space and a higher base speed. It is more expensive than a ram and cannot attack buildings. Like rams, it can only be converted by Monks at melee range.

## What beats Siege Towers
Melee units, which can stop it before it reaches the wall or destroy it quickly thanks to its negative melee armor. Magyar Huszars and Eagle Warriors are especially good at this. Mangudai, Mangonels and Bombard Cannons also beat it, and Bombard Towers and Trebuchets get through its pierce armor.

skirmisher.description:
An anti-archer foot archer trained at the Archery Range from the Feudal Age, available to every civilization. The Mapuche can also train it at the Settlement. It costs 25 food and 35 wood, no gold, and upgrades to the Elite Skirmisher.

Skirmishers have high base pierce armor and bonus damage against archers and Spearmen, which makes them a cheap answer to an archer-based opponent. Their attack is weak and slow and they cannot fire at close range, so they deal almost no damage to infantry and cavalry. Melee units and siege beat them.
skirmisher.tactics:
## When to make Skirmishers
Skirmishers are worth training when the opponent goes heavily into archers. Otherwise they make poor ranged support. Their 3 base pierce armor cuts down the damage they take from arrows, and the bonus damage does the rest. They work best for civilizations whose bonuses favor infantry or heavy cavalry, which can then handle the units Skirmishers cannot. Because they cost no gold they count as trash units, and in the late game, when gold runs out and armies rely on food and wood, they become much more important. Their low cost and quick training also let a player overwhelm an opponent with sheer numbers in some situations.

## Upgrades and bonuses
Skirmishers take the full line of archer upgrades: Fletching, Bodkin Arrow and Bracer for attack and range, the Blacksmith armor upgrades, Thumb Ring and Ballistics. Many civilizations improve them. Byzantine Skirmishers cost 25% less, Korean ones 50% less wood, Vietnamese ones have 20% more HP and Dravidian ones fire 25% faster. Inca can remove the minimum range with Andean Sling, and Aztecs gain attack and range from Atlatl.

## What beats Skirmishers
Melee units of nearly every kind, because Skirmishers barely damage infantry or cavalry and cannot shoot at point blank range. Spearmen take bonus damage from them but can exploit that minimum range, so a few Spearmen beat a few Skirmishers while large groups of Skirmishers win. Siege units also beat them.

slinger.description:
An anti-infantry foot archer trained at the Archery Range from the Castle Age. It is a regional unit for the South American civilizations: the Inca, Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi. It costs 50 food and 25 wood, no gold, has 35 HP, 4 attack and range 5, and has no upgrades.

Slingers deal bonus damage to infantry, Monks and siege. For these civilizations they are the only answer to infantry and Monks, and to shock infantry in particular. Like Skirmishers they have a minimum range, so cavalry and fast infantry can get to them, and their slow projectiles make them vulnerable to archers. Organ Guns deal bonus damage to them.
slinger.tactics:
## Using Slingers
Slingers are weaker against infantry than Hand Cannoneers and weaker against Monks than Light Cavalry, but they are what the South American civilizations have. They counter non-ranged siege such as rams, Armored Elephants and Siege Towers, and Trebuchets, which are inaccurate against units. Against ranged siege the fight depends on micro. As trash units they help late in the game, though the food cost can slow the early Castle Age. Ballistics affects their shots. Champi Warriors make a good partner against shock infantry: the Champis absorb damage while the Slingers deal it.

## Differences between civilizations
Inca Slingers cost 25% less food in the Castle Age and 30% in the Imperial Age, and get Andean Sling, which removes the minimum range and adds attack, and Fabric Shields for +1/+1 armor. They are probably the most well rounded. Mapuche Slingers have extra HP and pass-through damage with Malon, but no Bracer, so Onagers outrange them. Muisca Slingers have extra melee armor and, with Huaracas, +1 range and 50% faster training, which makes them the best against siege, though they lack Ring Archer Armor. Tupi Slingers refund 15% of their cost on death and fire 25% faster with Caciques.

## What beats Slingers
Cavalry, which closes the gap and exploits the minimum range. Archers handled by a skilled player, because the slow projectiles are easy to dodge. Organ Guns, with bonus damage against the skirmisher class. Ranged siege can beat them too, depending on micro.

spearman.description:
The Spearman is an anti-cavalry infantry unit that every civilization can train at the Barracks once the Feudal Age is reached. The Sicilians can also train it at the Donjon and the Mapuche at the Settlement. It costs 35 food and 25 wood and no gold, which makes it a trash unit. It has 45 HP, 3 attack and no armor, with +15 bonus damage against cavalry and elephant units and +12 against camel units. It upgrades to the Pikeman for 160 food and 90 gold.

It is a good early counter to cavalry and weak against nearly everything else. Without upgrades it even loses outright to a Villager with Loom.
spearman.tactics:
## Defending against cavalry
Spearmen are very cheap and easy to mass, so they can overwhelm enemy cavalry with numbers. They are useful for stopping early Scout Cavalry charges, and players mainly train them to defend their base against cavalry raids. Because they cost no gold, they can be added to a defense without taking gold away from other units. Castle Age cavalry such as Knights and Camel Riders is a different matter, and Spearmen struggle against it.

## Not a raiding unit
Their stats are lackluster, and they combine low movement speed with no range. They cannot catch anything that runs from them, so they should not be used for raiding. Keep them near what they protect.

## What beats Spearmen
Archers and other infantry. With no armor and very low base attack, Spearmen lose to most units that are not cavalry. An unupgraded Spearman loses even to a Villager with Loom, which makes it one of only two military units, along with the Skirmisher, that do.

steppe-lancer.description:
The Steppe Lancer is a light cavalry unit with a lance that lets it attack at a range of 1. It is a regional unit trained at the Stable from the Castle Age by the Cumans, Jurchens, Khitans, Mongols and Tatars, and all five can upgrade it to the Elite Steppe Lancer in the Imperial Age.

It costs 70 food and 40 gold, cheaper than a Knight, and has 60 HP, 9 attack and a speed of 1.45. It is fast and good against infantry, Light Cavalry, Villagers and siege, and very good at tearing down walls and buildings in groups. With 0/1 armor it is fragile, and it loses to archers, stronger cavalry, Pikemen and camels.
steppe-lancer.tactics:
## Using Steppe Lancers
Steppe Lancers work either in large groups, where the back rows attack past the front row like Kamayuks, or in small packs for quick raids. Their speed and range let them hit and run like Cavalry Archers. Masses do well at choke points and behind sturdier units such as Knights, attacking over their backs. Since more of them can attack a target at once, they break Palisade Walls and buildings much faster than most units, which makes them good at opening a walled base.

Against melee units, careful control matters. Only the Camel Rider and Light Cavalry lines are fast enough to catch them, and Crossbowmen are too slow to force a fight, so they are hard to answer early in the Castle Age. Against Pikemen they can hit and run, and against clumped units they can do the same.

## Civilization differences
Cumans train them much faster with Steppe Husbandry and mass them easily from cheap Stables. Jurchens get a faster attack and rely on them as their main cavalry before a Castle. Khitan Lancers hit hardest in the Castle Age but lack Bloodlines. Mongol Lancers have the most HP and are a core unit early in the Castle Age. Tatar ones have the most armor but are more of a tactical unit next to Keshiks and mounted archers.

## What beats Steppe Lancers
Knights, camel units and Cavalry Archers are the best answers. Archers in general punish their low pierce armor, and Pikemen hurt them when they cannot keep their distance.

tarkan.description:
The Hun unique cavalry, trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, and at the Stable once Marauders is researched. The Elite upgrade comes in the Imperial Age. A Tarkan costs 60 food and 60 gold and has 100 HP (150 as Elite), 8 attack (11 as Elite), 1/3 armor (1/4 as Elite) and an attack bonus against buildings, with extra against stone defenses and Castles.

It sits between Light Cavalry and Knights in cost and stats and specializes in destroying buildings. High pierce armor makes it good against archers, siege and Light Cavalry, while infantry, heavy cavalry and Camel Riders beat it.
tarkan.tactics:
## Raiding buildings
Use Tarkans for quick raids and hit and run on towns, buildings and forward camps. They knock down defensive buildings with relative ease and can deal with archers sent to stop them. At home they are useful against an opponent who brings siege weapons in numbers. The Huns also have Paladins for melee combat, so Tarkans are best kept on their main job of destroying buildings. Castle Tarkans train in 14 seconds; with Marauders they also come from the Stable, where the Hun team bonus makes them 20% faster to train. Blacksmith attack and armor upgrades, Bloodlines and Husbandry all apply.

## Against archers
The Elite Tarkan has one more pierce armor than the Paladin and only 10 HP less, so it also works against archer civilizations, although it kills archers more slowly than a Paladin does.

## What beats Tarkans
Genoese Crossbowmen tear them apart with their bonus damage against cavalry. Infantry, heavy cavalry, Camel Riders and Mamelukes also beat them in a straight melee fight.

teutonic-knight.description:
The Teuton unique unit, a slow and heavily armored infantry unit trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to the Elite Teutonic Knight in the Imperial Age for 950 food and 500 gold. It costs 85 food and 30 gold and trains in 12 seconds.

It starts with 90 HP, 14 attack and 8 melee armor, and the Elite version has 110 HP, 17 attack and 10 melee armor. That makes it the most powerful infantry unit in the game, able to beat almost any melee unit one on one. Its speed of 0.8 is its biggest weakness: ranged units can hit and run against it, and it cannot force fights.
teutonic-knight.tactics:
## Strengths and limits
Fully upgraded, a Teutonic Knight has 110 HP, 21 attack, 13 melee armor and 6 pierce armor. It beats fully upgraded Paladins more effectively than fully upgraded Halberdiers do, although Halberdiers are much more cost-effective against cavalry. It is slower than nearly every unit that is not a Monk or siege weapon and has no raiding potential, so it is a poor offensive unit to build an army around. It is also one of the most expensive infantry units. Elite Skirmishers do too little damage to be a threat to it.

## Siege support
Siege weapons are the best partner. With Ironclad's extra melee armor they can cover the Teutonic Knights against almost any threat: Scorpions and Mangonels deal with archers, and Bombard Cannons with enemy siege. The cheaper Halberdier competes for the same role. The biggest danger to this combination is enemy siege, especially Bombard Cannons and long range Onagers, which hit the whole army hard and can shell slow Teutonic Knights on their way in.

## Against Monks
Teutonic Knights have built-in conversion resistance on top of the Teuton team bonus, so no conversion can happen before the 11th conversion interval, and one is guaranteed by the 13th. The Teutons lack Light Cavalry and have poor archers, but Heresy is available if needed.

## What beats Teutonic Knights
Ranged units, which can kite it, along with Scorpions and Mangonels. War Elephants and Cataphracts beat it in melee, and Samurai and Jaguar Warriors use their bonuses to win mass battles. Leitis ignore melee armor completely. Obuchs strip armor with every hit and set it up for other units, though a Teutonic Knight beats an Obuch on its own. The Urumi Swordsman's charge attack and the armor ignoring attack from Wootz Steel cause trouble, and Liao Dao bleeding and Lamellar Armor damage reflection make its melee armor nearly worthless.

thirisadai.description:
The Dravidian unique ship, a large warship trained at the Dock in the Imperial Age for 180 wood and 60 gold. It fires five arrows at once, a main arrow and four extra ones that deal 1 damage each, and it has no Elite upgrade.

It costs twice as much as a Galleon but has 250 HP, 11 pierce armor and extra armor against anti-ship attacks, and it beats Galleons fairly easily for equal resources. It is slower than the Galley line, so faster ships can outmaneuver it. Turtle Ships, Longships, massed Fire Ships and Demolition Ships are its main threats.
thirisadai.tactics:
## An Imperial Age power spike
Thirisadai need no unit upgrades, so a Dravidian player can skip the Galleon upgrade and its research time and still field a stronger ship as soon as the Imperial Age arrives, while the opponent's ships wait on upgrades. The saved resources can go into Chemistry, Elite Cannon Galleon, Heavy Demolition Ship and Shipwright. A Thirisadai also uses half the population of Galleons for equal resources, which matters late in the Imperial Age. Because the Dravidians have a full navy tech tree, it remains a strong late-game addition after their other naval bonuses are used up. Not having it in the Castle Age offsets the savings.

## Fighting other ships
Thirisadai beat Galleons and Caravels, since the Caravel's pass-through damage does little against heavily armored ships, and they also do well against Cannon Galleons and units and buildings on the shoreline. Their durability makes fights last longer, which helps a Dravidian player unload massed Demolition Ships into a group of enemy ships. The same tactic also works for the opponent against them.

## What beats Thirisadai
Turtle Ships beat them one on one and for equal resources, and Longships win for equal resources. Fast Fire Ships handle them fairly easily in large numbers. Demolition Ships are cost-effective if they hit several at once, since two direct hits leave a Thirisadai barely afloat. On land, Castles, towers, Onagers and Bombard Cannons outgun them, and Monks can convert them.

throwing-axeman.description:
The Frankish unique unit, an infantry soldier trained at the Castle from the Castle Age and upgraded to Elite Throwing Axeman in the Imperial Age. It costs 55 food and 25 gold and has 60 HP, range 5 and 7 attack. The axes deal melee damage at range, so it can stand behind the front line like an archer while being countered like infantry.

Few units have much more melee armor than pierce armor, which helps its damage. It hits hard for a ranged unit, especially against buildings, and takes more hits than most archers. The short range leaves it open to other ranged units, and heavy cavalry such as Paladins is effective against it.
throwing-axeman.tactics:
## Using Throwing Axemen
Throwing Axemen fill the back-line role the Franks' weak Crossbowmen cannot. They are much cheaper than Hand Cannoneers and perform about as well in combat. Their best job is supporting Frankish Paladins: Camel Riders and Halberdiers, the usual answers to Paladins, both have low melee armor and fall quickly to axes, while the Paladins protect the axemen from what threatens them. They also kill siege weapons easily if they can close the gap without being shot down. The long attack delay makes kiting melee units a poor idea. Blacksmith infantry upgrades, Squires and Arson all apply.

## What beats Throwing Axemen
Archers outrange them and they have no base pierce armor. Scorpions, Mangonels and Slingers punish them in the same way. Heavy melee units with high melee armor or strong infantry bonuses, such as Jaguar Warriors, Boyars, Cataphracts, Samurai, Teutonic Knights and Paladins, shrug off the axes and win in close combat.

trade-cart.description:
The Trade Cart is an economic unit trained at the Market from the Feudal Age by all civilizations. It costs 100 wood and 50 gold, takes 51 seconds to train and has 70 HP and no armor. Its look depends on the civilization.

Trade Carts generate gold by travelling to another player's Market and back to their owner's. The farther apart the two Markets are, the more gold each trip brings, and the amount grows almost with the square of the distance. Mines and Relics run out on most maps, so trade becomes very important in long games, and trade routes are a prime target for attacks.
trade-cart.tactics:
## Setting up a trade route
Trade Carts pick up gold at the other player's Market and drop it at their owner's Market. They can trade with allied, neutral and enemy civilizations, but trading with an enemy is a bad idea unless that enemy has resigned, since the carts are likely to be killed at the enemy Market. The two Markets need to be at least 5 tiles apart to earn one gold per trip, although trade also works in fractions of gold that add up over time. The most a single trip can bring is 517 gold, with both Markets at the very edges of a ludicrous sized map.

## Trade Carts and Trade Cogs
Trade Cogs trade between Docks, move faster at 1.65 against 1.25 and benefit from Careening, Shipwright and Dry Dock. A single Trade Cog earns about as much as a single Trade Cart, but Cogs bump into each other and lose efficiency as more of them share a route. Extra Docks built for warships can also disrupt their routes, while there is no reason to build extra Markets. Land routes can be covered by defensive structures and the player's bases, while water routes are open to enemy warships. When a long enough landmass exists, Trade Carts are almost always the better choice.

## What beats Trade Carts
Any force that reaches the route. With 70 HP and no armor, Trade Carts cannot defend themselves, and because late game gold depends on trade, opponents make trade routes a primary target. Guard the route accordingly.

trade-cog.description:
The Trade Cog is a civilian ship that every civilization can train at the Dock from the Feudal Age. It earns gold by sailing between your Dock and another player's Dock, and the farther apart the Docks are, the more gold each trip brings. The Docks must be at least five tiles apart to earn anything.

It costs 100 wood and 50 gold and has 80 HP, 0/6 armor and a speed of 1.65. Trade matters a lot in late games because gold mines run out on most maps. The Trade Cog has no attack, so trade routes need protection from enemy warships.
trade-cog.tactics:
## Setting up sea trade
Trade Cogs can trade with allied, neutral and enemy players, but trading with an enemy is a bad idea unless they have resigned, since the Cogs will likely be sunk at the enemy Dock. Trade routes are a main target for attacks and need guarding. Careening and Dry Dock add pierce armor, Carvel Hull, Clinker Construction and Caravan add speed, and Shipwright makes them cheaper and faster to train.

## Compared with the Trade Cart
The Trade Cog is faster than a Trade Cart and benefits from Dock technologies. A single Trade Cog earns about as much as a single Trade Cart, but Cogs bump into each other and tend to follow the shoreline, so they lose efficiency quickly as more of them share a route. A Trade Cog always returns to a particular Dock, so extra Docks built for warships can disrupt a route, while there is no reason to build extra Markets. Land routes can also be covered by defensive structures and bases, while open water leaves Cogs exposed. Whether to trade by sea or by land depends on the map and the available routes.

## What beats Trade Cogs
Enemy warships, because sea trade routes are open and hard to defend. Any attack that reaches the route cuts your gold income, and unarmed Cogs cannot fight back.

transport-ship.description:
A ship trained at the Dock from the Dark Age, available to all civilizations, that carries up to 20 land units or herdable animals across water. It costs 125 wood and has 70 HP and 0/2 armor, and it cannot attack.

It is used for overseas raids, scouting, sneak attacks and rescuing units from a lost fight, and on maps with large bodies of water such as Archipelago and Islands it is the only way to move units between islands. If it sinks, every unit on board is lost, so it should be escorted by warships such as Galleys or Fire Ships.
transport-ship.tactics:
## Using Transport Ships
Load the units onto the ship, move it to the target shore and use the Unload button. Transports also make good decoys: put a cheap unit in each of several Transport Ships and let the enemy chase them, which draws the main force away from the real target. Careening and Dry Dock add pierce armor, Carvel Hull and Clinker Construction add speed, and Shipwright makes them cheaper and faster to build. Saracen Transport Ships have double HP and carry 20 more units.

## Conversion
If a loaded Transport Ship is converted, the units inside are not. The new owner has to destroy the ship to kill them, or can keep the ship and hold that population hostage, since the enemy cannot use it while the units are stuck inside. In free for all games, some players sail a converted Transport full of enemy units to a common enemy's base.

## What beats Transport Ships
Enemy warships, since the Transport cannot fight back and has few HP. Monks can convert it. Losing the ship loses everything aboard, which is why it needs an escort.

trebuchet.description:
A long range siege weapon trained at the Castle in the Imperial Age by every civilization except Shu, Wei and Wu, which have the Traction Trebuchet instead. It costs 200 wood and 200 gold and has the longest base range and the highest attack of any unit, with a range of 16 and a minimum range of 4.

Its 200 attack plus +250 against buildings makes it the safest way to destroy Castles. It must unpack to fire and pack to move, which takes about 11 seconds either way. It is slow, inaccurate against units, fires once every 10 seconds and is defenseless against most units that reach it.
trebuchet.tactics:
## Taking down fortifications
The Trebuchet's main role is destroying enemy Castles from a safe distance, a job only the Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon can also do. Siege Engineers raises its range to 17, and Tatar Trebuchets with Timurid Siegecraft reach 19. Its poor mobility makes it worse than the Siege Ram or Bombard Cannon for tearing down the rest of a base. Packing and unpacking can be canceled instantly to move to safety or keep firing, and the Japanese Kataparuto cuts the time to about 2.8 seconds. Trebuchets can also destroy trees, though Onagers do that better.

## Shooting at units
A Trebuchet shot kills almost any unit, Mangonels and packed Trebuchets included, while rams have enough pierce armor to survive one. Low accuracy makes this unreliable. Use Attack Ground, because ordering a direct attack on a unit lets the target flee or dodge. Briton Trebuchets with Warwolf deal area damage and can wreck massed archers. When Trebuchets are used offensively, a standing army must guard them, and Villagers nearby can repair them.

## What beats Trebuchets
Bombard Cannons work best, since their range lets them hit Trebuchets without dealing with the guards. Onagers are viable but limited by their shorter range. Cavalry and fast infantry such as Woad Raiders and Ghulams have the speed and damage to reach them, as long as they watch for defenders, and Mangudai have an attack bonus against them. Infantry and rams are a last resort because they are slow and give the enemy time to pack up or respond with an army. Archers are ineffective because of the Trebuchet's high pierce armor and HP.

turtle-ship.description:
The second Korean unique unit, a heavily armored gunpowder siege ship trained at the Dock from the Castle Age for 152 wood and 130 gold. It can be upgraded to Elite Turtle Ship in the Imperial Age. Each attack cycle fires a cannonball with splash damage and then two volleys of rockets, and the cannon can hurt friendly units.

Unlike the Cannon Galleon it has no minimum range and excels against other warships. It has 260 HP (350 for Elite) and extra armor that cancels the anti-ship bonus damage of most ships and towers. Its weak points are its short range, slow speed and high cost.
turtle-ship.tactics:
## Holding the middle of the fleet
Against Galleons the Turtle Ship deals nearly twice the damage a Galleon does, and five times as much against Fast Fire Ships. The rockets punish enemy micro that would otherwise dodge the cannonballs. Neither attack is affected by Ballistics. Its bonus armor against anti-ship attacks (+8, or +11 for Elite) cancels the bonus damage of War Galleys, Fire Ships and towers without Heated Shot.

A navy of only Turtle Ships is a costly mistake. They work best in the middle of the fleet, soaking damage and dealing heavy damage, with Fast Fire Ships or Carracks in front and Galleons alongside to add range and stop enemy hit-and-run. Shinkichon adds 1 range and 2 rockets, and Siege Engineers adds another point of range.

## What beats Turtle Ships
Massed Fast Fire Ships are the best answer, since they are cheaper and faster and deal comparable damage. The Koreans have no Demolition Ships, so they lack a hard counter to Fire Ships. Galleons can hit and run against the slow Turtle Ship, and Demolition Ships can outmaneuver its large hitbox and hurt groups of them, though they are not a good counter in large numbers. Carracks beat them for equal resources. From the shore, Bombard Cannons, Monks, Castles and towers are all good choices, and Condottieri can fight them in the shallows.

two-handed-swordsman.description:
The fourth tier of the Militia line, upgraded from the Long Swordsman at the Barracks once the Imperial Age is reached, for 200 food and 100 gold. It upgrades further to the Champion. It costs 50 food and 20 gold and has 65 HP, 12 attack, 1/1 armor and bonus damage against shock infantry and buildings.

The upgrade adds +3 attack and is decent for its cost, but the unit is not seen often because the Champion upgrade becomes available right after it. It beats Elite Skirmishers, Halberdiers, Heavy Camel Riders, Elite Eagle Warriors and buildings, and loses to archers, Heavy Scorpions and heavily armored melee units.
two-handed-swordsman.tactics:
## When to stop here
The Two-Handed Swordsman shows up in the early Imperial Age when the Champion upgrade is not needed yet, for example to answer a Halberdier and ram push or an all-in on Eagle Warriors. Against Eagles, Cavaliers with Bloodlines are sometimes preferred.

## Malay and Bulgarians
The Malay and Bulgarians can use it in large numbers. The Malay unique technology Forced Levy swaps the 20 gold cost of the Militia line for 20 more food, so in late game trash wars a swarm of Two-Handed Swordsmen easily beats Halberdiers, Hussars and Elite Skirmishers. The Bulgarians get every Militia line upgrade for free, and Bagains adds +5 melee armor, which helps them in both the early and late Imperial Age.

## What beats Two-Handed Swordsmen
Archers and Heavy Scorpions, since the swordsman is slow and has little pierce armor. Heavily armored or specialised melee units such as Cataphracts, Jaguar Warriors, Boyars and Teutonic Knights win in close combat. Hussars hold up reasonably against them as well.

urumi-swordsman.description:
The Urumi Swordsman is the first unique unit of the Dravidians, an infantry unit trained at the Castle from the Castle Age. It costs 65 food and 20 gold, trains in 9 seconds and has 55 HP, 9 attack and 1/0 armor. Its attack charges up over time, and the first hit on a unit deals +12 damage with a splash in a small radius. The Elite upgrade in the Imperial Age costs 900 food and 450 gold, adds HP and attack and raises the charge to +15, refilling in 20 seconds instead of 24.

It is a glass cannon with high burst damage, low durability and no pierce armor.
urumi-swordsman.tactics:
## Two good uses
Urumi Swordsmen deal much of their damage up front with the charge attack. The first good use is against tightly packed groups of weak units such as archers. Too few Urumis will not reach them, but a successful charge deals hundreds of HP of damage in seconds, which takes at least roughly equal numbers. The second is defense: guarding siege and elephant units, especially Armored Elephants. Attackers run around the Urumis to reach the weaker units, which maximizes the splash, and against Pikemen they defend better than any other unit. Once the charge is spent their strength drops fast, so a few units more or less can decide between a crushing win and a crushing loss.
